items.title: 13.2.2   Duplicate elements
items.text:
Question

Given an integer array that may contain duplicate elements, return all distinct permutations.

Suppose the input is \([1, 1, 2]\). To distinguish the two occurrences of \(1\), denote the second \(1\) by \(\hat{1}\).

As shown in Figure 13-7, half the permutations generated by the previous method are duplicates.

Figure 13-7   Duplicate permutations

How can we remove these duplicates? A straightforward approach is to use a hash set to deduplicate the results. However, this is inelegant: branches that generate duplicate permutations are unnecessary and should be identified and pruned in advance, improving efficiency.

items.title: 1.   Pruning equal elements
items.text:
In Figure 13-8, choosing \(1\) or \(\hat{1}\) in the first round is equivalent: every permutation produced under one choice is duplicated under the other. We should therefore prune \(\hat{1}\).

Similarly, after choosing \(2\) in the first round, choosing either \(1\) or \(\hat{1}\) in the second produces duplicate branches. Prune the second-round choice of \(\hat{1}\) as well.

In essence, within any one round of choices, we want to try only one of the elements with the same value.

Figure 13-8   Pruning duplicate permutations

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
items.text:
Building on the previous solution, create a hash set duplicated in each round to record the values already tried in that round and prune repeated values:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby permutations_ii.py
def backtrack(
    state: list[int], choices: list[int], selected: list[bool], res: list[list[int]]
):
    """Backtracking: permutations II"""
    # Record a solution when the state length equals the number of elements
    if len(state) == len(choices):
        res.append(list(state))
        return
    # Iterate over all choices
    duplicated = set[int]()
    for i, choice in enumerate(choices):
        # Prune: do not reuse an element or choose the same value again at this depth
        if not selected[i] and choice not in duplicated:
            # Try: make a choice and update the state
            duplicated.add(choice)  # Record the chosen value
            selected[i] = True
            state.append(choice)
            # Proceed to the next choice
            backtrack(state, choices, selected, res)
            # Backtrack: undo the choice and restore the previous state
            selected[i] = False
            state.pop()

def permutations_ii(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    """Permutations II"""
    res = []
    backtrack(state=[], choices=nums, selected=[False] * len(nums), res=res)
    return res

    for (int i = 0; i < choices.size(); i++) {

        if (!selected[i] && duplicated.find(choice) == duplicated.end()) {

            selected[i] = true;

            selected[i] = false;
            state.pop_back();

    }
}

If all elements are distinct, \(n\) elements have \(n!\) permutations, where the exclamation mark denotes factorial. Recording each result requires copying a list of length \(n\), taking \(O(n)\) time. The time complexity is therefore \(O(n!n)\).

The maximum recursion depth is \(n\), requiring \(O(n)\) space for stack frames. The array selected uses \(O(n)\) space. At most \(n\) duplicated sets exist at once, using \(O(n^2)\) space. The space complexity is therefore \(O(n^2)\).

items.title: 3.   Comparing the two pruning methods
items.text:
Although both selected and duplicated are used for pruning, they serve different purposes.

  • Pruning repeated selections: There is only one selected array throughout the search. It records which elements are in the current state, preventing the same element from appearing twice in state.
  • Pruning equal elements: Each round of choices (each call to backtrack) has its own duplicated set. It records the values already chosen in that round's for loop, ensuring that equal elements are tried only once in that round.

Figure 13-9 shows the scope of each pruning condition. Each node represents a choice, and the nodes along a path from root to leaf form a permutation.

Figure 13-9   Scope of the two pruning conditions

items.title: 13.3.1   Distinct elements
items.text:
Question

Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive target integer target, find all combinations whose elements sum to target. The array has no duplicate elements, and each element may be chosen multiple times. Return the combinations as a list containing no duplicates.

For example, with input \(\{3, 4, 5\}\) and target \(9\), the solutions are \(\{3, 3, 3\}, \{4, 5\}\). Keep two points in mind.

  • Each input element may be chosen an unlimited number of times.
  • Element order does not matter: \(\{4, 5\}\) and \(\{5, 4\}\) represent the same subset.

items.title: 1.   Starting from the permutations solution
items.text:
As with permutations, we can view generating a subset as a sequence of choices. Update the sum as we make choices, and record the subset when the sum equals target.

Unlike permutations, each element may be chosen an unlimited number of times, so we do not need a Boolean selected list. A small modification to the permutations code gives an initial solution:

def backtrack(
    state: list[int],
    target: int,
    total: int,
    choices: list[int],
    res: list[list[int]],
):
    """Backtracking: subset sum I"""
    # Record a solution when the subset sum equals target
    if total == target:
        res.append(list(state))
        return
    # Iterate over all choices
    for i in range(len(choices)):
        # Prune: skip this choice if the subset sum would exceed target
        if total + choices[i] > target:
            continue
        # Try: make a choice and update the sum total
        state.append(choices[i])
        # Proceed to the next choice
        backtrack(state, target, total + choices[i], choices, res)
        # Backtrack: undo the choice and restore the previous state
        state.pop()

    backtrack(state, target, total, nums, res)

    # Backtrack: undo the choice and restore the previous state
    state.pop
  end
end

For input array \([3, 4, 5]\) and target \(9\), this code returns \([3, 3, 3], [4, 5], [5, 4]\). It finds all subsets summing to \(9\), but includes the duplicate subsets \([4, 5]\) and \([5, 4]\).

The search distinguishes the order of choices, whereas subsets do not. As shown in Figure 13-10, choosing \(4\) then \(5\) and choosing \(5\) then \(4\) follow different branches but produce the same subset.

Figure 13-10   Subset search and pruning when the sum exceeds the target

One straightforward way to remove duplicate subsets is to deduplicate the result list. However, this is inefficient for two reasons.

  • With many array elements, especially when target is large, the search generates many duplicate subsets.
  • Comparing subsets (arrays) is expensive: we must sort them first, then compare their elements one by one.

items.title: 2.   Pruning duplicate subsets
items.text:
Instead, we can eliminate duplicates by pruning during the search. As shown in Figure 13-11, duplicates arise when array elements are chosen in different orders, as in the following example.

  1. Choosing \(3\) and then \(4\) in the first two rounds generates all subsets beginning with these choices, denoted by \([3, 4, \dots]\).
  2. Later, after choosing \(4\) first, we should skip \(3\) in the second round, because subsets \([4, 3, \dots]\) duplicate those generated in step 1..

At each level of the search, choices are tried from left to right, so branches farther to the right have more choices pruned.

  1. Choosing \(3\) and then \(5\) generates subsets \([3, 5, \dots]\).
  2. Choosing \(4\) and then \(5\) generates subsets \([4, 5, \dots]\).
  3. If \(5\) is chosen first, skip both \(3\) and \(4\) in the second round, because \([5, 3, \dots]\) and \([5, 4, \dots]\) duplicate the subsets described in steps 1. and 2..

Figure 13-11   Duplicate subsets caused by different choice orders

In general, for input \([x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n]\), a sequence of choices \([x_{i_1}, x_{i_2}, \dots, x_{i_m}]\) must satisfy \(i_1 \leq i_2 \leq \dots \leq i_m\). Any sequence violating this condition creates a duplicate and should be pruned.

items.title: 3.   Code implementation
items.text:
To implement this pruning, introduce start to specify where iteration begins. After choosing \(x_{i}\), begin the next round at index \(i\). This enforces \(i_1 \leq i_2 \leq \dots \leq i_m\) and ensures that each subset is unique.

We also make two further improvements.

  • Sort nums before starting the search. While iterating over choices, stop the loop as soon as the subset sum exceeds target, because all later elements are larger and would also exceed it.
  • Remove the sum variable total and track the sum by subtracting from target. Record a solution when target reaches \(0\).
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby subset_sum_i.py
def backtrack(
    state: list[int], target: int, choices: list[int], start: int, res: list[list[int]]
):
    """Backtracking: subset sum I"""
    # Record a solution when the remaining target is zero
    if target == 0:
        res.append(list(state))
        return
    # Iterate over all choices
    # Pruning 2: iterate from start to avoid generating duplicate subsets
    for i in range(start, len(choices)):
        # Pruning 1: exit the loop if this choice exceeds the remaining target
        # The array is sorted, so later elements are at least as large and also exceed the remaining target
        if target - choices[i] < 0:
            break
        # Try: make a choice and update target and start
        state.append(choices[i])
        # Proceed to the next choice
        backtrack(state, target - choices[i], choices, i, res)
        # Backtrack: undo the choice and restore the previous state
        state.pop()

    state = []  # State (subset)
    nums.sort()  # Sort nums
    start = 0  # Starting index for iteration
    res = []  # Result list (list of subsets)
    backtrack(state, target, nums, start, res)
    return res

func backtrackSubsetSumI(start, target int, state, choices *[]int, res *[][]int) {
    // Record a solution when the subset reaches the original target sum (remaining target is zero)
    if target == 0 {
        newState := append([]int{}, *state...)
        *res = append(*res, newState)
        return
    }
    // Iterate over all choices
    // Pruning 2: iterate from start to avoid generating duplicate subsets
    for i := start; i < len(*choices); i++ {
        // Pruning 1: exit the loop if this choice exceeds the remaining target
        // The array is sorted, so later elements are at least as large and also exceed the remaining target
        if target-(*choices)[i] < 0 {
            break

        // Try: make a choice and update target and start
        *state = append(*state, (*choices)[i])
        // Proceed to the next choice
        backtrackSubsetSumI(i, target-(*choices)[i], state, choices, res)
        // Backtrack: undo the choice and restore the previous state
        *state = (*state)[:len(*state)-1]
    }

items.title: 13.3.2   Duplicate elements
items.text:
Question

Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive target integer target, find all combinations whose elements sum to target. The array may contain duplicate elements, and each element may be chosen only once. Return the combinations as a list containing no duplicates.

Unlike the previous problem, the input may contain duplicate elements, which introduces a new issue. For array \([4, \hat{4}, 5]\) and target \(9\), for example, the existing code produces \([4, 5], [\hat{4}, 5]\): duplicate subsets.

These duplicates occur because equal elements are tried more than once in a single round. In Figure 13-13, the first round has three choices, two of which are \(4\). They generate duplicate branches and therefore duplicate subsets. The two occurrences of \(4\) in the second round cause the same problem.

Figure 13-13   Duplicate subsets caused by equal elements

items.title: 1.   Pruning equal elements
items.text:
To solve this, try each value only once in each round. The implementation uses the fact that equal elements are adjacent in a sorted array. Within a round, if an element equals the preceding element, that value has already been tried, so skip the current element.

In addition, each array element may be chosen only once. Fortunately, start can enforce this constraint too: after choosing \(x_{i}\), begin the next round at index \(i + 1\). This both eliminates duplicate subsets and prevents reusing an element.

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Backtracking is fundamentally exhaustive search. It traverses the solution space depth first to find solutions meeting the requirements, records them when found, and continues until all solutions are found or traversal is complete.
  • Backtracking alternates between trying a choice and undoing it. It explores choices through depth-first search; when a constraint is violated, it undoes the last choice, restores the previous state, and tries another choice. Trying and undoing are opposite operations.
  • Backtracking problems usually have multiple constraints that enable pruning. Pruning stops unnecessary branches early and can greatly improve search efficiency.
  • Backtracking is mainly used for search and constraint satisfaction problems. It can also solve combinatorial optimization problems, though more efficient or more effective approaches often exist.
  • The permutations problem asks for every possible ordering of a collection's elements. An array tracks whether each element has been selected, pruning branches that select the same element again and ensuring each is used only once.
  • If the input contains equal elements, permutation generation produces duplicate results. We must try each value only once per round, usually by using a hash set.
  • The subset sum problem asks for all subsets of a collection whose sum equals a target. Subsets disregard order, but the search generates all orderings, producing duplicates. Sorting the data before backtracking and using a variable to mark each round's starting index allows us to prune duplicate-generating branches.
  • Equal elements also produce duplicate subsets. Because the array is sorted, we can prune by comparing adjacent elements, ensuring that each value is tried only once per round.
  • The \(n\)-queens problem asks for arrangements of \(n\) queens on an \(n \times n\) chessboard such that no two queens can attack each other. It imposes row, column, and both diagonal constraints. Placing queens row by row ensures exactly one queen per row.
  • Column and diagonal constraints are handled similarly. An array records whether each column contains a queen, indicating whether a chosen square is valid. Two more arrays track queens on diagonals in each direction. The main challenge is identifying the relationship between row and column indices for squares on the same diagonal.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: How are backtracking and recursion related?

Broadly speaking, backtracking is an algorithmic strategy, while recursion is a tool.

  • Backtracking is usually implemented recursively. It is one application of recursion, specifically to search problems.
  • Recursion expresses the idea of decomposing a problem into subproblems. It is commonly used in divide and conquer, backtracking, and dynamic programming (memoized recursion).

def sum_iter(n: int) -> int:
    """Sum using iteration"""
    res = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        res += i
    return res

def sum_recur(n: int) -> int:
    """Sum using recursion"""
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    return n + sum_recur(n - 1)

  1. When the iterative function runs with n = 4, what is the value of the accumulator res at the end of each iteration?
  2. When the recursive function runs with n = 4, what values does the parameter n take, in order? How is the result computed as the calls return, starting from the deepest call?
  3. What are the time and space complexities of each approach? Explain using the execution steps from questions 1 and 2.
Reference answer

  1. The loop variable i takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 in order. At the end of each iteration, res becomes 1, 3, 6, 10, respectively, so the iterative function returns 10.

  2. The parameter n follows the sequence 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. The deepest call returns 1. The remaining calls then compute 2 + 1 = 3, 3 + 3 = 6, and 4 + 6 = 10, in order. At the deepest point, all four function calls are still active.

  3. Both functions perform a number of iterations or calls proportional to \(n\), so both have time complexity \(O(n)\). Their space complexities differ: the iterative version uses only a constant number of variables, giving \(O(1)\). In the recursive version, earlier calls must wait for their results until the base case is reached. The call stack therefore holds up to \(n\) calls at once, giving space complexity \(O(n)\).

    When analyzing space complexity, consider the space used by recursive calls as well as the variables in the code.

items.title: 3.   Which reversal method uses less space?
items.text:
There are two ways to reverse all the elements in an array nums:

  1. Create an array res of the same length, copy the elements into it in reverse order, and return it.

  2. Move two indices, i and j, inward from the beginning and end, swapping nums[i] with nums[j] in pairs.

    What is the space complexity of each approach? Which operation is in-place?

Reference answer

  1. An auxiliary array as long as the input is needed, giving space complexity \(O(n)\).

  2. Only two index variables are used, giving space complexity \(O(1)\). This is an in-place operation.

    Keep in mind that in-place reversal modifies the input array. Prefer it only when modifying the input is allowed. If the original array must be preserved, the copying cost of approach 1 is unavoidable.

items.title: 1.   Fibonacci number
items.text:
The Fibonacci sequence satisfies \(F(0)=0\), \(F(1)=1\), and, for \(n\ge2\), \(F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2)\).

Given a nonnegative integer n, use a loop to compute and return \(F(n)\) without recursion.

Hints
  1. Handle n equal to 0 or 1 separately first.
  2. Computing the next term requires only the previous two terms; there is no need to store the entire sequence.
  3. When updating the two variables, take care not to overwrite an old value before you have finished using it.

items.title: 2.2   Iteration and recursion
items.text: Algorithms often repeat tasks, and repetition is closely tied to complexity analysis. Before introducing time and space complexity, let's examine two basic ways to repeat work in a program: iteration and recursion.

items.title: 2.2.1   Iteration
items.text: Iteration is a control structure for repeating a task. A program repeatedly executes a block of code while a condition holds, stopping when it no longer does.

items.title: 1.   For loops
items.text:
A for loop is one of the most common forms of iteration, especially when the number of iterations is known in advance.

    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        res += i
    return res

items.title: 2.   While loops
items.text:
Like for, a while loop implements iteration. Before each iteration, it checks a condition: if true, execution continues; otherwise, the loop ends.

    res = 0
    i = 1  # Initialize the loop control variable
    # Sum 1, 2, ..., n-1, n in a loop
    while i <= n:
        res += i
        i += 1  # Update the loop control variable
    return res

items.title: 2.2.2   Recursion
items.text:
Recursion is an algorithmic strategy in which a function calls itself to solve a problem. It has two main phases.

  1. Descent: The function calls itself more deeply, usually with smaller or simpler arguments, until a base case is reached.
  2. Return: Once the base case is reached, calls return from the deepest level upward, combining results along the way.

In implementation, recursive code has three main elements.

  1. Base case: Determines when descent stops and returning begins.
  2. Recursive call: The function calls itself, usually with smaller or simpler arguments.
  3. Returned result: The current level returns its result to the previous level.

In the following code, calling recur(n) computes \(1 + 2 + \dots + n\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby recursion.py
def recur(n: int) -> int:
    """Recursion"""
    # Base case
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    # Recurse: make a recursive call
    res = recur(n - 1)
    # Unwind: return the result
    return n + res

}

Figure 2-3 illustrates the recursive process.

Figure 2-3   Recursive process of the summation function

Iteration and recursion can produce the same answer, but represent two different ways of thinking about and solving a problem.

  • Iteration works bottom up, starting with basic steps and repeatedly performing or accumulating them until the task is complete.
  • Recursion works top down, dividing the original problem into smaller subproblems of the same form, then repeating the division until reaching base cases with known solutions.

For the summation example, let \(f(n) = 1 + 2 + \dots + n\).

  • Iteration: Loop from \(1\) to \(n\), accumulating the sum at each step to obtain \(f(n)\).
  • Recursion: Decompose the problem as \(f(n) = n + f(n-1)\) and keep doing so recursively until the base case \(f(1) = 1\).

items.title: 1.   The call stack
items.text:
Each time a recursive function calls itself, the system allocates memory for the new call's local variables, return address, and other information. This has two consequences.

  • The call's context is stored in a stack frame until it returns. Recursion therefore usually uses more memory than iteration.
  • Each recursive call adds overhead. Recursion is therefore usually slower than a loop.

As shown in Figure 2-4, before the base case is reached, \(n\) recursive calls remain active at once: the recursion depth is \(n\).

Figure 2-4   Depth of recursive calls

Programming languages usually limit recursion depth, and excessively deep recursion may cause a stack overflow.

items.title: 2.   Tail recursion
items.text:
Interestingly, if the recursive call is the last operation before a function returns, a compiler or interpreter can optimize it to use as little space as iteration. This is called tail recursion.

  • Ordinary recursion: After a call returns, its caller must continue executing code, so the caller's context must be preserved.
  • Tail recursion: Nothing remains to be done after the recursive call returns, so the caller's context need not be retained.

For \(1 + 2 + \dots + n\), passing the accumulated result res as a parameter gives a tail-recursive solution:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby recursion.py
def tail_recur(n, res):
    """Tail recursion"""
    # Base case
    if n == 0:
        return res
    # Tail-recursive call
    return tail_recur(n - 1, res + n)

}

Figure 2-5 illustrates tail recursion. Ordinary and tail recursion perform their additions at different points.

items.title: 3.   Recursion trees
items.text:
For divide-and-conquer problems, recursion often provides a more intuitive approach and more readable code than iteration. Consider the Fibonacci sequence.

Question

Given the Fibonacci sequence \(0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots\), find its \(n\)-th number.

Let \(f(n)\) be its \(n\)-th number. Two facts follow.

  • The first two numbers are \(f(1) = 0\) and \(f(2) = 1\).
  • Every later number is the sum of the two preceding numbers: \(f(n) = f(n - 1) + f(n - 2)\).

Use the recurrence for recursive calls and the first two numbers as base cases. Calling fib(n) then returns the \(n\)-th Fibonacci number:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby recursion.py
def fib(n: int) -> int:
    """Fibonacci sequence: recursion"""
    # Base cases: f(1) = 0, f(2) = 1
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return n - 1
    # Recursive calls: f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2)
    res = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    # Return the result f(n)
    return res

    // Return the result f(n)
    return res;
}

  • In algorithms, searching, sorting, backtracking, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and many other techniques use this idea directly or indirectly.
  • In data structures, recursion naturally handles linked lists, trees, and graphs because divide-and-conquer reasoning suits them well.

items.title: 2.2.3   Comparing iteration and recursion
items.text:
Table 2-1 summarizes their differences in implementation, performance, and suitability.

Table 2-1   Comparing iteration and recursion

Iteration Recursion Implementation Loops A function calls itself Time efficiency Usually high, with no function-call overhead Each call adds overhead Memory use Usually a fixed amount of memory Accumulated calls may require many stack frames Suitable problems Simple repetitive tasks, with straightforward, readable code Subproblem decomposition, including trees, graphs, divide and conquer, and backtracking; concise, clear structure

Tip

If the following discussion feels difficult, return to it after reading the section on stacks.

How are iteration and recursion connected? In the summation example, additions occur during the return phase. The first function called is the last to finish its addition, matching a stack's last-in, first-out behavior.

The terms call stack and stack frame already suggest this close relationship.

  1. Descent: A function call adds a new stack frame to the call stack, holding local variables, parameters, the return address, and other data.
  2. Return: When the function finishes, its frame is removed, restoring the caller's execution context.

Thus, an explicit stack can simulate the call stack, converting recursion into iteration:

        # Simulate recursive calls by pushing onto the stack
        stack.append(i)
    # Simulate unwinding and accumulating the result
    while stack:
        # Simulate unwinding by popping from the stack
        res += stack.pop()

    return res

The resulting iterative code is more complicated. Although iteration and recursion can often be converted into each other, doing so is not always worthwhile.

  • The converted code may be harder to understand and less readable.
  • Simulating the call stack can be very difficult for complex problems.

The choice between iteration and recursion depends on the problem. In practice, weigh their strengths and weaknesses and choose the approach that fits the situation.

items.title: 2.1   Evaluating algorithm efficiency
items.text:
Algorithm design pursues two goals in sequence.

  1. Find a solution: The algorithm must reliably produce correct results across the specified input range.
  2. Find the best solution: When several approaches exist, we want the most efficient algorithm possible.

Once correctness is established, efficiency becomes a primary measure of an algorithm's quality. It has two dimensions.

  • Time efficiency: How long the algorithm takes to run.
  • Space efficiency: How much memory it uses.

Our goal is to design data structures and algorithms that are both fast and economical with memory. Evaluating efficiency effectively lets us compare algorithms and guide their design and optimization.

There are two main evaluation methods: practical testing and theoretical estimation.

items.title: 2.1.1   Practical testing
items.text:
Suppose algorithms A and B solve the same problem. The most direct comparison is to run both on a computer and measure runtime and memory use. This reflects actual behavior, but has substantial limitations.

First, it is difficult to remove the influence of the test environment. Hardware affects performance: a highly parallel algorithm benefits from a multicore CPU, while a memory-intensive algorithm benefits from faster RAM. Results may differ across machines, so a fair average would require testing on many kinds of hardware, which is impractical.

Second, comprehensive testing consumes substantial resources. Efficiency changes with input size. Algorithm A may be faster than B for small inputs, while the reverse holds for large inputs. A convincing conclusion requires testing many input sizes, consuming considerable computing resources.

items.title: 2.1.2   Theoretical estimation
items.text:
Given these limitations, we can estimate efficiency through calculation alone. This is called asymptotic complexity analysis, or simply complexity analysis.

Complexity analysis relates an algorithm's time and space requirements to its input size. It describes how runtime and memory use grow as the input gets larger. We can unpack this definition into three points.

  • Time and space resources correspond to time complexity and space complexity.
  • Growth in input size means complexity relates efficiency to the amount of input data.
  • Growth trends mean we study how quickly time or space increases, rather than its exact value.

Complexity analysis overcomes limitations of practical testing in several ways.

  • It does not require running code, saving energy and computing resources.
  • It is independent of the test environment, so its conclusions apply across platforms.
  • It reveals efficiency at different input sizes, especially for large inputs.

Tip

If complexity still feels unclear, do not worry. The following sections will explain it in detail.

Complexity analysis gives us a yardstick for evaluating the time and space an algorithm needs and comparing different algorithms.

As a mathematical concept, complexity can be abstract and challenging for beginners. This makes it a difficult topic to introduce first. Yet discussing a data structure or algorithm's properties inevitably involves runtime and memory use.

Before studying data structures and algorithms in depth, build an initial understanding of complexity analysis so that you can analyze simple algorithms.

items.title: 2.4   Space complexity
items.text: Space complexity measures how an algorithm's memory use grows as the input gets larger. It is much like time complexity, with memory usage replacing runtime.

items.title: 2.4.1   Space used by an algorithm
items.text:
The memory an algorithm uses during execution falls into these main categories.

  • Input space: Stores the input data.
  • Temporary space: Stores variables, objects, function contexts, and other working data.
  • Output space: Stores the output data.

Space complexity generally counts temporary space plus output space.

Temporary space can be divided further into three parts.

  • Temporary data: Constants, variables, objects, and other data used during execution.
  • Stack frames: Context data for function calls. Each call creates a frame at the top of the stack, which is released when the function returns.
  • Instruction space: Compiled program instructions, usually ignored in the analysis.

We usually count temporary data, stack frames, and output data when analyzing space complexity, as shown in Figure 2-15.

items.title: 2.4.2   Deriving space complexity
items.text:
The approach is much like time complexity analysis, except that we count memory used rather than operations performed.

Unlike time complexity, we usually focus only on worst-case space complexity. Memory is a hard requirement: enough must be available for every valid input.

In the following code, "worst case" has two meanings.

  1. The worst input: When \(n < 10\), space complexity is \(O(1)\). When \(n > 10\), initializing nums requires \(O(n)\) space, so worst-case space complexity is \(O(n)\).
  2. Peak memory during execution: Before the final line, the program uses \(O(1)\) space. Initializing nums raises usage to \(O(n)\), so worst-case space complexity is \(O(n)\).

def function

    0

### The loop uses O(1) space ###

end

### The recursion uses O(n) space ###

    return if n == 1
    recur(n - 1)
end

Both loop() and recur() take \(O(n)\) time, but their space complexities differ.

  • loop() calls function() \(n\) times. Each call returns and releases its stack frame before the next iteration, so space complexity remains \(O(1)\).
  • During recur(), \(n\) calls can remain active at once, using \(O(n)\) space for stack frames.

items.title: 2.4.3   Common complexity classes
items.text:
For input size \(n\), Figure 2-16 shows common space complexities in increasing order of growth.

\[ \begin{aligned} & O(1) < O(\log n) < O(n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) \newline & \text{Constant} < \text{Logarithmic} < \text{Linear} < \text{Quadratic} < \text{Exponential} \end{aligned} \]

Figure 2-16   Common space complexity classes

items.title: 1.   Constant space \(O(1)\)
items.text:

items.title: 2.   Linear space \(O(n)\)
items.text:
Linear space commonly occurs in arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues whose element counts are proportional to \(n\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby space_complexity.py
def linear(n: int):
    """Linear complexity"""
    # A list of length n occupies O(n) space
    nums = [0] * n
    # A hash table with n entries occupies O(n) space
    hmap = dict[int, str]()
    for i in range(n):
        hmap[i] = str(i)

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        nodes.push_back(ListNode(i));
    }
    // A hash table with n entries occupies O(n) space

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

}

    int val;
    UT_hash_handle hh; // Implemented using uthash.h
} HashTable;

void linear(int n) {
    // An array of length n uses O(n) space
    int *nums = malloc(sizeof(int) * n);
    free(nums);

    // A list of length n occupies O(n) space
    ListNode **nodes = malloc(sizeof(ListNode *) * n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        nodes[i] = newListNode(i);
    }
    // Free memory
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        free(nodes[i]);
    }
    free(nodes);

    // A hash table with n entries occupies O(n) space
    HashTable *h = NULL;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        HashTable *tmp = malloc(sizeof(HashTable));
        tmp->key = i;
        tmp->val = i;
        HASH_ADD_INT(h, key, tmp);
    }

    // Free memory
    HashTable *curr, *tmp;
    HASH_ITER(hh, h, curr, tmp) {
        HASH_DEL(h, curr);
        free(curr);
    }
}

Quadratic space commonly occurs in matrices and graphs whose element counts grow with the square of \(n\):

    // The two-dimensional list occupies O(n^2) space

        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            tmp.push_back(0);
        }
        numMatrix.push_back(tmp);
    }
}

items.title: 5.   Logarithmic space \(O(\log n)\)
items.text:
Logarithmic space often appears in divide-and-conquer algorithms. For example, merge sort splits an array of length \(n\) in half at each recursive step, producing a recursion tree of height \(\log n\) and using \(O(\log n)\) space for stack frames.

Another example is converting a number to a string. A positive integer \(n\) has \(\lfloor \log_{10} n \rfloor + 1\) digits, giving a string of length \(\lfloor \log_{10} n \rfloor + 1\). The space complexity is therefore \(O(\log_{10} n + 1) = O(\log n)\).

items.title: 2.4.4   Balancing time and space
items.text:
Ideally, we would minimize both time and space complexity. In practice, optimizing both simultaneously is usually difficult.

Reducing time complexity often increases space complexity, and vice versa. Using more memory to run faster is called trading space for time; accepting slower execution to use less memory is trading time for space.

The choice depends on which resource matters more. Time is usually more valuable than space, so trading space for time is common. For very large datasets, however, keeping space complexity under control is also crucial.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
Evaluating algorithm efficiency

  • Time and space efficiency are the two main measures of algorithm quality.
  • Practical testing measures efficiency, but cannot easily remove environmental effects and consumes substantial computing resources.
  • Complexity analysis avoids those limitations, applies across platforms, and reveals efficiency at different input sizes.

Time complexity

  • Time complexity describes how runtime grows with input size. It is useful for evaluating efficiency, but may not distinguish algorithms accurately for small inputs or equal complexity classes.
  • Worst-case time complexity is expressed with big-\(O\) notation, an asymptotic upper bound describing the growth of the operation count \(T(n)\) as \(n\) tends to positive infinity.
  • Deriving time complexity takes two steps: count operations, then determine the asymptotic upper bound.
  • Common complexities, from slower to faster growth, include \(O(1)\), \(O(\log n)\), \(O(n)\), \(O(n \log n)\), \(O(n^2)\), \(O(2^n)\), and \(O(n!)\).
  • Some algorithms' complexity depends on the input's arrangement. We distinguish worst-case, best-case, and average-case complexity. Best-case complexity is rarely used because reaching it generally requires strict input conditions.
  • Average-case complexity describes performance on random inputs and is closest to typical practical behavior. Calculating it requires an input distribution and its mathematical expectation.

Space complexity

  • Like time complexity, space complexity describes a growth trend: how memory usage increases with input size.
  • Memory used during execution includes input, temporary, and output space. Input space is usually excluded from space complexity. Temporary space includes temporary data, stack frames, and instructions; stack frames usually affect complexity only in recursive functions.
  • We usually consider worst-case space complexity, measuring memory under the worst input and at the moment of maximum usage.
  • Common space complexities, from slower to faster growth, include \(O(1)\), \(O(\log n)\), \(O(n)\), \(O(n^2)\), and \(O(2^n)\).

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Does tail recursion have \(O(1)\) space complexity?

In theory, tail recursion can be optimized to \(O(1)\) space. However, most languages, including Java, Python, C++, Go, and C#, do not automatically optimize tail recursion, so its space complexity is usually treated as \(O(n)\).

Q: What is the difference between a function and a method?

A function can run independently, with all arguments passed explicitly. A method is associated with an object, receives that object implicitly when called, and can operate on the instance's data.

Here are examples from several common languages.

  • C is procedural and has no built-in object-oriented model, so it has functions only. We can simulate object-oriented programming with structures (struct); functions associated with a structure then act like methods in other languages.
  • Java and C# are object-oriented, and executable blocks (methods) are usually part of a class. Static methods behave like functions: they belong to the class and cannot access a particular instance's variables directly.
  • C++ and Python support both procedural programming with functions and object-oriented programming with methods.

Q: Does the common space complexity chart show absolute memory usage?

No. It illustrates growth trends rather than absolute amounts of memory.

For \(n = 8\), the plotted values may not match the corresponding functions exactly. Each curve includes a constant term that adjusts it to a visually convenient range.

In practice, these constant terms are usually unknown, so complexity alone cannot generally identify the best solution for \(n = 8\). For \(n = 8^5\), the choice is easier because growth rates dominate.

Q: Do algorithms sometimes trade time for space, or space for time, depending on the application?

Most practical applications trade space for time. Database indexes, for example, often use B+ trees or hash indexes, consuming substantial memory to achieve \(O(\log n)\) or even \(O(1)\) query time.

When memory is scarce, the reverse tradeoff may be useful. In embedded development, an engineer might replace a hash table with sequential array search to save memory, accepting slower lookups.

items.title: 2.3   Time complexity
items.text:
Runtime gives a direct, accurate picture of an algorithm's efficiency. How might we predict the runtime of a piece of code precisely?

  1. Specify the execution platform, including hardware, programming language, and system environment, all of which affect performance.
  2. Determine the time required by each operation: for example, addition + might take 1 ns, multiplication * 10 ns, and print() 5 ns.
  3. Count every operation in the code and sum their execution times to obtain the total runtime.

For example, consider the following code with input size \(n\):

    a = 2      # 1 ns

    a = a * 2  # 10 ns
    # Repeat n times
    for _ in range(n):  # 1 ns
        print(0)        # 5 ns

void algorithm(int n) {

    a = a + 1;  // 1 ns
    a = a * 2;  // 10 ns

        cout << 0 << endl;         // 5 ns
    }
}

\[ 1 + 1 + 10 + (1 + 5) \times n = 6n + 12 \]

In practice, calculating runtime this way is neither suitable nor realistic. We do not want estimates tied to one platform, since algorithms run on many platforms. Also, the time taken by each operation is difficult to determine, making accurate prediction very hard.

items.title: 2.3.1   Measuring growth in runtime

Figure 2-7   Runtime growth of algorithms A, B, and C

How does time complexity analysis differ from calculating runtime directly?

  • Time complexity evaluates efficiency effectively. Algorithm B grows linearly, becoming slower than A when \(n > 1\) and slower than C when \(n > 1000000\). With sufficiently large input size \(n\), a constant-time algorithm will outperform a linear-time one. This is what a growth trend tells us.
  • Time complexity is easier to derive. The execution platform and kinds of elementary operations do not determine the growth trend. We can treat each elementary operation as taking the same unit of time, reducing runtime estimation to operation counting and greatly simplifying analysis.
  • Time complexity has limitations. Algorithms A and C have the same complexity but very different runtimes. Although B has higher complexity than C, it is much faster for small \(n\). Complexity alone may not settle such comparisons. Even so, it remains the most effective and widely used way to evaluate algorithm efficiency.

items.title: 2.3.2   Asymptotic upper bounds
items.text:
Consider this function with input size \(n\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby 
def algorithm(n: int):
    a = 1      # +1
    a = a + 1  # +1
    a = a * 2  # +1
    # Repeat n times
    for i in range(n):  # +1
        print(0)        # +1

void algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +1
    a = a + 1;  // +1
    a = a * 2;  // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        cout << 0 << endl;    // +1
    }
}

void algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +1
    a = a + 1;  // +1
    a = a * 2;  // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        System.out.println(0);    // +1
    }
}

void Algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +1
    a = a + 1;  // +1
    a = a * 2;  // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {   // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        Console.WriteLine(0);   // +1
    }
}

func algorithm(n int) {
    a := 1      // +1
    a = a + 1   // +1
    a = a * 2   // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for i := 0; i < n; i++ {   // +1
        fmt.Println(a)         // +1
    }
}

func algorithm(n: Int) {
    var a = 1 // +1
    a = a + 1 // +1
    a = a * 2 // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for _ in 0 ..< n { // +1
        print(0) // +1
    }
}

function algorithm(n) {
    var a = 1; // +1
    a += 1; // +1
    a *= 2; // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for(let i = 0; i < n; i++){ // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        console.log(0); // +1
    }
}

function algorithm(n: number): void{
    var a: number = 1; // +1
    a += 1; // +1
    a *= 2; // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for(let i = 0; i < n; i++){ // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        console.log(0); // +1
    }
}

  int a = 1; // +1
  a = a + 1; // +1
  a = a * 2; // +1
  // Repeat n times
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
    print(0); // +1
  }
}

fn algorithm(n: i32) {
    let mut a = 1;   // +1
    a = a + 1;      // +1
    a = a * 2;      // +1

    // Repeat n times
    for _ in 0..n { // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        println!("{}", 0); // +1
    }
}

void algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +1
    a = a + 1;  // +1
    a = a * 2;  // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {   // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        printf("%d", 0);            // +1
    }
}

fun algorithm(n: Int) {
    var a = 1 // +1
    a = a + 1 // +1
    a = a * 2 // +1
    // Repeat n times
    for (i in 0..<n) { // +1 (i ++ executes each iteration)
        println(0) // +1
    }
}

def algorithm(n)
    a = 1       # +1
    a = a + 1   # +1
    a = a * 2   # +1
    # Repeat n times
    (0...n).each do # +1
        puts 0      # +1
    end
end

Let \(T(n)\) be the operation count as a function of input size \(n\). For the function above:

\[ T(n) = 3 + 2n \]

Since \(T(n)\) is a first-degree function, runtime grows linearly, giving linear time complexity.

We write linear time complexity as \(O(n)\). This is called big-\(O\) notation, and it gives an asymptotic upper bound on \(T(n)\).

Time complexity analysis essentially finds an asymptotic upper bound on the operation count \(T(n)\). It has a precise mathematical definition.

Asymptotic upper bound

If a positive real constant \(c\) and a real number \(n_0\) exist such that \(T(n) \leq c \cdot f(n)\) for all \(n > n_0\), then \(f(n)\) is an asymptotic upper bound on \(T(n)\), written \(T(n) = O(f(n))\).

As shown in Figure 2-8, we seek a function \(f(n)\) such that, as \(n\) tends to infinity, \(T(n)\) and \(f(n)\) have the same order of growth, differing only by a constant factor \(c\).

Figure 2-8   Asymptotic upper bound of a function

items.title: 2.3.3   How to derive time complexity
items.text:
The mathematics of asymptotic bounds may feel unfamiliar. Do not worry if it is not fully clear yet: learn the practical method first, and its meaning will become clearer with practice.

Once we identify \(f(n)\), the time complexity is \(O(f(n))\). Finding the asymptotic upper bound \(f(n)\) takes two steps: count operations, then determine the bound.

items.title: 1.   Step 1: Count operations
items.text:
We can count code operations line by line. Since the constant factor \(c\) in \(c \cdot f(n)\) may be arbitrarily large, coefficients and constant terms in \(T(n)\) can be ignored. This gives three useful shortcuts.

  1. Ignore constant terms in \(T(n)\). They are independent of \(n\) and do not affect complexity.
  2. Drop coefficients. For example, \(2n\) or \(5n + 1\) iterations can be counted simply as \(n\), because the coefficient of \(n\) does not affect complexity.
  3. Multiply for nested loops. Multiply the outer and inner iteration counts, applying shortcuts 1. and 2. to each level.

We can apply these shortcuts to the following function:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby 
def algorithm(n: int):
    a = 1      # +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n  # +0 (shortcut 1)
    # +n (shortcut 2)
    for i in range(5 * n + 1):
        print(0)
    # +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for i in range(2 * n):
        for j in range(n + 1):
            print(0)

void algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)
    for (int i = 0; i < 5 * n + 1; i++) {
        cout << 0 << endl;
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n + 1; j++) {
            cout << 0 << endl;
        }
    }
}

void algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)
    for (int i = 0; i < 5 * n + 1; i++) {
        System.out.println(0);
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n + 1; j++) {
            System.out.println(0);
        }
    }
}

void Algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)
    for (int i = 0; i < 5 * n + 1; i++) {
        Console.WriteLine(0);
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n + 1; j++) {
            Console.WriteLine(0);
        }
    }
}

func algorithm(n int) {
    a := 1     // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)

        fmt.Println(0)
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)

            fmt.Println(0)
        }
    }
}

    var a = 1 // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)

        print(0)
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for _ in 0 ..< (2 * n) {
        for _ in 0 ..< (n + 1) {
            print(0)
        }
    }
}

    let a = 1;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)

        console.log(0);
    }

        for (let j = 0; j < n + 1; j++) {
            console.log(0);
        }
    }
}

function algorithm(n: number): void {
    let a = 1;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)
    for (let i = 0; i < 5 * n + 1; i++) {
        console.log(0);
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)

        for (let j = 0; j < n + 1; j++) {
            console.log(0);
        }
    }
}

void algorithm(int n) {
  int a = 1; // +0 (shortcut 1)
  a = a + n; // +0 (shortcut 1)
  // +n (shortcut 2)
  for (int i = 0; i < 5 * n + 1; i++) {
    print(0);
  }
  // +n*n (shortcut 3)
  for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n + 1; j++) {
      print(0);
    }
  }
}

    let mut a = 1;     // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n;        // +0 (shortcut 1)

    // +n (shortcut 2)
    for i in 0..(5 * n + 1) {
        println!("{}", 0);
    }

    // +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for i in 0..(2 * n) {
        for j in 0..(n + 1) {
            println!("{}", 0);
        }
    }
}

void algorithm(int n) {
    int a = 1;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n;  // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)
    for (int i = 0; i < 5 * n + 1; i++) {
        printf("%d", 0);
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n + 1; j++) {
            printf("%d", 0);
        }
    }
}

fun algorithm(n: Int) {
    var a = 1   // +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n   // +0 (shortcut 1)
    // +n (shortcut 2)
    for (i in 0..<5 * n + 1) {
        println(0)
    }
    // +n*n (shortcut 3)
    for (i in 0..<2 * n) {
        for (j in 0..<n + 1) {
            println(0)
        }
    }
}

def algorithm(n)
    a = 1       # +0 (shortcut 1)
    a = a + n   # +0 (shortcut 1)
    # +n (shortcut 2)
    (0...(5 * n + 1)).each do { puts 0 }
    # +n*n (shortcut 3)
    (0...(2 * n)).each do
        (0...(n + 1)).each do { puts 0 }
    end
end

The formulas below compare full and simplified counts. Both give time complexity \(O(n^2)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} T(n) & = 2n(n + 1) + (5n + 1) + 2 & \text{Full count (-.-|||)} \newline & = 2n^2 + 7n + 3 \newline T(n) & = n^2 + n & \text{Shortcut count (o.O)} \end{aligned} \]

items.title: 2.   Step 2: Determine the asymptotic upper bound
items.text:
The highest-order term in \(T(n)\) determines time complexity. As \(n\) tends to infinity, that term dominates, and the others become negligible.

Table 2-2 includes deliberately extreme coefficients to emphasize that coefficients cannot overcome growth order. As \(n\) tends to infinity, those constants become insignificant.

Table 2-2   Operation counts and their time complexities

Operation count \(T(n)\) Time complexity \(O(f(n))\) \(100000\) \(O(1)\) \(3n + 2\) \(O(n)\) \(2n^2 + 3n + 2\) \(O(n^2)\) \(n^3 + 10000n^2\) \(O(n^3)\) \(2^n + 10000n^{10000}\) \(O(2^n)\)

items.title: 2.3.4   Common complexity classes
items.text:
For input size \(n\), common time complexities are shown below in increasing order of growth.

\[ \begin{aligned} & O(1) < O(\log n) < O(n) < O(n \log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!) \newline & \text{Constant} < \text{Logarithmic} < \text{Linear} < \text{Linearithmic} < \text{Quadratic} < \text{Exponential} < \text{Factorial} \end{aligned} \]

items.title: 1.   Constant time \(O(1)\)
items.text:

items.title: 3.   Quadratic time \(O(n^2)\)
items.text:
A quadratic operation count grows with the square of input size \(n\). It commonly appears in nested loops where both levels take \(O(n)\) time, giving \(O(n^2)\) overall:

def quadratic(n: int) -> int:
    """Quadratic complexity"""
    count = 0
    # The number of iterations is proportional to the square of the input size n
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            count += 1
    return count

            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

Figure 2-10   Constant, linear, and quadratic time complexity

In bubble sort, for example, the outer loop runs \(n - 1\) times, while the inner loop runs \(n-1\), \(n-2\), \(\dots\), \(2\), and \(1\) times, averaging \(n / 2\). The resulting complexity is \(O((n - 1) n / 2) = O(n^2)\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby time_complexity.py
def bubble_sort(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """Quadratic complexity (bubble sort)"""
    count = 0  # Counter
    # Outer loop: the unsorted range is [0, i]
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1, 0, -1):
        # Inner loop: move the largest element in the unsorted range [0, i] to its right end through swaps
        for j in range(i):
            if nums[j] > nums[j + 1]:
                # Swap nums[j] and nums[j + 1]
                tmp: int = nums[j]
                nums[j] = nums[j + 1]
                nums[j + 1] = tmp
                count += 3  # Swapping two elements takes 3 elementary operations
    return count

items.title: 4.   Exponential time \(O(2^n)\)
items.text:
Cell division is a classic example of exponential growth. Starting with \(1\) cell, one round produces \(2\), two rounds produce \(4\), and after \(n\) rounds there are \(2^n\) cells.

The figure and code below simulate cell division in \(O(2^n)\) time. The input \(n\) is the number of rounds, while the returned count is the total number of individual divisions.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby time_complexity.py
def exponential(n: int) -> int:
    """Exponential complexity (iterative implementation)"""
    count = 0
    base = 1
    # Each cell divides into two per round, giving the sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 2^(n-1)
    for _ in range(n):
        for _ in range(base):
            count += 1
        base *= 2
    # count = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + .. + 2^(n-1) = 2^n - 1
    return count

        for (int j = 0; j < base; j++) {
            count++;
        }
        base *= 2;
    }
    // count = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + .. + 2^(n-1) = 2^n - 1
    return count;
}

Exponential growth is very rapid and common in exhaustive approaches such as brute-force search and backtracking. It is unacceptable for large inputs, which usually require approaches such as dynamic programming or greedy algorithms.

items.title: 5.   Logarithmic time \(O(\log n)\)
items.text:
Logarithmic growth corresponds to repeatedly halving a quantity, the reverse of exponential growth. Starting with input size \(n\), halving each round gives \(\log_2 n\) iterations, the inverse of \(2^n\).

The figure and code below simulate repeated halving, taking \(O(\log_2 n)\) time, usually written \(O(\log n)\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby time_complexity.py
def logarithmic(n: int) -> int:
    """Logarithmic complexity (iterative implementation)"""
    count = 0
    while n > 1:
        n = n / 2
        count += 1
    return count

Logarithmic time often arises in divide-and-conquer algorithms, reflecting the idea of dividing a problem into smaller, simpler parts. It grows slowly and is highly desirable, second only to constant time among these classes.

What is the base of \(O(\log n)\)?

More precisely, reducing the size by a factor of \(m\) gives \(O(\log_m n)\). The change-of-base formula shows that different fixed bases yield the same complexity:

\[ O(\log_m n) = O(\log_k n / \log_k m) = O(\log_k n) \]

Thus, changing the base \(m\) does not affect the complexity. We usually omit \(m\) and simply write \(O(\log n)\).

items.title: 6.   Linearithmic time \(O(n \log n)\)
items.text:
Linearithmic time often appears when one level of a nested process takes \(O(\log n)\) and another takes \(O(n)\). An example follows:

def linear_log_recur(n: int) -> int:
    """Linearithmic complexity"""
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    # Split into two subproblems, each half the original size
    count = linear_log_recur(n // 2) + linear_log_recur(n // 2)
    # The current subproblem includes n operations
    for _ in range(n):
        count += 1
    return count

items.title: 7.   Factorial time \(O(n!)\)
items.text:
Factorial growth arises when generating every permutation of \(n\) distinct elements. The number of permutations is:

\[ n! = n \times (n - 1) \times (n - 2) \times \dots \times 2 \times 1 \]

Algorithms with factorial time complexity are usually implemented recursively. As the figure and code below show, each call creates \(n\) branches at the first level, \(n - 1\) at the second, and so on until level \(n\):

def factorial_recur(n: int) -> int:
    """Factorial complexity (recursive implementation)"""
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    count = 0
    # Split one problem into n subproblems
    for _ in range(n):
        count += factorial_recur(n - 1)
    return count

items.title: 2.3.5   Worst-case, best-case, and average-case time complexity
items.text:
An algorithm's efficiency often depends on how its input data is arranged. Suppose nums is an array of length \(n\) containing every integer from \(1\) through \(n\) exactly once in a random order. The task is to return the index of \(1\). We can conclude the following.

  • If nums = [?, ?, ..., 1], with \(1\) last, we must traverse the whole array, giving worst-case time complexity \(O(n)\).
  • If nums = [1, ?, ?, ...], with \(1\) first, no further traversal is needed regardless of array length, giving best-case time complexity \(\Omega(1)\).

Worst-case time complexity corresponds to an asymptotic upper bound, expressed with big-\(O\) notation. Best-case time complexity corresponds to an asymptotic lower bound, expressed with \(\Omega\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby worst_best_time_complexity.py
def random_numbers(n: int) -> list[int]:
    """Generate an array containing 1, 2, ..., n in shuffled order"""
    # Generate the array nums = 1, 2, 3, ..., n
    nums = [i for i in range(1, n + 1)]
    # Randomly shuffle the array elements
    random.shuffle(nums)
    return nums

def find_one(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """Find the index of the number 1 in array nums"""
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        # When 1 is at the start of the array, the best-case time complexity is O(1)
        # When 1 is at the end of the array, the worst-case time complexity is O(n)
        if nums[i] == 1:
            return i
    return -1

    val res = arrayOfNulls<Int>(n)
    for (i in 0..<n) {
        res[i] = nums[i]
    }
    return res
}

/* Find the index of the number 1 in array nums */
fun findOne(nums: Array<Int?>): Int {
    for (i in nums.indices) {
        // When 1 is at the start of the array, the best-case time complexity is O(1)
        // When 1 is at the end of the array, the worst-case time complexity is O(n)
        if (nums[i] == 1)
            return i
    }
    return -1
}
worst_best_time_complexity.rb
### Generate an array containing 1, 2, ..., n in shuffled order ###
def random_numbers(n)
  # Generate the array nums = 1, 2, 3, ..., n
  nums = Array.new(n) { |i| i + 1 }
  # Randomly shuffle the array elements
  nums.shuffle!
end

### Find the index of the number 1 in array nums ###
def find_one(nums)
  for i in 0...nums.length
    # When 1 is at the start of the array, the best-case time complexity is O(1)
    # When 1 is at the end of the array, the worst-case time complexity is O(n)
    return i if nums[i] == 1
  end

  -1
end
Visualize execution

View full screen >

Best-case complexity is rarely used in practice because it may occur only with low probability and can be misleading. Worst-case complexity is more useful because it gives a safe performance bound, allowing us to use the algorithm with confidence.

In this example, both the worst and best cases occur only for particular arrangements, perhaps with low probability, and may not reflect ordinary performance. Average-case complexity describes performance on random inputs and is expressed with \(\Theta\).

For some algorithms, the average case is easy to derive. In the example above, \(1\) is equally likely to occur at any index in the shuffled array. The average number of iterations is half the array length, \(n / 2\), giving \(\Theta(n / 2) = \Theta(n)\).

For more complex algorithms, average-case complexity can be difficult to calculate because the overall expectation under the input distribution is hard to derive. In such cases, we usually judge efficiency by worst-case complexity.

Why is \(\Theta\) rarely seen?

Perhaps because \(O\) is so familiar, it is often used for average-case complexity too. Strictly speaking, this usage is not standard. In this book and other resources, read a statement such as "average-case time complexity \(O(n)\)" as \(\Theta(n)\).

items.title: Chapter 3.   Data structures
items.text:
Abstract

Data structures provide a framework that is both sturdy and versatile.

They offer a blueprint for organizing data, a foundation on which algorithms come to life.

items.title: 3.2   Basic data types
items.text:
Computer data comes in many forms: text, images, video, audio, 3D models, and more. Although organized differently, all these forms are built from basic data types.

Basic data types are types on which the CPU can operate directly and which algorithms use directly. The main types include the following.

  • Integer types: byte, short, int, and long.
  • Floating-point types: float and double, used to represent fractional numbers.
  • The character type char, used for letters in different languages, punctuation, and even emoji.
  • The Boolean type bool, used for yes-or-no values.

Basic data types are stored in binary form. One binary digit is \(1\) bit. In the vast majority of modern operating systems, \(1\) byte consists of \(8\) bits.

A basic data type's value range depends on the space it occupies. Taking Java as an example:

  • An integer byte occupies \(1\) byte = \(8\) bits and can represent \(2^{8}\) distinct values.
  • An integer int occupies \(4\) bytes = \(32\) bits and can represent \(2^{32}\) distinct values.

Table 3-1 lists storage sizes, value ranges, and default values for Java's basic data types. There is no need to memorize it; understand the general picture and refer back when needed.

Table 3-1   Storage sizes and value ranges of basic data types

Type Name Storage size Minimum value Maximum value Default value Integer byte 1 byte \(-2^7\) (\(-128\)) \(2^7 - 1\) (\(127\)) \(0\) short 2 bytes \(-2^{15}\) \(2^{15} - 1\) \(0\) int 4 bytes \(-2^{31}\) \(2^{31} - 1\) \(0\) long 8 bytes \(-2^{63}\) \(2^{63} - 1\) \(0\) Floating-point float 4 bytes \(1.175 \times 10^{-38}\) \(3.403 \times 10^{38}\) \(0.0\text{f}\) double 8 bytes \(2.225 \times 10^{-308}\) \(1.798 \times 10^{308}\) \(0.0\) Character char 2 bytes \(0\) \(2^{16} - 1\) \(0\) Boolean bool 1 byte \(\text{false}\) \(\text{true}\) \(\text{false}\)

Table 3-1 describes Java's basic data types. Each programming language defines its own types, whose sizes, value ranges, and default values may differ.

  • In Python, an int can be arbitrarily large, limited only by available memory. A float is a 64-bit double-precision number. There is no char type: a single character is a str of length 1.
  • C and C++ do not fix the sizes of basic data types; they vary by implementation and platform. Table 3-1 follows the LP64 data model, used by 64-bit Unix operating systems including Linux and macOS.
  • A char occupies 1 byte in C and C++. In most programming languages, character size depends on the encoding used; see the character encoding section.
  • Although a Boolean needs only 1 bit (\(0\) or \(1\)), it usually occupies 1 byte in memory because modern CPUs typically use a byte as the smallest addressable memory unit.

How do basic data types relate to data structures? A data structure is a way to organize and store data in a computer. The emphasis is on structure, rather than the data itself.

To represent a row of numbers, an array comes naturally to mind. Its linear structure captures adjacency and ordering, regardless of whether the stored values are integers (int), fractional numbers (float), or characters (char).

In other words, basic data types specify what kind of data is stored, while data structures specify how it is organized. The following code uses the same data structure, an array, for different basic types, including int, float, char, and bool.
