items.title: 3.4   Character encoding *
items.text: All computer data is stored as binary numbers, including characters of type char. To represent characters, we need a character set that assigns each character a unique binary number. The computer can then convert numbers to characters by looking them up.

items.title: 3.4.1   ASCII character set
items.text:
ASCII, short for American Standard Code for Information Interchange, was the earliest character set. It uses 7 bits (the lower 7 bits of a byte) per character, allowing up to 128 characters. As shown in Figure 3-6, ASCII includes uppercase and lowercase English letters, digits 0 ~ 9, punctuation, and control characters such as newlines and tabs.

Figure 3-6   ASCII codes

However, ASCII can represent only English text. As computers spread worldwide, EASCII character sets emerged to support more languages. Extending ASCII from 7 bits to 8 allowed 256 distinct characters.

Different regions developed their own EASCII character sets. The first 128 characters remained identical to ASCII, while the remaining 128 varied to meet different languages' needs.

items.title: 3.4.2   GBK character set
items.text:
Eventually, even EASCII proved too small for many languages. Chinese, for example, has nearly 100,000 characters, with thousands used daily. In 1980, China's National Bureau of Standards released GB2312, containing 6,763 Chinese characters and meeting most basic needs for processing Chinese text.

GB2312 could not handle some rare and traditional characters. GBK extended it to 21,886 Chinese characters. In GBK encoding, ASCII characters use one byte, and Chinese characters use two.

items.title: 3.4.3   Unicode character set
items.text:
As computing grew, character sets and encoding standards proliferated, creating problems. Most covered only particular languages and did not work well in multilingual settings. Multiple standards also existed for the same language, so exchanging text between computers using different encodings could produce garbled text.

Researchers asked: could a sufficiently comprehensive character set, containing all the world's languages and symbols, solve both multilingual compatibility and garbled-text problems? This idea led to Unicode.

Unicode, whose Chinese name means "unified code", can theoretically accommodate over a million characters. It aims to bring the world's characters into one universal set for processing and displaying different languages, reducing garbled text caused by incompatible standards. Since its release in 1991, it has continued adding languages and characters. As of September 2022, Unicode contained 149,186 characters, including letters, symbols, and emoji.

As a universal character set, Unicode assigns each character a unique code point, or character number, from U+0000 to U+10FFFF. It does not, by itself, specify how these code points are stored in a computer. How can a system parse text containing code points of different lengths? For example, how does it distinguish one two-byte character from two one-byte characters?

One straightforward solution is to store every character in a fixed-width encoding. In Figure 3-7, each character in "Hello" occupies 1 byte, while each in "算法" occupies 2 bytes. Padding the high bits with zeros lets us encode every character in "Hello 算法" with 2 bytes. The system can then read one character every 2 bytes to recover the phrase.

Figure 3-7   Example of Unicode encoding

ASCII has already shown that English text needs only 1 byte per character. This scheme would double its storage compared with ASCII, wasting memory. We therefore need a more efficient Unicode encoding.

items.title: 3.4.4   UTF-8 encoding
items.text:
UTF-8 is now the most widely used Unicode encoding worldwide. It is variable-length, using 1 to 4 bytes per character depending on the character. ASCII characters need 1 byte, Latin and Greek letters need 2, common Chinese characters need 3, and some less common characters need 4.

UTF-8's rules have two cases.

  • For a one-byte character, set the highest bit to \(0\) and the remaining 7 bits to its Unicode code point. ASCII occupies the first 128 Unicode code points, so UTF-8 is backward-compatible with ASCII. UTF-8 can therefore decode old ASCII text.
  • For an \(n\)-byte character, where \(n > 1\), set the first byte's leading \(n\) bits to \(1\) and the next bit, \(n + 1\), to \(0\). Starting with the second byte, set the leading 2 bits of every byte to \(10\). Fill the remaining bits with the character's Unicode code point.

Figure 3-8 shows UTF-8 for "Hello算法". Since the leading \(n\) bits are \(1\), the system can determine the character length \(n\) by counting the leading \(1\) bits.

Why do all remaining bytes begin with \(10\)? This \(10\) acts as a check marker. If decoding starts at the wrong byte, the leading \(10\) helps the system quickly detect the problem.

The prefix \(10\) works as a marker because no character's first byte can begin with \(10\) under UTF-8's rules. To see this by contradiction, suppose it did begin with \(10\). The single leading one would imply a length of \(1\) byte, corresponding to ASCII, but an ASCII byte must begin with \(0\), a contradiction.

Figure 3-8   Example of UTF-8 encoding

Two other common encodings are:

  • UTF-16: Uses 2 or 4 bytes per character. ASCII and common non-English characters use 2 bytes; some characters require 4. For a two-byte character, its UTF-16 encoding equals its Unicode code point.
  • UTF-32: Uses 4 bytes for every character. It therefore takes more space than UTF-8 or UTF-16, especially for text containing mostly ASCII characters.

In terms of storage, UTF-8 is efficient for English characters because each uses only 1 byte. UTF-16 is more efficient for some non-English characters, such as Chinese, using 2 bytes where UTF-8 may require 3.

In terms of compatibility, UTF-8 is the most widely supported, and many tools and libraries prioritize it.

items.title: 3.4.5   Character encoding in programming languages
items.text:
Historically, most programming languages have stored strings at runtime using fixed-width encodings such as UTF-16 or UTF-32. Fixed-width encoding lets us treat a string as an array, with the following advantages.

  • Random access: UTF-16 strings support straightforward random access. With variable-length UTF-8, finding the \(i\)-th character requires traversing from the beginning to the \(i\)-th character, taking \(O(n)\) time.
  • Character counting: Similarly, finding the length of a UTF-16 string is an \(O(1)\) operation, while finding the character count of a UTF-8 string requires traversing the whole string.
  • String operations: Operations such as splitting, concatenation, insertion, and deletion are easier on UTF-16 strings. With UTF-8, they usually require extra work to avoid producing invalid encodings.

The design of string representations is an interesting subject involving many factors.

  • Java's String uses UTF-16, with 2 bytes per character. When Java was designed, 16 bits were thought sufficient for every character. This turned out to be incorrect: Unicode later expanded beyond 16 bits, so a Java character may now require a pair of 16-bit values called a surrogate pair.
  • JavaScript and TypeScript use UTF-16 for similar historical reasons. When Netscape introduced JavaScript in 1995, Unicode was still young, and 16 bits could represent all its characters at the time.
  • C# uses UTF-16 largely because Microsoft designed .NET, and many Microsoft technologies, including Windows, use UTF-16 extensively.

Having underestimated the number of characters, these languages had to adopt surrogate pairs for Unicode characters beyond 16 bits. This was a compromise. A character in such a string may occupy 2 or 4 bytes, losing the benefit of fixed width, and handling surrogate pairs requires additional code, making programming and debugging more complex.

For these reasons, some languages use different representations.

  • Python's str uses Unicode with a flexible representation whose character width depends on the largest code point in the string. If all characters are ASCII, each uses 1 byte. If some exceed ASCII but all lie within the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), each uses 2 bytes. If any lie outside the BMP, each uses 4 bytes.
  • Go's string uses UTF-8 internally. Go also provides rune to represent a single Unicode code point.
  • Rust's str and String use UTF-8 internally, while char represents a single Unicode code point.

These descriptions concern string storage within programming languages. How strings are stored in files or transmitted over a network is a separate question. For file storage and network transmission, strings are usually encoded as UTF-8 for compatibility and space efficiency.

items.title: 3.1   Classifying data structures
items.text: Common data structures include arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, and graphs. They can be classified by their logical structure and physical structure.

items.title: 3.1.1   Logical structure: linear and nonlinear
items.text:
Logical structure describes the relationships between data elements. Arrays and linked lists arrange data in sequence, expressing linear relationships. Trees arrange data hierarchically from top to bottom, expressing ancestry and descent. Graphs consist of vertices and edges that express complex network relationships.

As shown in Figure 3-1, logical structures fall into two broad categories: linear and nonlinear. A linear structure arranges data in a logical sequence; a nonlinear structure does not.

  • Linear data structures: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, and hash tables. Elements have one-to-one sequential relationships.
  • Nonlinear data structures: Trees, heaps, graphs, and hash tables.

Nonlinear data structures can be divided further into tree and network structures.

  • Tree structures: Trees, heaps, and hash tables, with one-to-many relationships.
  • Network structures: Graphs, with many-to-many relationships.

Figure 3-1   Linear and nonlinear data structures

items.title: 3.1.2   Physical structure: contiguous and scattered storage
items.text:
While an algorithm runs, the data it processes is mainly stored in memory. Figure 3-2 shows a memory module, with each black chip containing storage space. We can imagine memory as a huge Excel spreadsheet, where each cell holds a certain amount of data.

The system uses memory addresses to access data at particular locations. As shown in Figure 3-2, the computer assigns each cell a number according to specific rules, giving every memory location a unique address. Programs use these addresses to access data.

Figure 3-2   Memory module, storage space, and memory addresses

Tip

The Excel spreadsheet analogy is a simplification. Real memory is more complex and involves address spaces, memory management, caching, virtual memory, and physical memory.

Memory is a resource used by all programs. When a program occupies a region of memory, other programs usually cannot use that region at the same time. Memory resources are therefore an important consideration when designing data structures and algorithms. For example, an algorithm's peak memory usage should not exceed the system's available memory. If no large contiguous region is available, the chosen data structure must support scattered storage.

As shown in Figure 3-3, physical structure describes how data is stored in computer memory: either contiguously (arrays) or in scattered locations (linked lists). It determines how data can be accessed, updated, inserted, and deleted. The two storage forms have complementary strengths in time and space efficiency.

Figure 3-3   Contiguous and scattered storage

All data structures are implemented using arrays, linked lists, or a combination of the two. For example, stacks and queues can use either arrays or linked lists, while hash tables may use both.

  • Array-based implementations: Stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, graphs, matrices, tensors (arrays with dimension \(\geq 3\)), and more.
  • Linked-list-based implementations: Stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, graphs, and more.

A linked list can change length during execution after initialization, so it is called a dynamic data structure. An array's length is fixed after initialization, so it is called a static data structure. However, reallocating memory can change an array's length, providing a degree of dynamic behavior.

Tip

If physical structure feels difficult to understand, read the next chapter first and then return to this section.

items.title: 1.   Relationships between data in everyday situations
items.text:
For each situation below, choose a linear, tree, or network structure based on the relationships between the data, and explain your choice:

  1. Students stand in a line, each concerned only with the people immediately in front of and behind them.
  2. A school is organized in a hierarchy: school → grade → class.
  3. City roads connect intersections. An intersection can lead to several others, and the roads may form cycles.
Reference answer

  1. A linear structure. Apart from the first and last people, each person has exactly one neighbor in front and one behind, forming a line of relationships.

  2. A tree structure. Each class belongs to a grade, and each grade belongs to the school, forming a hierarchy from top to bottom.

  3. A network structure. An intersection can connect to several others, and routes can form cycles. These relationships cannot be arranged in a single sequence or a strict hierarchy.

    To identify a structure, first examine the relationships between its elements, rather than how much memory it occupies.

items.title: 2.   Storing a logical sequence in memory
items.text:
Consider two simplified memory layouts for storing the logical sequence A → B → C:

  • Layout A: A, B, C are stored in memory cells numbered 20, 21, 22, respectively.
  • Layout B: A, B, C are stored in cells numbered 20, 7, 31, respectively. A records the location of B, and B records the location of C.
  1. Which layout uses contiguous storage, and which uses noncontiguous storage?
  2. Which layout is more like an array, and which is more like a linked list?
  3. The cell numbers in layout B are not in ascending order. Why can it still represent the logical sequence A → B → C?
Reference answer

  1. Layout A uses consecutive memory cells, so its storage is contiguous. In layout B, nodes occupy separate locations, so its storage is noncontiguous.

  2. Layout A is more like an array; layout B is more like a linked list.

  3. The logical order is determined by the links recorded between nodes, not by the numerical order of their memory cell numbers. The location stored in A leads to B, and the location stored in B leads to C, so we can still visit A, B, C in sequence.

    This also shows that logical and physical structure are two ways of looking at the same data.

items.title: 3.   Data types and structures in homework records
items.text:
A study group records whether four students have submitted their homework, in seating order:

[true, false, true, true]

  1. Which basic data type is suitable for each element?
  2. These four elements form a sequence in seating order. What logical structure does this use?
  3. If the group later records homework scores instead, as [90, 0, 85, 100], has the type of content changed, or the way it is organized? Explain.
Reference answer

  1. Each element represents only yes or no, so the Boolean type bool is appropriate.

  2. The elements form a linear structure in seating order and can be stored in an array.

  3. The content type has changed: the elements are now integers instead of Boolean values. Their organization has not changed. The data still forms a sequence in seating order and can still use the linear structure of an array.

    A basic data type describes what is stored; a data structure describes how the data is organized.

items.title: 1.   Counting ones in a binary representation
items.text:
Given a nonnegative integer n, count the ones in its binary representation.

Use bitwise operations. Do not convert the binary representation to a string or use a built-in function that counts the ones directly.

Hints
  1. n & 1 extracts the rightmost bit of n, allowing you to check whether it is 1.
  2. Shifting right by one bit discards the current rightmost bit; most languages use the >> operator.
  3. After implementing the method that checks each bit and shifts right, observe that n & (n - 1) changes the rightmost 1 in n to 0.

LeetCode

items.title: 3.3   Number encoding *
items.text:
Tip

Sections marked with * in their titles are optional. If you are short on time or find them difficult, you can skip them initially and return after completing the required sections.

items.title: 3.3.1   Sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement
items.text:
The previous table showed that every integer type represents one more negative value than positive value. For example, byte ranges over \([-128, 127]\). Understanding this counterintuitive fact requires sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement.

First, integers are stored in two's complement form. Before explaining why, let's define the three representations.

  • Sign-magnitude: The highest bit is the sign: \(0\) for positive and \(1\) for negative. The remaining bits represent the magnitude.
  • One's complement: A positive number has the same representation as sign-magnitude. For a negative number, invert every bit except the sign bit of its sign-magnitude representation.
  • Two's complement: A positive number again has the same representation as sign-magnitude. For a negative number, add \(1\) to its one's complement.

Figure 3-4 shows how to convert among these representations.

Figure 3-4   Converting between sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement

Although sign-magnitude is intuitive, it has limitations. First, negative sign-magnitude values cannot be used directly in ordinary binary arithmetic. For example, directly adding \(1 + (-2)\) in this representation gives \(-3\), which is clearly wrong.

\[ egin{aligned} & 1 + (-2) ewline & ightarrow 0000 \; 0001 + 1000 \; 0010 ewline & = 1000 \; 0011 ewline & ightarrow -3 \end{aligned} \]

To address this, computers introduced one's complement. Convert the operands to one's complement, calculate \(1 + (-2)\), and convert the result back to sign-magnitude to obtain the correct answer, \(-1\).

\[ egin{aligned} & 1 + (-2) ewline & ightarrow 0000 \; 0001 \; ext{(sign-magnitude)} + 1000 \; 0010 \; ext{(sign-magnitude)} ewline & = 0000 \; 0001 \; ext{(one's complement)} + 1111 \; 1101 \; ext{(one's complement)} ewline & = 1111 \; 1110 \; ext{(one's complement)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0001 \; ext{(sign-magnitude)} ewline & ightarrow -1 \end{aligned} \]

Second, sign-magnitude has two representations of zero, \(+0\) and \(-0\). Two binary encodings for zero can create ambiguity. Conditional checks may be wrong if they do not handle both forms, while special handling requires extra checks that can reduce efficiency.

\[ egin{aligned} +0 & ightarrow 0000 \; 0000 ewline -0 & ightarrow 1000 \; 0000 \end{aligned} \]

One's complement also has positive and negative zero, so computers introduced two's complement. Consider converting negative zero through all three representations:

\[ egin{aligned} -0 ightarrow \; & 1000 \; 0000 \; ext{(sign-magnitude)} ewline = \; & 1111 \; 1111 \; ext{(one's complement)} ewline = 1 \; & 0000 \; 0000 \; ext{(two's complement)} ewline \end{aligned} \]

Adding \(1\) to the one's complement of negative zero produces a carry. A byte has only 8 bits, so the \(1\) carried into the ninth bit is discarded. Negative zero's two's complement is therefore \(0000 \; 0000\), the same as positive zero. Two's complement has only one zero, eliminating the ambiguity.

One question remains: if byte ranges over \([-128, 127]\), where does the extra negative value \(-128\) come from? Every integer in \([-127, +127]\) has sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement representations, and its sign-magnitude and two's complement forms can be converted into each other.

However, the two's complement value \(1000 \; 0000\) is an exception with no corresponding sign-magnitude form. Applying the conversion gives \(0000 \; 0000\), but that represents \(0\), whose two's complement should be itself. The special pattern \(1000 \; 0000\) is defined to represent \(-128\). Indeed, two's complement addition of \((-1) + (-127)\) gives \(-128\).

\[ egin{aligned} & (-127) + (-1) ewline & ightarrow 1111 \; 1111 \; ext{(sign-magnitude)} + 1000 \; 0001 \; ext{(sign-magnitude)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0000 \; ext{(one's complement)} + 1111 \; 1110 \; ext{(one's complement)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0001 \; ext{(two's complement)} + 1111 \; 1111 \; ext{(two's complement)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0000 \; ext{(two's complement)} ewline & ightarrow -128 \end{aligned} \]

All the calculations above use addition. This points to an important fact: computer arithmetic circuits are largely built around addition. Compared with operations such as multiplication, division, and subtraction, addition is simpler to implement in hardware, easier to parallelize, and faster.

This does not mean computers can only add. Combining addition with basic logical operations makes other arithmetic possible. For example, subtraction \(a - b\) becomes addition \(a + (-b)\), while multiplication and division can be expressed as repeated additions or subtractions.

We can now summarize why computers use two's complement. It lets the same circuitry and operations handle both positive and negative addition, without dedicated subtraction circuitry or special handling for positive and negative zero. This simplifies hardware and improves efficiency.

Two's complement is an elegant design. Space limits our discussion here, but interested readers are encouraged to explore it further.

items.title: 3.3.2   Floating-point encoding
items.text:
Both int and float occupy 4 bytes, yet float has a much wider range. This seems surprising: since float also represents fractions, should its range not be smaller?

The reason is that float uses a different representation. Write a 32-bit binary number as:

\[ b_{31} b_{30} b_{29} \ldots b_2 b_1 b_0 \]

Under IEEE 754, a 32-bit float has three parts.

  • Sign \(\mathrm{S}\): 1 bit, corresponding to \(b_{31}\).
  • Exponent \(\mathrm{E}\): 8 bits, corresponding to \(b_{30} b_{29} \ldots b_{23}\).
  • Fraction \(\mathrm{N}\): 23 bits, corresponding to \(b_{22} b_{21} \ldots b_0\).

The value represented by the binary float is:

\[ \text {val} = (-1)^{b_{31}} \times 2^{\left(b_{30} b_{29} \ldots b_{23}\right)_2-127} \times\left(1 . b_{22} b_{21} \ldots b_0\right)_2 \]

In decimal notation, this becomes:

\[ \text {val}=(-1)^{\mathrm{S}} \times 2^{\mathrm{E} -127} \times (1 + \mathrm{N}) \]

The components have these ranges:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{S} \in & \{ 0, 1\}, \quad \mathrm{E} \in \{ 1, 2, \dots, 254 \} \newline (1 + \mathrm{N}) = & (1 + \sum_{i=1}^{23} b_{23-i} 2^{-i}) \subset [1, 2 - 2^{-23}] \end{aligned} \]

Figure 3-5   Example of an IEEE 754 float calculation

In Figure 3-5, \(\mathrm{S} = 0\), \(\mathrm{E} = 124\), and \(\mathrm{N} = 2^{-2} + 2^{-3} = 0.375\), giving:

\[ \text { val } = (-1)^0 \times 2^{124 - 127} \times (1 + 0.375) = 0.171875 \]

We can now answer the original question: the exponent gives float a much wider range than int. The largest positive float is \(2^{254 - 127} \times (2 - 2^{-23}) \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\); changing the sign bit gives the most negative value.

The wider range of float comes at the cost of precision. An int uses all 32 bits to represent evenly spaced integer values. Because float includes an exponent, the gap between adjacent representable values tends to grow as their magnitude increases.

As shown in Table 3-2, exponent values \(\mathrm{E} = 0\) and \(\mathrm{E} = 255\) have special meanings, representing zero, infinity, and \(\mathrm{NaN}\), among other values.

Table 3-2   Meanings of exponent values

Exponent E Fraction \(\mathrm{N} = 0\) Fraction \(\mathrm{N} \ne 0\) Formula \(0\) \(\pm 0\) Subnormal number \((-1)^{\mathrm{S}} \times 2^{-126} \times (0.\mathrm{N})\) \(1, 2, \dots, 254\) Normal number Normal number \((-1)^{\mathrm{S}} \times 2^{(\mathrm{E} -127)} \times (1.\mathrm{N})\) \(255\) \(\pm \infty\) \(\mathrm{NaN}\)

Subnormal numbers substantially improve precision near zero. The smallest positive normal number is \(2^{-126}\), and the smallest positive subnormal number is \(2^{-126} \times 2^{-23}\).

Double-precision double uses a similar representation, which we will not detail here.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Data structures can be classified by logical and physical structure. Logical structure describes relationships between data elements, while physical structure describes how data is stored in memory.
  • Common logical structures are linear, tree, and network structures. We usually classify data structures as linear (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues) or nonlinear (trees, graphs, heaps). A hash table implementation may contain both linear and nonlinear structures.
  • During execution, data resides in computer memory. Each location has a memory address, which programs use to access its data.
  • The two main physical structures are contiguous storage (arrays) and scattered storage (linked lists). All data structures are implemented using arrays, linked lists, or both.
  • Basic data types include integers (byte, short, int, long), floating-point numbers (float, double), characters (char), and Booleans (bool). Their value ranges depend on storage size and representation.
  • Sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement are three ways to encode numbers, and can be converted into one another. In sign-magnitude representation, the highest bit is the sign and the remaining bits give the magnitude.
  • Integers are stored in two's complement. This lets the computer handle positive and negative addition uniformly, avoids separate hardware circuitry for subtraction, and eliminates the ambiguity of positive and negative zero.
  • A floating-point encoding consists of 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. The exponent provides a much wider range than integers, at the cost of precision.
  • ASCII was the earliest English character set. It uses 1 byte and contains 128 characters. GBK is a common Chinese character set with over 20,000 Chinese characters. Unicode aims to provide a comprehensive character standard for the world's languages, avoiding garbled text caused by incompatible encodings.
  • UTF-8 is the most popular Unicode encoding and is widely compatible. Its variable length makes it extensible and space-efficient. UTF-16 and UTF-32 use fixed lengths. For Chinese text, UTF-16 uses less space than UTF-8. Languages such as Java and C# use UTF-16 by default.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Why can a hash table contain both linear and nonlinear data structures?

A hash table is built on an array. To handle hash collisions, it may use separate chaining, discussed later in the Hash collisions section: each array bucket points to a linked list, which may be converted to a tree (usually a red-black tree) if it grows beyond a threshold.

From a storage perspective, each bucket in the underlying array may contain a value, a linked list, or a tree. A hash table may therefore contain both linear structures (arrays and linked lists) and nonlinear structures (trees).

Q: Does char occupy 1 byte?

The size of char depends on the programming language's encoding. For example, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, and C# use UTF-16 to store Unicode code points, so their char type occupies 2 bytes.

Q: Is calling array-based structures static misleading? A stack supports dynamic operations such as pushing and popping.

A stack does support dynamic data operations, but its underlying structure remains static in length. Although array-based structures can add and remove elements dynamically, their capacity is fixed. When the data exceeds the allocated capacity, a larger array must be created and the old contents copied into it.

Q: When we create a stack or queue without specifying its size, why is it still called a static data structure?

In high-level languages, the class automatically chooses an initial capacity for a stack or queue. For example, Java's ArrayList typically starts with a capacity of 10. Resizing is also automatic; see the later section on lists.

Q: Converting sign-magnitude to two's complement uses "invert, then add 1". Its inverse should be "subtract 1, then invert", so why does "invert, then add 1" also work in the reverse direction?

These conversions are really computations of a complement. If \(a + b = c\), we call \(a\) the complement of \(b\) with respect to \(c\), and conversely \(b\) the complement of \(a\) with respect to \(c\).

Consider the \(n = 4\)-bit binary number \(0010\). Treating it as sign-magnitude and disregarding the sign bit, we obtain its two's complement by inverting and adding 1:

\[ 0010 \rightarrow 1101 \rightarrow 1110 \]

The two representations sum to \(0010 + 1110 = 10000\). Thus, \(1110\) is the complement of \(0010\) with respect to \(10000\). The "invert, then add 1" operation computes the complement with respect to \(10000\).

What is the complement of \(1110\) with respect to \(10000\)? We can again invert and add 1:

\[ 1110 \rightarrow 0001 \rightarrow 0010 \]

The two representations are complements of each other with respect to \(10000\), so conversion in either direction can use the same operation: invert, then add 1.

Of course, we can also recover the sign-magnitude form of \(1110\) by the inverse operation: subtract 1, then invert.

\[ 1110 \rightarrow 1101 \rightarrow 0010 \]

Both "invert, then add 1" and "subtract 1, then invert" compute the complement with respect to \(10000\), so they are equivalent.

In essence, inverting computes the complement with respect to \(1111\), since sign-magnitude + one's complement = 1111. Adding 1 to the one's complement then gives the complement with respect to \(10000\).

The example uses \(n = 4\), but the reasoning extends to binary numbers of any bit width.

items.title: Chapter 12.   Divide and conquer
items.text:
Abstract

A difficult problem is broken down layer by layer, becoming simpler with each division.

Divide and conquer reveals an important truth: start with the simple parts, and complexity becomes manageable.

items.title: 12.2   Divide-and-conquer search
items.text:
We have learned that search algorithms fall into two broad categories.

  • Brute-force search: Traverses a data structure, taking \(O(n)\) time.
  • Adaptive search: Uses a particular organization of data or prior information to achieve \(O(\log n)\) or even \(O(1)\) time.

In fact, search algorithms that run in \(O(\log n)\) time are usually based on divide and conquer, as seen in binary search and trees.

  • Each step of binary search reduces the problem of finding a target in an array to a smaller problem of finding it in half of the array. This continues until the array is empty or the target is found.
  • Trees exemplify divide and conquer. In data structures such as binary search trees, AVL trees, and heaps, various operations take \(O(\log n)\) time.

Binary search uses divide and conquer in the following way.

  • The problem can be divided: By comparing the middle element with the target, binary search recursively reduces the original problem of searching an array to the subproblem of searching half of that array.
  • The subproblems are independent: Binary search handles only one subproblem at each step, unaffected by other subproblems.
  • The subproblem solutions need not be combined: Binary search seeks a particular element, so there is no need to combine solutions. Solving the subproblem also solves the original problem.

Divide and conquer makes searching faster because brute-force search eliminates only one option per step, whereas divide-and-conquer search can eliminate half the options.

items.title: 1.   Implementing binary search with divide and conquer
items.text:
Earlier chapters implemented binary search iteratively. We will now implement it recursively using divide and conquer.

Question

Given a sorted array nums of length \(n\) with distinct elements, find the element target.

From a divide-and-conquer perspective, let \(f(i, j)\) denote the subproblem for the search interval \([i, j]\).

Starting with the original problem \(f(0, n-1)\), perform binary search as follows.

  1. Calculate the midpoint \(m\) of the search interval \([i, j]\) and use it to eliminate half the interval.
  2. Recursively solve the subproblem of half the size, either \(f(i, m-1)\) or \(f(m+1, j)\).
  3. Repeat steps 1. and 2., returning when target is found or the interval is empty.

Figure 12-4 shows the divide-and-conquer process for finding \(6\) in an array using binary search.

Figure 12-4   Divide-and-conquer process for binary search

In the implementation, we define a recursive function dfs() to solve \(f(i, j)\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_recur.py
def dfs(nums: list[int], target: int, i: int, j: int) -> int:
    """Binary search: problem f(i, j)"""
    # If the interval is empty, the target is absent; return -1
    if i > j:
        return -1
    # Calculate the midpoint index m
    m = (i + j) // 2
    if nums[m] < target:
        # Recurse on subproblem f(m+1, j)
        return dfs(nums, target, m + 1, j)
    elif nums[m] > target:
        # Recurse on subproblem f(i, m-1)
        return dfs(nums, target, i, m - 1)
    else:
        # The target element was found; return its index
        return m

def binary_search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    """Binary search"""
    n = len(nums)
    # Solve problem f(0, n-1)
    return dfs(nums, target, 0, n - 1)

items.title: 12.3   Building a binary tree
items.text:
Question

Given a binary tree's preorder traversal preorder and inorder traversal inorder, reconstruct the tree and return its root node. Assume that all node values are distinct, as shown in Figure 12-5.

Figure 12-5   Example input for reconstructing a binary tree

items.title: 1.   Identifying a divide-and-conquer problem
items.text:
Reconstructing a binary tree from preorder and inorder is a typical divide-and-conquer problem.

  • The problem can be divided: We can split the original problem into two subproblems, building the left subtree and building the right subtree, plus one operation: initializing the root node. Each subtree can be divided in the same way into smaller subtrees, until we reach the smallest subproblem, an empty subtree.
  • The subproblems are independent: The left and right subtrees are independent and do not overlap. To build the left subtree, we need only the portions of the preorder and inorder traversals corresponding to it. The same applies to the right subtree.
  • The subproblem solutions can be combined: Once we have built the left and right subtrees, we can attach them to the root to obtain the solution to the original problem.

items.title: 2.   Dividing the subtrees
items.text:
The analysis above shows that divide and conquer applies, but how do we use preorder and inorder to separate the left and right subtrees?

By definition, both preorder and inorder consist of three parts.

  • Preorder: [ root | left subtree | right subtree ]. For the tree above, this is [ 3 | 9 | 2 1 7 ].
  • Inorder: [ left subtree | root | right subtree ]. For the tree above, this is [ 9 | 3 | 1 2 7 ].

Using the example above, we can divide the traversals with the steps shown in Figure 12-6.

  1. The first element in the preorder traversal, 3, is the root value.
  2. Find the index of root value 3 in inorder, then use it to divide inorder into [ 9 | 3 | 1 2 7 ].
  3. This division of inorder tells us that the left and right subtrees have 1 and 3 nodes, respectively, allowing us to divide preorder into [ 3 | 9 | 2 1 7 ].

Figure 12-6   Separating subtrees in preorder and inorder traversals

items.title: 3.   Describing subtree intervals with variables
items.text:
Using this method, we have identified the index intervals for the root, left subtree, and right subtree in preorder and inorder. We need a few pointer variables to describe these intervals.

  • Let \(i\) be the index of the current tree's root in preorder.
  • Let \(m\) be the index of the current tree's root in inorder.
  • Let \([l, r]\) be the interval occupied by the current tree in inorder.

As shown in Table 12-1, these variables describe the root index in preorder and each subtree's interval in inorder.

Table 12-1   Root and subtree indices in preorder and inorder traversals

Root index in preorder Subtree interval in inorder Current tree \(i\) \([l, r]\) Left subtree \(i + 1\) \([l, m-1]\) Right subtree \(i + 1 + (m - l)\) \([m+1, r]\)

The term \((m-l)\) in the right subtree's root index is the number of nodes in the left subtree. Figure 12-7 helps illustrate this.

Figure 12-7   Index intervals for the root and the left and right subtrees

items.title: 4.   Code implementation
items.text:
To find \(m\) efficiently, we use a hash table hmap mapping each element of inorder to its index:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby build_tree.py
def dfs(
    preorder: list[int],
    inorder_map: dict[int, int],
    i: int,
    l: int,
    r: int,
) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Build a binary tree: divide and conquer"""
    # Stop when the subtree interval is empty
    if r - l < 0:
        return None
    # Initialize the root node
    root = TreeNode(preorder[i])
    # Look up m to separate the left and right subtrees
    m = inorder_map[preorder[i]]
    # Subproblem: build the left subtree
    root.left = dfs(preorder, inorder_map, i + 1, l, m - 1)
    # Subproblem: build the right subtree
    root.right = dfs(preorder, inorder_map, i + 1 + m - l, m + 1, r)
    # Return the root node
    return root

def build_tree(preorder: list[int], inorder: list[int]) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Build a binary tree"""
    # Initialize a hash table mapping each element in inorder to its index
    inorder_map = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(inorder)}
    root = dfs(preorder, inorder_map, 0, 0, len(inorder) - 1)
    return root

    // Stop when the subtree interval is empty
    if (r - l < 0)

For a tree with \(n\) nodes, initializing each node (executing one call to dfs()) takes \(O(1)\) time. The overall time complexity is therefore \(O(n)\).

The hash table maps inorder elements to indices, requiring \(O(n)\) space. In the worst case, the binary tree degenerates into a linked list, and the recursion depth reaches \(n\), using \(O(n)\) space for stack frames. The overall space complexity is therefore \(O(n)\).

items.title: 12.1   Divide and conquer
items.text:
Divide and conquer is a fundamental and widely used algorithmic strategy. Usually implemented recursively, it has two stages: dividing the problem and combining its solutions.

  1. Divide (the partitioning stage): Recursively split the original problem into two or more subproblems until the smallest subproblems are reached.
  2. Conquer (the combining stage): Starting with the known solutions to the smallest subproblems, combine solutions from the bottom up to construct the solution to the original problem.

As shown in Figure 12-1, merge sort is a classic application of divide and conquer.

  1. Divide: Recursively split the original array (the original problem) into two subarrays (subproblems) until each subarray contains just one element (the smallest subproblem).
  2. Conquer: Merge the sorted subarrays (subproblem solutions) from the bottom up to obtain the sorted original array (the solution to the original problem).

Figure 12-1   Divide-and-conquer strategy in merge sort

items.title: 12.1.1   Recognizing divide-and-conquer problems
items.text:
The following criteria usually help determine whether divide and conquer is suitable for a problem.

  1. The problem can be divided: The original problem can be split into smaller, similar subproblems, which can in turn be divided recursively in the same way.
  2. The subproblems are independent: They neither overlap nor depend on one another, so they can be solved independently.
  3. The subproblem solutions can be combined: Combining them yields the solution to the original problem.

Merge sort clearly satisfies all three criteria.

  1. The problem can be divided: Recursively split an array (the original problem) into two subarrays (subproblems).
  2. The subproblems are independent: Each subarray can be sorted independently.
  3. The subproblem solutions can be combined: Merge the two sorted subarrays (subproblem solutions) into a single sorted array (the solution to the original problem).

items.title: 12.1.2   Improving efficiency with divide and conquer
items.text:
Divide and conquer not only solves algorithmic problems effectively, but often improves efficiency as well. Quick sort, merge sort, and heap sort outperform selection sort, bubble sort, and insertion sort because they use this strategy.

This raises a question: why does divide and conquer improve efficiency, and what is the underlying reason? Why is dividing a large problem, solving its subproblems, and combining their solutions faster than solving it directly? We can examine this from two perspectives: the number of operations and parallel computation.

items.title: 1.   Reducing the number of operations
items.text:
Consider bubble sort, which takes \(O(n^2)\) time to sort an array of length \(n\). Suppose we split the array at its midpoint, as shown in Figure 12-2. Splitting takes \(O(n)\) time, sorting each half takes \(O((n / 2)^2)\) time, and merging the halves takes \(O(n)\) time. The total time complexity is:

\[ O(n + (\frac{n}{2})^2 \times 2 + n) = O(\frac{n^2}{2} + 2n) \]

Figure 12-2   Bubble sort before and after dividing the array

Now consider the following inequality, whose left and right sides represent the total operation counts before and after division:

\[ \begin{aligned} n^2 & > \frac{n^2}{2} + 2n \newline n^2 - \frac{n^2}{2} - 2n & > 0 \newline n(n - 4) & > 0 \end{aligned} \]

When \(n > 4\), dividing the array reduces the number of operations and should make sorting faster. The time complexity is still quadratic, \(O(n^2)\); only the constant factor has decreased.

What if we keep splitting each subarray into two at its midpoint until every subarray contains just one element? This is precisely the idea behind merge sort, which takes \(O(n \log n)\) time.

What if we introduce more split points, dividing the original array evenly into \(k\) subarrays? This resembles bucket sort, which is well suited to sorting large amounts of data and can theoretically achieve \(O(n + k)\) time.

items.title: 2.   Using parallel computation
items.text:
The subproblems produced by divide and conquer are independent, so they can usually be solved in parallel. Thus, divide and conquer can both reduce time complexity and help the operating system parallelize the work.

Parallelization is especially effective on multicore or multiprocessor systems. Multiple subproblems can be processed simultaneously, making fuller use of computing resources and substantially reducing total runtime.

For example, in the bucket sort shown in Figure 12-3, a large dataset is evenly distributed among buckets. The sorting tasks for different buckets can then be assigned to different computing units, and their results combined afterward.

Figure 12-3   Parallel computation in bucket sort

items.title: 12.1.3   Common applications of divide and conquer
items.text:
Divide and conquer solves many classic algorithmic problems.

  • Closest pair of points: Divide a set of points into two parts, find the closest pair within each part, then find the closest pair spanning the two parts.
  • Large integer multiplication: Karatsuba's algorithm, for example, breaks multiplication of large integers into several smaller integer multiplications and additions.
  • Matrix multiplication: Strassen's algorithm, for example, breaks multiplication of large matrices into multiple smaller matrix multiplications and additions.
  • Tower of Hanoi: This problem can be solved recursively and is a classic application of divide and conquer.
  • Counting inversions: In a sequence, an earlier number and a later number form an inversion if the earlier one is larger. Inversions can be counted using divide and conquer with merge sort.

Divide and conquer is also widely used in designing algorithms and data structures.

  • Binary search: Split a sorted array at its middle index, compare the middle element with the target to decide which half to discard, then repeat the same operation on the remaining interval.
  • Merge sort: This was described at the start of the section.
  • Quick sort: Choose a pivot and divide the array into two subarrays, one containing elements smaller than the pivot and the other containing larger elements. Repeat the division on both parts until each subarray contains just one element.
  • Bucket sort: Distribute data among multiple buckets, sort the elements in each bucket, and then take the elements from the buckets in order to obtain a sorted array.
  • Trees: Operations such as search, insertion, and deletion in binary search trees, AVL trees, red-black trees, B-trees, and B+ trees can be viewed as applications of divide and conquer.
  • Heaps: A heap is a special kind of complete binary tree. Its operations, such as insertion, deletion, and heapification, implicitly use divide and conquer.
  • Hash tables: Although hash tables do not directly use divide and conquer, some collision-handling strategies use it indirectly. For example, long linked lists in separate chaining may be converted into red-black trees to speed up lookups.

As we can see, divide and conquer quietly underlies many algorithms and data structures, often without being explicitly named.

items.title: 1.   Which tasks suit divide and conquer?
items.text:
A student wants to solve the following tasks by splitting each in half, solving the halves separately, and combining the results. For each task, decide whether divide and conquer is suitable, is possible but does not reduce the total work, or is unsuitable because the halves cannot be solved independently. Explain.

  1. Sort an unsorted array.
  2. Find the maximum value in an array.
  3. Execute a sequence of stack operations push(x) and pop() in order, outputting the element returned by each pop().
Reference answer
  1. Suitable: split in half, sort the halves independently, and merge in \(O(n)\) time. This is exactly merge sort.
  2. Possible, but without reducing the total work: the two halves must still examine all \(n\) elements between them, taking \(O(n)\) time, just like a direct scan.
  3. The halves cannot be solved independently: the stack contents at the start of the second half depend on the results of the first half. The second half therefore cannot run independently of the first half's result.

items.text:

    if n % 2 == 0:
        return half * half
    return half * half * x

Run it with x = 3 and n = 5:

  1. What values does n take in successive recursive calls?
  2. Starting with the deepest call, what value does each call return?
  3. Why should the recursive result be saved in half instead of making the same recursive call on each side of the multiplication?
Reference answer

  1. The parameter follows 5 → 2 → 1 → 0, halving the exponent each time until the base case is reached.

  2. When n = 0, the return value is 1. When n = 1, it is \(1×1×3=3\). When n = 2, it is \(3×3=9\); when n = 5, it is \(9×9×3=243\).

  3. Calling the same subproblem on both sides of the multiplication repeats exactly the same computation. Saving the result in half means each level makes only one recursive call, with recursion depth approximately \(\log n\). Making two calls would cause substantial repeated computation.

items.title: 3.   Splitting traversal sequences into left and right subtrees
items.text:
A binary tree with distinct node values has these preorder and inorder traversals:

  • Preorder: [A, B, D, E, C]
  • Inorder: [D, B, E, A, C]

Split only at the root level; there is no need to recurse further or draw the entire tree.

  1. What is the root node?
  2. Which parts of the inorder sequence belong to the left and right subtrees?
  3. Which parts of the preorder sequence belong to the left and right subtrees? What are the root's immediate children?
Reference answer

  1. The first node in preorder is the root, so the root is A.

  2. A splits the inorder sequence into two parts: [D, B, E] for the left subtree and [C] for the right subtree.

  3. The left subtree has three nodes, so the three preorder elements after root A belong to the left subtree: [B, D, E]. The remaining [C] belongs to the right subtree. Thus, the root's left child is B, and its right child is C.

items.title: 1.   Fast exponentiation
items.text:
Given a real number x and an integer n, compute \(x^n\) without calling a built-in power function. Use recursive divide and conquer: halve the exponent at each step and reuse the computed subproblem result. For this problem, \(x^0=1\), including when x = 0. When n < 0, x != 0 is guaranteed, and the answer can be expressed as \((1/x)^{-n}\).

Hints
  1. When n is 0, the answer is 1.
  2. After computing x to the power n // 2, save it in half instead of making the recursive call a second time.
  3. When n < 0, first replace x with 1 / x and n with -n. In C++ or Java, you can convert n to a 64-bit integer first to avoid overflow when negating the smallest 32-bit integer.

LeetCode

items.title: 12.4   Tower of Hanoi
items.text:
In merge sort and binary tree reconstruction, we divided the original problem into two subproblems, each half its size. The Tower of Hanoi uses a different division strategy.

Question

Given three rods called A, B, and C, initially rod A holds \(n\) disks arranged from smallest at the top to largest at the bottom. Move all \(n\) disks to rod C while preserving their order, as shown in Figure 12-10. The following rules apply.

  1. A disk can only be removed from the top of one rod and placed on top of another.
  2. Only one disk may be moved at a time.
  3. A smaller disk must always be above a larger disk.

Figure 12-10   Example of the Tower of Hanoi

Let \(f(i)\) denote a Tower of Hanoi problem of size \(i\). For example, \(f(3)\) means moving \(3\) disks from A to C.

items.title: 1.   Considering the base cases
items.text:
For \(f(1)\), with just one disk, simply move it directly from A to C, as shown in Figure 12-11.

<1><2>

Figure 12-11   Solution for a problem of size 1

For \(f(2)\), with two disks, we need to use B because the smaller disk must remain above the larger one, as shown in Figure 12-12.

  1. Move the smaller top disk from A to B.
  2. Move the larger disk from A to C.
  3. Move the smaller disk from B to C.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 12-12   Solution for a problem of size 2

We can summarize the solution to \(f(2)\) as moving two disks from A to C using B. Here, C is the destination rod and B is the auxiliary rod.

items.title: 2.   Dividing the problem
items.text:
For \(f(3)\), with three disks, the situation is a little more complicated.

Since we know how to solve \(f(1)\) and \(f(2)\), we can use divide and conquer: treat the top two disks on A as a group and follow the steps in Figure 12-13. This moves all three disks from A to C.

  1. Use B as the destination and C as the auxiliary rod to move two disks from A to B.
  2. Move the remaining disk directly from A to C.
  3. Use C as the destination and A as the auxiliary rod to move two disks from B to C.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 12-13   Solution for a problem of size 3

In essence, we have divided \(f(3)\) into two \(f(2)\) subproblems and one \(f(1)\) subproblem. Solving these three subproblems in order solves the original problem. This shows that the subproblems are independent and their solutions can be combined.

We can now state the divide-and-conquer strategy for the Tower of Hanoi, illustrated in Figure 12-14: divide \(f(n)\) into two subproblems \(f(n-1)\) and one subproblem \(f(1)\), then solve them in this order.

  1. Move \(n-1\) disks from A to B using C.
  2. Move the remaining \(1\) disk directly from A to C.
  3. Move \(n-1\) disks from B to C using A.

Each of the two \(f(n-1)\) subproblems can be divided recursively in the same way until we reach the smallest subproblem, \(f(1)\). The solution to \(f(1)\) is a single move.

Figure 12-14   Divide-and-conquer strategy for the Tower of Hanoi

items.title: 3.   Code implementation
items.text:
We define a recursive function dfs(i, src, buf, tar) that moves the top \(i\) disks from rod src to destination rod tar using auxiliary rod buf:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby hanota.py
def move(src: list[int], tar: list[int]):
    """Move one disk"""
    # Take a disk from the top of src
    pan = src.pop()
    # Place the disk on top of tar
    tar.append(pan)

def dfs(i: int, src: list[int], buf: list[int], tar: list[int]):
    """Solve the Tower of Hanoi problem f(i)"""
    # If this subproblem has only one disk to move, move it directly from src to tar
    if i == 1:
        move(src, tar)
        return
    # Subproblem f(i-1): move the top i-1 disks from src to buf using tar
    dfs(i - 1, src, tar, buf)
    # Subproblem f(1): move the remaining disk of this subproblem from src to tar
    move(src, tar)
    # Subproblem f(i-1): move the top i-1 disks from buf to tar using src
    dfs(i - 1, buf, src, tar)

def solve_hanota(A: list[int], B: list[int], C: list[int]):
    """Solve the Tower of Hanoi problem"""
    n = len(A)
    # Move the top n disks from A to C using B
    dfs(n, A, B, C)

Quote

The Tower of Hanoi comes from an ancient legend. In a temple in ancient India, monks had three tall diamond rods and \(64\) gold disks of different sizes. They continually moved the disks, believing that the world would end when the last disk was placed in its correct position.

Even at one move per second, however, this would take about \(2^{64} \approx 1.84×10^{19}\) seconds, or roughly \(585\) billion years, far longer than current estimates of the age of the universe. If the legend is true, we should have little reason to worry about the end of the world.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Divide and conquer is a common algorithm design strategy with two stages: dividing the problem and combining solutions. It is usually implemented recursively.
  • To recognize a divide-and-conquer problem, ask whether it can be divided, whether the subproblems are independent, and whether their solutions can be combined.
  • Merge sort is a classic example. It recursively divides an array into two equally sized subarrays until each contains one element, then merges them level by level to complete the sort.
  • Divide and conquer often improves efficiency by reducing the number of operations and making it easier to parallelize the work.
  • Divide and conquer solves many algorithmic problems and appears widely in the design of data structures and algorithms.
  • Adaptive search is more efficient than brute-force search. Search algorithms with \(O(\log n)\) time complexity are usually based on divide and conquer.
  • Binary search is another classic example, with no step for combining subproblem solutions. It can be implemented through recursive divide and conquer.
  • Reconstructing a binary tree can be divided into building its left and right subtrees. This is achieved by partitioning index intervals in the preorder and inorder traversals.
  • A Tower of Hanoi problem of size \(n\) can be divided into two subproblems of size \(n-1\) and one of size \(1\). Solving these three subproblems in order solves the original problem.

items.text:
Abstract

Streams flow into rivers, and rivers flow into the sea.

Dynamic programming brings together solutions to small problems to answer a larger one, guiding us step by step to the other shore.

items.title: 14.2   Properties of dynamic programming problems
items.text:
The previous section showed how dynamic programming solves a problem by decomposing it into subproblems. Decomposition is a general algorithmic idea, but divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and backtracking use it differently.

  • Divide and conquer recursively splits a problem into independent subproblems until the smallest ones are reached, then combines their solutions as the recursion returns to solve the original problem.
  • Dynamic programming also decomposes problems recursively. Its main difference from divide and conquer is that its subproblems depend on one another, and many overlapping subproblems appear during decomposition.
  • Backtracking enumerates possible solutions by trying choices and undoing them, using pruning to avoid unnecessary branches. A solution consists of a sequence of decisions, and the prefix before each decision can be viewed as a subproblem.

Dynamic programming is often used for optimization problems. Besides overlapping subproblems, these problems have two key properties: optimal substructure and the no-aftereffect property.

items.title: 14.2.1   Optimal substructure
items.text:
Let's modify the climbing stairs problem slightly to illustrate optimal substructure more clearly.

Minimum cost to climb stairs

Given a staircase, you can climb \(1\) or \(2\) steps at a time. Each step has a nonnegative integer indicating the cost paid on that step. A nonnegative integer array \(cost\) gives the costs: \(cost[i]\) is the cost of step \(i\), and \(cost[0]\) refers to the ground (the starting point). What is the minimum cost of reaching the top?

As shown in Figure 14-6, if steps \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\) cost \(1\), \(10\), and \(1\), respectively, the minimum cost of reaching step \(3\) from the ground is \(2\).

Figure 14-6   Minimum cost of reaching step 3

Let \(dp[i]\) be the total cost of reaching step \(i\). Since step \(i\) can only be reached from step \(i - 1\) or \(i - 2\), \(dp[i]\) must be either \(dp[i - 1] + cost[i]\) or \(dp[i - 2] + cost[i]\). To minimize the cost, choose the smaller of the two:

\[ dp[i] = \min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]) + cost[i] \]

This introduces the meaning of optimal substructure: an optimal solution to the original problem is constructed from optimal solutions to its subproblems.

This problem clearly has optimal substructure: choose the better of \(dp[i-1]\) and \(dp[i-2]\) and use it to construct the optimal solution \(dp[i]\).

Does the climbing stairs problem from the previous section also have optimal substructure? Its goal is to count solutions, so it seems to be a counting problem. But rephrase the goal as finding the maximum number of solutions, and although the problem remains equivalent, optimal substructure becomes apparent: the maximum number of ways to reach step \(n\) is the sum of the maximum numbers for steps \(n-1\) and \(n-2\). The interpretation of optimal substructure is therefore flexible and can vary by problem.

The state transition equation, together with the initial states \(dp[1] = cost[1]\) and \(dp[2] = cost[2]\), gives the following dynamic programming code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_cost_climbing_stairs_dp.py
def min_cost_climbing_stairs_dp(cost: list[int]) -> int:
    """Minimum cost to climb stairs: dynamic programming"""
    n = len(cost) - 1
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return cost[n]
    # Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)

items.title: 14.2.2   No-aftereffect property
items.text:
The no-aftereffect property is central to effective dynamic programming: given a fully specified state, its future depends only on that state, not on the sequence of states that led to it.

In the climbing stairs problem, state \(i\) can lead to \(i+1\) or \(i+2\), corresponding to moves of \(1\) or \(2\) steps. Neither choice requires us to consider states before \(i\): they do not affect the future of state \(i\).

Adding a constraint changes the situation.

Climbing stairs with a constraint

Given a staircase with \(n\) steps, you may climb \(1\) or \(2\) steps at a time, but may not make two consecutive moves of \(1\) step. How many ways are there to reach the top?

As shown in Figure 14-8, only \(2\) ways remain to reach step \(3\): taking \(1\) step three times in a row violates the constraint and is discarded.

Figure 14-8   Number of ways to reach step 3 with the constraint

If the previous move climbed \(1\) step, the next must climb \(2\) steps. Thus, the next choice cannot be determined by the current state (the current step number) alone; it also depends on the preceding state (the previous step number).

The no-aftereffect property no longer holds with this state definition, and \(dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]\) is no longer valid. Using \(dp[i-1]\) means taking \(1\) step now, but it includes many ways in which the preceding move also took \(1\) step. We cannot simply add all of \(dp[i-1]\) to \(dp[i]\) without violating the constraint.

We therefore expand the state definition: state \([i, j]\) means we are on step \(i\) and the previous move climbed \(j\) steps, where \(j \in \{1, 2\}\). This distinguishes whether the preceding move climbed \(1\) or \(2\) steps, allowing us to determine how the current state could have been reached.

  • If the previous move climbed \(1\) step, the move before it must have climbed \(2\) steps. Thus, \(dp[i, 1]\) can only come from \(dp[i-1, 2]\).
  • If the previous move climbed \(2\) steps, the move before it could have climbed \(1\) or \(2\) steps. Thus, \(dp[i, 2]\) can come from \(dp[i-2, 1]\) or \(dp[i-2, 2]\).

As shown in Figure 14-9, \(dp[i, j]\) now counts the ways to reach state \([i, j]\). The state transition equations are:

\[ \begin{cases} dp[i, 1] = dp[i-1, 2] \\ dp[i, 2] = dp[i-2, 1] + dp[i-2, 2] \end{cases} \]

Figure 14-9   Recurrence with the constraint

Finally, return \(dp[n, 1] + dp[n, 2]\), the total number of ways to reach step \(n\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_constraint_dp.py
def climbing_stairs_constraint_dp(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs with constraints: dynamic programming"""
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return 1
    # Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions
    dp = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # Initial states: set the solutions to the smallest subproblems
    dp[1][1], dp[1][2] = 1, 0
    dp[2][1], dp[2][2] = 0, 1
    # State transitions: solve progressively larger subproblems using smaller ones
    for i in range(3, n + 1):
        dp[i][1] = dp[i - 1][2]
        dp[i][2] = dp[i - 2][1] + dp[i - 2][2]
    return dp[n][1] + dp[n][2]

  List<List<int>> dp = List.generate(n + 1, (index) => List.filled(3, 0));
  // Initial states: set the solutions to the smallest subproblems
  dp[1][1] = 1;
  dp[1][2] = 0;
  dp[2][1] = 0;
  dp[2][2] = 1;
  // State transitions: solve progressively larger subproblems using smaller ones
  for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) {
    dp[i][1] = dp[i - 1][2];
    dp[i][2] = dp[i - 2][1] + dp[i - 2][2];
  }
  return dp[n][1] + dp[n][2];
}

In this example, only one preceding state mattered, so expanding the state definition restored the no-aftereffect property. Some problems, however, depend much more strongly on their history.

Climbing stairs that generate obstacles

Given a staircase with \(n\) steps, you may climb \(1\) or \(2\) steps at a time. Whenever you reach step \(i\), the system places an obstacle on step \(2i\), and you may never land on step \(2i\) afterward. For example, if your first two moves land on steps \(2\) and \(3\), then steps \(4\) and \(6\) are blocked for all later moves. How many ways are there to reach the top?

Here, each next move depends on all previous states, because every move places an obstacle higher up and affects future moves. Such problems are often difficult to solve with dynamic programming.

Many complex combinatorial optimization problems, such as the traveling salesperson problem, do not satisfy the no-aftereffect property. For such problems, we often choose other methods, such as heuristic search, genetic algorithms, or reinforcement learning, to obtain useful locally optimal solutions within a limited time.

items.title: 14.3   Solving dynamic programming problems
items.text:
The previous two sections introduced the main properties of dynamic programming problems. We will now explore two practical questions.

  1. How can we recognize a dynamic programming problem?
  2. Where should we start, and what are the steps for solving one?

items.title: 14.3.1   Recognizing the problem
items.text:
In general, a problem is suitable for dynamic programming if it has overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, and the no-aftereffect property. These can be difficult to identify directly from a problem statement, so we usually start with a broader test: could backtracking (exhaustive search) solve it?

Problems suited to backtracking usually fit a decision tree model. They can be represented as a tree in which each node is a decision and each path is a sequence of decisions.

In other words, if a problem has clear choices and a solution is produced through a sequence of them, it fits the decision tree model and can usually be solved by backtracking.

Beyond this, some signs make dynamic programming more promising.

  • The problem asks for an optimum, such as a maximum, minimum, greatest number, or smallest number.
  • States can be represented by a list, a multidimensional matrix, or a tree, and a recurrence relates each state to nearby states.

Other signs make it less promising.

  • The goal is to find all possible solutions rather than an optimal one.
  • The problem explicitly involves permutations or combinations and asks for multiple concrete arrangements.

If a problem fits the decision tree model and has clear positive signs, we can tentatively treat it as a dynamic programming problem and verify that assumption while solving it.

items.title: 14.3.2   Steps for solving the problem
items.text:
The process varies with the problem's nature and difficulty, but usually includes describing the decisions, defining states, creating a \(dp\) table, deriving a state transition equation, and identifying boundary conditions.

To make these steps concrete, we will use the classic minimum path sum problem.

Question

Given an \(n \times m\) grid grid, each cell contains a nonnegative integer representing its cost. A robot starts at the top-left cell and can move one cell down or right at a time until it reaches the bottom-right cell. Return the minimum path sum from the top-left to the bottom-right.

In the example shown in Figure 14-10, the minimum path sum is \(13\).

Figure 14-10   Example input for minimum path sum

Step 1: Identify each decision, define the state, and establish the \(dp\) table

Each decision moves one cell down or right. If the current cell has indices \([i, j]\), the next indices are \([i+1, j]\) or \([i, j+1]\). The state therefore contains two variables, the row and column indices, and is denoted by \([i, j]\).

State \([i, j]\) corresponds to the subproblem of finding the minimum path sum from the starting point \([0, 0]\) to \([i, j]\). Its solution is \(dp[i, j]\).

This gives the two-dimensional \(dp\) matrix shown in Figure 14-11, with the same dimensions as the input \(grid\).

Figure 14-11   State definition and dp table

Note

Dynamic programming and backtracking can be described as sequences of decisions. A state consists of the decision variables and should contain every variable needed to describe progress, with enough information to derive the next state.

Each state corresponds to a subproblem. A \(dp\) table stores the solutions to all subproblems, with one dimension of the \(dp\) table for each independent state variable. In essence, the \(dp\) table maps states to subproblem solutions.

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the state transition equation

State \([i, j]\) can only be reached from the cell above, \([i-1, j]\), or the cell to the left, \([i, j-1]\). The optimal substructure is therefore that the minimum path sum to \([i, j]\) is determined by the smaller of the minimum path sums to \([i, j-1]\) and \([i-1, j]\).

This gives the state transition equation illustrated in Figure 14-12:

\[ dp[i, j] = \min(dp[i-1, j], dp[i, j-1]) + grid[i, j] \]

Figure 14-12   Optimal substructure and state transition equation

Note

Using the defined \(dp\) table, examine the relationship between the original problem and its subproblems. Find how to construct an optimal solution from optimal subproblem solutions: this is the optimal substructure.

Once we identify optimal substructure, we can use it to build the state transition equation.

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and evaluation order

A state in the first row can only come from its left, and a state in the first column can only come from above. Thus, the first row \(i = 0\) and first column \(j = 0\) define the boundary conditions.

As shown in Figure 14-13, each cell depends on the cells to its left and above. We therefore traverse the matrix with an outer loop over rows and an inner loop over columns.

Figure 14-13   Boundary conditions and evaluation order

Note

Boundary conditions initialize the \(dp\) table in dynamic programming and support pruning in search.

The key to choosing an evaluation order is ensuring that all smaller subproblems needed by the current state have already been solved correctly.

We could now write the dynamic programming solution directly. However, decomposing a problem is a top-down way of thinking, so implementing "brute-force search \(\rightarrow\) memoized search \(\rightarrow\) dynamic programming" often follows our reasoning more naturally.

items.title: 1.   Method 1: Brute-force search
items.text:
Starting from \([i, j]\), recursively decompose the problem into smaller states \([i-1, j]\) and \([i, j-1]\). The recursive function has the following elements.

  • Parameters: The state \([i, j]\).
  • Return value: The minimum path sum \(dp[i, j]\) from \([0, 0]\) to \([i, j]\).
  • Base case: When \(i = 0\) and \(j = 0\), return \(grid[0, 0]\).
  • Pruning: If \(i < 0\) or \(j < 0\), the indices are out of bounds. Return cost \(+\infty\) to mark the path as infeasible.

The implementation is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dfs(grid: list[list[int]], i: int, j: int) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum: brute-force search"""
    # Stop searching at the top-left cell
    if i == 0 and j == 0:
        return grid[0][0]
    # If a row or column index is out of bounds, return a cost of +∞
    if i < 0 or j < 0:
        return inf
    # Calculate the minimum path costs from the top-left corner to (i-1, j) and (i, j-1)
    up = min_path_sum_dfs(grid, i - 1, j)
    left = min_path_sum_dfs(grid, i, j - 1)
    # Return the minimum path cost from the top-left corner to (i, j)
    return min(left, up) + grid[i][j]

/* Minimum path sum: brute-force search */

    // Stop searching at the top-left cell
    if (i == 0 && j == 0) {

    }
    // If a row or column index is out of bounds, return a cost of +∞
    if (i < 0 || j < 0) {

    }

    return min(left, up) != INT_MAX ? min(left, up) + grid[i][j] : INT_MAX;
}

Figure 14-14 shows the recursion tree rooted at \(dp[2, 1]\). It includes overlapping subproblems, whose number grows rapidly with the size of grid.

The underlying reason for overlapping subproblems is that multiple paths can reach the same cell from the top-left corner.

Figure 14-14   Recursion tree for brute-force search

Each state offers two choices, down and right, and reaching the bottom-right corner takes \(m + n - 2\) moves. The worst-case time complexity is therefore \(O(2^{m + n})\), where \(n\) and \(m\) are the numbers of rows and columns. This estimate ignores the grid boundaries, where only one choice remains, so the actual number of paths is smaller.

items.title: 2.   Method 2: Memoized search
items.text:
Introduce a memoization table mem with the same dimensions as grid to store subproblem solutions and prune repeated subproblems:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dfs_mem(
    grid: list[list[int]], mem: list[list[int]], i: int, j: int
) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum: memoized search"""
    # Stop searching at the top-left cell
    if i == 0 and j == 0:
        return grid[0][0]
    # If a row or column index is out of bounds, return a cost of +∞
    if i < 0 or j < 0:
        return inf
    # If a result has already been recorded, return it directly
    if mem[i][j] != -1:
        return mem[i][j]
    # Minimum path costs to the cells on the left and above
    up = min_path_sum_dfs_mem(grid, mem, i - 1, j)
    left = min_path_sum_dfs_mem(grid, mem, i, j - 1)
    # Record and return the minimum path cost from the top-left corner to (i, j)
    mem[i][j] = min(left, up) + grid[i][j]
    return mem[i][j]

    mem[i][j] = int(math.Min(float64(left), float64(up))) + grid[i][j]
    return mem[i][j]
}

  # If a row or column index is out of bounds, return a cost of +∞

  mem[i][j] = [left, up].min + grid[i][j]

items.title: 3.   Method 3: Dynamic programming
items.text:
The following code implements dynamic programming iteratively:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dp(grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum: dynamic programming"""
    n, m = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * m for _ in range(n)]
    dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]
    # State transitions: first row
    for j in range(1, m):
        dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 1] + grid[0][j]
    # State transitions: first column
    for i in range(1, n):
        dp[i][0] = dp[i - 1][0] + grid[i][0]
    # State transitions: remaining rows and columns
    for i in range(1, n):
        for j in range(1, m):
            dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j - 1], dp[i - 1][j]) + grid[i][j]
    return dp[n - 1][m - 1]

items.title: 4.   Space optimization
items.text:
Each cell depends only on the cells to its left and above, so a single-row array is enough to represent the \(dp\) table.

Because dp stores only one row of states, we cannot initialize the entire first column in advance. Instead, update its entry when processing each row:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dp_comp(grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum: space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n, m = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * m
    # State transitions: first row
    dp[0] = grid[0][0]
    for j in range(1, m):
        dp[j] = dp[j - 1] + grid[0][j]
    # State transitions: remaining rows
    for i in range(1, n):
        # State transitions: first column
        dp[0] = dp[0] + grid[i][0]
        # State transitions: remaining columns
        for j in range(1, m):
            dp[j] = min(dp[j - 1], dp[j]) + grid[i][j]
    return dp[m - 1]
