items.title: 14.6   Edit distance problem
items.text:
Edit distance, also called Levenshtein distance, is the minimum number of edits needed to transform one string into another. It is commonly used in information retrieval and natural language processing to measure similarity between sequences.

Question

Given two strings \(s\) and \(t\), return the minimum number of edits needed to transform \(s\) into \(t\).

Three edits are allowed: insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character with any other character.

As shown in Figure 14-27, transforming kitten into sitting takes 3 edits: 2 replacements and 1 insertion. Transforming hello into algo also takes 3 edits: 2 replacements and 1 deletion.

Figure 14-27   Examples of edit distance

Edit distance fits naturally into a decision tree model. Strings are nodes, and each decision (an edit) is an edge.

As shown in Figure 14-28, without restrictions on the edits, each node can have many outgoing edges, one for each possible operation. Thus, many paths can transform hello into algo.

From the decision tree perspective, the goal is to find the shortest path between nodes hello and algo.

Figure 14-28   Edit distance as a decision tree

items.title: 1.   Dynamic programming approach
items.text:
Step 1: Identify each decision, define the state, and establish the \(dp\) table

Each decision applies one edit to string \(s\).

We want each edit to reduce the problem's size so that we can form subproblems. Let the lengths of \(s\) and \(t\) be \(n\) and \(m\). First consider their last characters, \(s[n-1]\) and \(t[m-1]\).

  • If \(s[n-1]\) and \(t[m-1]\) match, skip them and consider \(s[n-2]\) and \(t[m-2]\).
  • If \(s[n-1]\) and \(t[m-1]\) differ, apply an edit to \(s\) (insertion, deletion, or replacement) to match the endings, allowing us to move on to a smaller problem.

Each decision (edit) in \(s\) changes the characters still to be matched in \(s\) and \(t\). The state therefore specifies the \(i\)-th and \(j\)-th characters currently under consideration in \(s\) and \(t\), denoted by \([i, j]\).

State \([i, j]\) represents the subproblem of finding the minimum number of edits needed to transform the first \(i\) characters of \(s\) into the first \(j\) characters of \(t\).

This gives a two-dimensional \(dp\) table of size \((n+1) \times (m+1)\).

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the state transition equation

For subproblem \(dp[i, j]\), the final characters are \(s[i-1]\) and \(t[j-1]\). The three possible edits give the cases shown in Figure 14-29.

  1. Insert \(t[j-1]\) after \(s[i-1]\), leaving subproblem \(dp[i, j-1]\).
  2. Delete \(s[i-1]\), leaving subproblem \(dp[i-1, j]\).
  3. Replace \(s[i-1]\) with \(t[j-1]\), leaving subproblem \(dp[i-1, j-1]\).

Figure 14-29   State transitions for edit distance

The optimal substructure follows: the minimum edit count \(dp[i, j]\) is the smallest of \(dp[i, j-1]\), \(dp[i-1, j]\), and \(dp[i-1, j-1]\), plus \(1\) for the current edit. The state transition equation is:

\[ dp[i, j] = \min(dp[i, j-1], dp[i-1, j], dp[i-1, j-1]) + 1 \]

When \(s[i-1]\) and \(t[j-1]\) match, no edit is needed for the current characters, and the state transition equation becomes:

\[ dp[i, j] = dp[i-1, j-1] \]

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and evaluation order

If both strings are empty, \(0\) edits are needed, so \(dp[0, 0] = 0\). If \(s\) is empty but \(t\) is not, the minimum edit count is the length of \(t\), giving the first row \(dp[0, j] = j\). If \(s\) is nonempty but \(t\) is empty, the count is the length of \(s\), giving the first column \(dp[i, 0] = i\).

The solution \(dp[i, j]\) depends on entries to its left, above, and upper left, so two nested loops can traverse the \(dp\) table in increasing index order.

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
3.   Space optimization
items.text:
The state \(dp[i,j]\) depends on \(dp[i-1, j]\) above, \(dp[i, j-1]\) to the left, and \(dp[i-1, j-1]\) at the upper left. Forward iteration loses \(dp[i-1, j-1]\), while backward iteration cannot compute \(dp[i, j-1]\) in advance. Neither order alone is sufficient.

We can use a variable leftup to preserve the upper-left solution \(dp[i-1, j-1]\), leaving only the left and upper entries to consider. The situation then matches unbounded knapsack, and forward iteration works. The code is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby edit_distance.py
def edit_distance_dp_comp(s: str, t: str) -> int:
    """Edit distance: space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n, m = len(s), len(t)
    dp = [0] * (m + 1)
    # State transitions: first row
    for j in range(1, m + 1):
        dp[j] = j
    # State transitions: remaining rows
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # State transitions: first column
        leftup = dp[0]  # Temporarily store dp[i-1, j-1]
        dp[0] += 1
        # State transitions: remaining columns
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            temp = dp[j]
            if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:
                # If the two characters are equal, skip both of them
                dp[j] = leftup
            else:
                # Minimum edits = the minimum among the insertion, deletion, and replacement subproblems + 1
                dp[j] = min(dp[j - 1], dp[j], leftup) + 1
            leftup = temp  # Update to dp[i-1, j-1] for the next iteration
    return dp[m]

  (1...(m + 1)).each { |j| dp[j] = j }
  # State transitions: remaining rows
  for i in 1...(n + 1)
    # State transitions: first column
    leftup = dp.first # Temporarily store dp[i-1, j-1]
    dp[0] += 1
    # State transitions: remaining columns
    for j in 1...(m + 1)
      temp = dp[j]
      if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]
        # If the two characters are equal, skip both of them
        dp[j] = leftup
      else
        # Minimum edits = the minimum among the insertion, deletion, and replacement subproblems + 1
        dp[j] = [dp[j - 1], dp[j], leftup].min + 1
      end
      leftup = temp # Update to dp[i-1, j-1] for the next iteration
    end
  end
  dp[m]
end

items.title: 1.   When is dynamic programming a good fit?
items.text:
A student says, “Whenever you can write a recurrence relation, you should use dynamic programming.” For each task below, decide whether dynamic programming, backtracking, or a loop or mathematical formula without a dp table is the best fit. Give one key reason for each choice.

  1. Find the minimum number of coins needed to make an amount of 6 using denominations [1, 3, 4]. Each denomination can be used any number of times.
  2. Output all permutations of [1, 2, 3].

  3. Calculate \(1 + 2 + \dots + n\).

    For the task you consider suitable for dynamic programming, also explain what dp[i] represents.

Reference answer

  1. Dynamic programming is a good fit. Let dp[i] be the minimum number of coins needed to make an amount of i. For each coin c whose denomination does not exceed i, consider dp[i-c] + 1 as a candidate answer, then take the minimum of these candidates. Different choices repeatedly lead to the same amounts, and an optimal solution for a larger amount can be built from optimal solutions for smaller amounts. The answer for an amount of 6 is 2: 3 + 3.

  2. Use backtracking. The task requires generating all 6 permutations individually. Backtracking systematically makes a choice, continues the search, then undoes the choice and explores other branches. Whatever method you use, outputting all the permutations requires enumerating them.

  3. A loop or the formula for an arithmetic series is sufficient. Although you can write S(i) = S(i-1) + i, calculating S(i) depends on just one smaller value, S(i-1). Each partial sum needs to be calculated only once, so there are no overlapping subproblems and no need for a dp table. Being able to write a recurrence does not mean you need dynamic programming.

items.title: 2.   How do you calculate a cell in the knapsack table?
items.text:
Consider a 0-1 knapsack problem with item weights wgt = [1, 2, 3], values val = [5, 11, 15], and a knapsack capacity of 4. Here, dp[i][c] is the maximum value obtainable using only the first \(i\) items with a capacity limit of \(c\). The knapsack does not have to be filled exactly.

Calculate just the state dp[3][4]. You are given dp[2][4] = 16 and dp[2][1] = 5.

  1. What is the candidate value if you do not take item 3?
  2. If you take item 3, how much capacity remains, and what is the candidate value?
  3. What should dp[3][4] be? Which items does this solution take?
Reference answer

  1. If you do not take item 3, use the result for the first two items. The candidate value is dp[2][4] = 16.

  2. Item 3 weighs 3, so taking it leaves a capacity of \(4-3=1\). The candidate value is dp[2][1] + 15 = 5 + 15 = 20.

  3. Comparing 16 and 20 gives dp[3][4] = 20. This solution takes items 1 and 3, with a total weight of \(1+3=4\) and a total value of \(5+15=20\).

    Calculating this state illustrates a single “take it or leave it” comparison in the 0-1 knapsack problem.

items.title: 3.   In what order should knapsack capacities be updated?
items.text:
A 0-1 knapsack problem has just one item, with weight 2 and value 5. The knapsack capacity is 4. Each item can be taken at most once, and the initial one-dimensional array is dp = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0].

A student processes this item by updating capacities from 2 to 4:

  • Updating dp[2] gives 5.
  • Updating dp[3] also gives 5.
  • When updating dp[4], the student uses the newly computed dp[2], obtaining dp[4] = 10.
  1. Is dp[4] = 10 correct? Why or why not?
  2. Given that each item can be taken at most once, what should dp[4] be?
  3. When processing each item, should capacities be updated from largest to smallest or from smallest to largest? What problem does this prevent?
Reference answer

  1. The result is incorrect. A value of 10 means taking the item worth 5 twice, which violates the condition that each item can be taken at most once.

  2. The knapsack can contain only this one item, so the correct value of dp[4] is 5.

  3. Update capacities from largest to smallest: 4, then 3, then 2. This ensures that when calculating dp[c], the value read from dp[c-2] is still the result from before the current item was processed. The current item therefore cannot be used more than once in the same round of updates.

items.title: 1.   Counting ways to climb stairs
items.text:
A staircase has n steps. You can climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time and must land exactly on step n. Calculate the number of different ways to climb the staircase. Assume n >= 1; two ways differ only in their sequence of 1-step and 2-step moves. Use a one-dimensional dynamic programming array. For now, do not use the space optimization that retains only two states.

Hints
  1. The final move to step i must be either a 1-step or a 2-step move.
  2. This gives dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].
  3. Handle n = 1 and n = 2 first, then fill the table starting at step 3.

items.text:
You are given arrays wgt and val of equal length. Item i has a positive integer weight wgt[i] and a nonnegative integer value val[i]. The knapsack capacity cap is a nonnegative integer. Each item can be taken at most once. Find the maximum total value that fits in the knapsack without exceeding cap in total weight. Use one-dimensional dynamic programming.

Hints
  1. Initialize an array dp of length cap + 1, where dp[c] is the maximum value obtainable with a capacity limit of c.
  2. When processing item i, compare dp[c] for leaving it out with dp[c-wgt[i]] + val[i] for taking it.
  3. Update capacities from largest to smallest to avoid taking the current item more than once in the same round.

items.title: 14.1   Introduction to dynamic programming
items.text:
Dynamic programming is an important algorithmic paradigm. It breaks a problem into smaller subproblems and stores their solutions to avoid repeated computation, greatly improving time efficiency.

We will start with a classic example, give a brute-force backtracking solution, identify its overlapping subproblems, and gradually derive a more efficient dynamic programming solution.

Climbing stairs

Given a staircase with \(n\) steps, you may climb \(1\) or \(2\) steps at a time. How many ways are there to reach the top?

As shown in Figure 14-1, a staircase with \(3\) steps has \(3\) possible ways to reach the top.

Figure 14-1   Number of ways to reach step 3

The goal is to count solutions, so we can use backtracking to enumerate every possibility. View climbing as a sequence of choices: starting from the ground, choose to climb \(1\) or \(2\) steps each time. Add \(1\) to the count whenever we reach the top, and prune any branch that goes beyond it. The code is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_backtrack.py
def backtrack(choices: list[int], state: int, n: int, res: list[int]) -> int:
    """Backtracking"""
    # When step n is reached, increase the number of ways by 1
    if state == n:
        res[0] += 1
    # Iterate over all choices
    for choice in choices:
        # Prune: do not go beyond step n
        if state + choice > n:
            continue
        # Try: make a choice and update the state
        backtrack(choices, state + choice, n, res)
        # Backtrack

def climbing_stairs_backtrack(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs: backtracking"""
    choices = [1, 2]  # Choose to climb 1 or 2 steps
    state = 0  # Start climbing from step 0
    res = [0]  # Use res[0] to record the number of ways
    backtrack(choices, state, n, res)
    return res[0]

items.title: 14.1.1   Method 1: Brute-force search
items.text:
Backtracking usually does not explicitly decompose the problem. Instead, it treats a solution as a sequence of decisions and searches all possible solutions through trial and pruning.

Let's analyze this problem through decomposition. Let \(dp[i]\) be the number of ways to reach step \(i\). The original problem is \(dp[i]\), and its subproblems include:

\[ dp[i-1], dp[i-2], \dots, dp[2], dp[1] \]

Since each move climbs \(1\) or \(2\) steps, when we stand on step \(i\), we must previously have been on step \(i - 1\) or \(i - 2\). In other words, step \(i\) can only be reached from step \(i -1\) or \(i - 2\).

This gives an important result: the number of ways to reach step \(i - 1\) plus the number of ways to reach step \(i - 2\) equals the number of ways to reach step \(i\). In symbols:

\[ dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] \]

Thus, the subproblems are linked by a recurrence: the solution to the original problem can be constructed from subproblem solutions. Figure 14-2 illustrates this relationship.

Figure 14-2   Recurrence for the number of ways

The recurrence gives a brute-force search solution. Starting at \(dp[n]\), recursively express a larger problem as the sum of two smaller ones until reaching \(dp[1]\) or \(dp[2]\). Their solutions are known: \(dp[1] = 1\) and \(dp[2] = 2\), meaning steps \(1\) and \(2\) can be reached in \(1\) and \(2\) ways, respectively.

Like the standard backtracking code, the following code performs depth-first search, but is more concise:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_dfs.py
def dfs(i: int) -> int:
    """Search"""
    # The values of dp[1] and dp[2] are known; return the corresponding value
    if i == 1 or i == 2:
        return i
    # dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]
    count = dfs(i - 1) + dfs(i - 2)
    return count

def climbing_stairs_dfs(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs: search"""
    return dfs(n)

Figure 14-3 shows the recursion tree for brute-force search. For \(dp[n]\), its depth is \(n\), and the time complexity is \(O(2^n)\). Exponential growth is explosive, so a relatively large \(n\) leads to a very long wait.

Figure 14-3   Recursion tree for climbing stairs

As Figure 14-3 shows, overlapping subproblems cause the exponential time complexity. For example, \(dp[9]\) splits into \(dp[8]\) and \(dp[7]\), while \(dp[8]\) splits into \(dp[7]\) and \(dp[6]\). Both contain \(dp[7]\).

These subproblems in turn contain smaller overlapping subproblems, and the pattern repeats at deeper levels of the recursion tree. Most of the computation is wasted on solving the same subproblems repeatedly.

items.title: 14.1.2   Method 2: Memoized search
items.text:
To improve efficiency, we want every overlapping subproblem to be solved only once. Introduce an array mem to record each solution and prune repeated subproblems during the search.

  1. The first time we calculate \(dp[i]\), store it in mem[i] for later use.
  2. When \(dp[i]\) is needed again, retrieve it directly from mem[i] instead of recomputing it.

The code is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_dfs_mem.py
def dfs(i: int, mem: list[int]) -> int:
    """Memoized search"""
    # The values of dp[1] and dp[2] are known; return the corresponding value
    if i == 1 or i == 2:
        return i
    # If dp[i] has been recorded, return it directly
    if mem[i] != -1:
        return mem[i]
    # dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]
    count = dfs(i - 1, mem) + dfs(i - 2, mem)
    # Record dp[i]
    mem[i] = count
    return count

def climbing_stairs_dfs_mem(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs: memoized search"""
    # mem[i] stores the number of ways to reach step i; -1 means no result has been recorded
    mem = [-1] * (n + 1)
    return dfs(n, mem)

items.title: 14.1.3   Method 3: Dynamic programming
items.text:
Memoized search is a top-down approach: start with the original problem (the root), recursively divide larger subproblems into smaller ones until reaching the smallest subproblems with known solutions (the leaves), then collect their solutions as recursion returns to construct the solution to the original problem.

In contrast, dynamic programming is a bottom-up approach: start with the smallest subproblem solutions and iteratively build solutions to larger subproblems until the original problem is solved.

Because this dynamic programming process does not backtrack, it needs only iterative loops, not recursion. In the following code, the array dp stores subproblem solutions, serving the same role as mem in memoized search:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_dp.py
def climbing_stairs_dp(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs: dynamic programming"""
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return n
    # Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    # Initial states: set the solutions to the smallest subproblems
    dp[1], dp[2] = 1, 2
    # State transitions: solve progressively larger subproblems using smaller ones
    for i in range(3, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]
    return dp[n]

}

Figure 14-5   Dynamic programming for climbing stairs

Like backtracking, dynamic programming uses states to represent stages of solving a problem. Each state corresponds to a subproblem and its locally optimal solution. For climbing stairs, the state is the current step number \(i\).

We can now summarize some common dynamic programming terminology.

  • The array dp is called the dp table, and \(dp[i]\) stores the solution to the subproblem for state \(i\).
  • The states for the smallest subproblems (steps \(1\) and \(2\)) are called the initial states.
  • The recurrence \(dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]\) is called the state transition equation.

items.title: 14.1.4   Space optimization
items.text:
You may have noticed that \(dp[i]\) depends only on \(dp[i-1]\) and \(dp[i-2]\), so we do not need an entire dp array storing every subproblem solution. Two variables updated as we proceed are enough. The code is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_dp.py
def climbing_stairs_dp_comp(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs: space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return n
    a, b = 1, 2
    for _ in range(3, n + 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b

    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) {
        int tmp = b;
        b = a + b;
        a = tmp;
    }
    return b;
}

In dynamic programming, a state often depends on only a limited number of preceding states. We can keep just those needed, reducing the storage dimensions to save memory. This technique is called using rolling variables or a rolling array.

items.title: 14.4   0-1 knapsack problem
items.text:
The knapsack problem is an excellent introduction to dynamic programming and one of its most common problem families. Variants include 0-1 knapsack, unbounded knapsack, and bounded knapsack.

We will begin with the most common variant, 0-1 knapsack.

Question

Given \(n\) items, where item \(i\) has weight \(wgt[i-1]\) and value \(val[i-1]\), and a knapsack of capacity \(cap\), each item may be chosen only once. What is the maximum total value that fits within the capacity?

As shown in Figure 14-17, item numbers \(i\) start at \(1\), while array indices start at \(0\). Item \(i\) therefore has weight \(wgt[i-1]\) and value \(val[i-1]\).

Figure 14-17   Example input for 0-1 knapsack

We can view 0-1 knapsack as \(n\) rounds of decisions, with two choices for each item: leave it out or put it in. It therefore fits the decision tree model.

The objective is to maximize value within a capacity limit, making dynamic programming a promising approach.

Step 1: Identify each decision, define the state, and establish the \(dp\) table

Leaving an item out keeps the available capacity unchanged; putting it in reduces the capacity. The state therefore consists of the current item number \(i\) and capacity \(c\), denoted by \([i, c]\).

State \([i, c]\) represents the subproblem of finding the maximum value obtainable from the first \(i\) items with capacity \(c\), denoted by \(dp[i, c]\).

We seek \(dp[n, cap]\), so we need a two-dimensional \(dp\) table of size \((n+1) \times (cap+1)\).

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the state transition equation

After deciding what to do with item \(i\), the remaining subproblem concerns the first \(i-1\) items. There are two cases.

  • Leave item \(i\) out: Capacity stays unchanged, and the remaining state is \([i-1, c]\).
  • Put item \(i\) in: Capacity decreases by \(wgt[i-1]\), value increases by \(val[i-1]\), and the remaining state is \([i-1, c-wgt[i-1]]\).

This reveals the optimal substructure: the maximum value \(dp[i, c]\) is the larger value obtained by leaving item \(i\) out or putting item \(i\) in. The state transition equation is:

\[ dp[i, c] = \max(dp[i-1, c], dp[i-1, c - wgt[i-1]] + val[i-1]) \]

If the current item's weight \(wgt[i - 1]\) exceeds the remaining capacity \(c\), the only option is to leave it out.

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and evaluation order

With no items or capacity \(0\), the maximum value is \(0\). Thus, the first column \(dp[i, 0]\) and first row \(dp[0, c]\) are both \(0\).

The current state \([i, c]\) depends on \([i-1, c]\) above and \([i-1, c-wgt[i-1]]\) to the upper left, so two nested loops can traverse the \(dp\) table in increasing index order.

We will now implement brute-force search, memoized search, and dynamic programming in that order.

items.title: 1.   Method 1: Brute-force search
items.text:
The search has the following elements.

  • Parameters: The state \([i, c]\).
  • Return value: The subproblem solution \(dp[i, c]\).
  • Base case: If there are no items left, \(i = 0\), or the remaining capacity is \(0\), stop recursion and return value \(0\).
  • Pruning: If the current item is heavier than the remaining capacity, only the choice to leave it out is allowed.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby knapsack.py
def knapsack_dfs(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], i: int, c: int) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack: brute-force search"""
    # If all items have been considered or no capacity remains, return value 0
    if i == 0 or c == 0:
        return 0
    # If the item exceeds the remaining capacity, it must be excluded
    if wgt[i - 1] > c:
        return knapsack_dfs(wgt, val, i - 1, c)
    # Calculate the maximum values obtained by excluding and including item i
    no = knapsack_dfs(wgt, val, i - 1, c)
    yes = knapsack_dfs(wgt, val, i - 1, c - wgt[i - 1]) + val[i - 1]
    # Return the larger value from the two choices
    return max(no, yes)

items.title: 2.   Method 2: Memoized search
items.text:
To solve each overlapping subproblem only once, use a memoization table mem, where mem[i][c] stores \(dp[i, c]\).

With memoization, the time complexity depends on the number of subproblems, giving \(O(n \times cap)\). The code is as follows:

def knapsack_dfs_mem(
    wgt: list[int], val: list[int], mem: list[list[int]], i: int, c: int
) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack: memoized search"""
    # If all items have been considered or no capacity remains, return value 0
    if i == 0 or c == 0:
        return 0
    # If a result has already been recorded, return it directly
    if mem[i][c] != -1:
        return mem[i][c]
    # If the item exceeds the remaining capacity, it must be excluded
    if wgt[i - 1] > c:
        return knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c)
    # Calculate the maximum values obtained by excluding and including item i
    no = knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c)
    yes = knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c - wgt[i - 1]) + val[i - 1]
    # Record and return the larger value from the two choices
    mem[i][c] = max(no, yes)
    return mem[i][c]

fn knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt: &[i32], val: &[i32], mem: &mut Vec<Vec<i32>>, i: usize, c: usize) -> i32 {
    // If all items have been considered or no capacity remains, return value 0
    if i == 0 || c == 0 {
        return 0;
    }
    // If a result has already been recorded, return it directly
    if mem[i][c] != -1 {
        return mem[i][c];
    }
    // If the item exceeds the remaining capacity, it must be excluded
    if wgt[i - 1] > c as i32 {
        return knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c);
    }
    // Calculate the maximum values obtained by excluding and including item i
    let no = knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c);
    let yes = knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c - wgt[i - 1] as usize) + val[i - 1];
    // Record and return the larger value from the two choices
    mem[i][c] = std::cmp::max(no, yes);
    mem[i][c]
}

items.title: 3.   Method 3: Dynamic programming
items.text:
Dynamic programming essentially fills the \(dp\) table using state transitions, as shown in the code below:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby knapsack.py
def knapsack_dp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack: dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * (cap + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # State transitions
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for c in range(1, cap + 1):
            if wgt[i - 1] > c:
                # If item i exceeds the remaining capacity, do not choose it
                dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value obtained by excluding and including item i
                dp[i][c] = max(dp[i - 1][c], dp[i - 1][c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[n][cap]

items.title: 4.   Space optimization
items.text:
Each state depends only on the previous row, so two rolling arrays reduce space complexity from \(O(n \times cap)\) to \(O(cap)\).

Can we go further and use just one array? Each state depends on entries directly above or to the upper left. With one array, when we begin processing row \(i\), it still holds the states from row \(i-1\).

  • With forward iteration, by the time we reach \(dp[i, j]\), the upper-left values \(dp[i-1, 1]\) ~ \(dp[i-1, j-1]\) may have been overwritten, making the transition incorrect.
  • With backward iteration, these values are not overwritten before they are needed, so transitions remain correct.

Figure 14-21 shows one array changing from row \(i = 1\) to row \(i = 2\). Consider how forward and backward iteration differ.

<1><2><3><4><5><6>

Figure 14-21   Space-optimized dynamic programming for 0-1 knapsack

In the implementation, simply remove the first dimension \(i\) from dp and reverse the inner loop:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby knapsack.py
def knapsack_dp_comp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack: space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * (cap + 1)
    # State transitions
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # Traverse in decreasing order
        for c in range(cap, 0, -1):
            if wgt[i - 1] > c:
                # If item i exceeds the remaining capacity, do not choose it
                dp[c] = dp[c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value obtained by excluding and including item i
                dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[cap]

    for c in cap.downto(1)
      if wgt[i - 1] > c
        # If item i exceeds the remaining capacity, do not choose it
        dp[c] = dp[c]
      else
        # Take the larger value obtained by excluding and including item i
        dp[c] = [dp[c], dp[c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1]].max
      end
    end
  end
  dp[cap]
end

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Dynamic programming decomposes problems and stores subproblem solutions to avoid repeated computation and improve efficiency.
  • Without a time limit, every dynamic programming problem can be solved by backtracking (brute-force search). However, the recursion tree contains many overlapping subproblems, making it very inefficient. Memoization stores computed solutions so that each overlapping subproblem is solved only once.
  • Memoized search is a top-down recursive approach, while the corresponding dynamic programming solution works bottom up, like filling a table. Since the current state depends only on certain nearby states, removing a dimension from the \(dp\) table can reduce space complexity.
  • Decomposing a problem into subproblems is a general algorithmic idea with different characteristics in divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and backtracking.
  • Dynamic programming problems have three key properties: overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, and the no-aftereffect property.
  • A problem has optimal substructure if its optimal solution can be constructed from optimal solutions to subproblems.
  • The no-aftereffect property means a state's future depends only on that state, not on the history leading to it. Many combinatorial optimization problems lack this property and cannot be solved quickly with dynamic programming.

Knapsack problems

  • Knapsack is one of the most typical dynamic programming problem families, with variants including 0-1, unbounded, and bounded knapsack.
  • In 0-1 knapsack, the state value is the maximum value obtainable from the first \(i\) items within capacity \(c\). The choices to exclude or include an item reveal optimal substructure and give the state transition equation. After space optimization, backward iteration is necessary because each state depends on entries above and to the upper left, which must not be overwritten prematurely.
  • Unbounded knapsack allows unlimited copies of each item, changing the transition for including an item. Because a state depends on entries directly above and to the left, space optimization requires forward iteration.
  • Coin change is a variant of unbounded knapsack. Minimizing the number of coins instead of maximizing value changes \(\max()\) to \(\min()\) in the transition. Requiring the target amount exactly, rather than staying within a capacity, calls for using \(amt + 1\) to represent an infeasible solution.
  • Coin change II counts combinations instead of minimizing coin count, so the transition replaces \(\min()\) with addition.

Edit distance

  • Edit distance (Levenshtein distance) measures similarity between strings. It is the minimum number of edits needed to turn one string into another, allowing insertion, deletion, and replacement.
  • The edit distance state is the minimum number of edits needed to transform the first \(i\) characters of \(s\) into the first \(j\) characters of \(t\). When \(s[i-1] \ne t[j-1]\), insertion, deletion, and replacement each leave a corresponding subproblem, revealing optimal substructure and the state transition equation. When \(s[i-1] = t[j-1]\), no edit is needed for those characters.
  • Edit distance depends on states above, to the left, and to the upper left, so neither forward nor backward iteration alone works after space optimization. A temporary variable preserves the upper-left state, reducing the situation to one like unbounded knapsack and allowing forward iteration.

items.title: 14.5   Unbounded knapsack problem
items.text: We will now solve another common knapsack variant, unbounded knapsack, and then examine a special case: coin change.

items.title: 14.5.1   Unbounded knapsack
items.text:
Question

Given \(n\) items, where item \(i\) has weight \(wgt[i-1]\) and value \(val[i-1]\), and a knapsack of capacity \(cap\), each item may be chosen repeatedly. What is the maximum value that fits within the capacity? An example is shown in Figure 14-22.

Figure 14-22   Example input for unbounded knapsack

items.title: 1.   Dynamic programming approach
items.text:
Unbounded knapsack is very similar to 0-1 knapsack. The only difference is that there is no limit on how many times an item may be chosen.

  • In 0-1 knapsack, there is only one of each item, so after including item \(i\), we can choose only from the first \(i-1\) items.
  • In unbounded knapsack, each item has an unlimited supply, so after including item \(i\), we can still choose from the first \(i\) items.

For unbounded knapsack, state \([i, c]\) has two cases.

  • Leave item \(i\) out: As in 0-1 knapsack, the remaining state is \([i-1, c]\).
  • Put item \(i\) in: Unlike 0-1 knapsack, the remaining state is \([i, c-wgt[i-1]]\).

The state transition equation becomes:

\[ dp[i, c] = \max(dp[i-1, c], dp[i, c - wgt[i-1]] + val[i-1]) \]

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
items.text:
Compared with 0-1 knapsack, only one \(i-1\) in the transition changes to \(i\); the rest of the code is identical:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby unbounded_knapsack.py
def unbounded_knapsack_dp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """Unbounded knapsack: dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * (cap + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # State transitions
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for c in range(1, cap + 1):
            if wgt[i - 1] > c:
                # If item i exceeds the remaining capacity, do not choose it
                dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value obtained by excluding and including item i
                dp[i][c] = max(dp[i - 1][c], dp[i][c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[n][cap]

items.title: 3.   Space optimization
items.text:
The current state depends on states to its left and above, so after space optimization, each row of the \(dp\) table must be processed in forward order.

This is the opposite of 0-1 knapsack. Use Figure 14-23 to understand the difference.

<1><2><3><4><5><6>

Figure 14-23   Space-optimized dynamic programming for unbounded knapsack

The implementation simply removes the first dimension of dp:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby unbounded_knapsack.py
def unbounded_knapsack_dp_comp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """Unbounded knapsack: space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * (cap + 1)
    # State transitions
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # Traverse in increasing order
        for c in range(1, cap + 1):
            if wgt[i - 1] > c:
                # If item i exceeds the remaining capacity, do not choose it
                dp[c] = dp[c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value obtained by excluding and including item i
                dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[cap]

def unbounded_knapsack_dp_comp(wgt, val, cap)
  n = wgt.length
  # Initialize the dp table
  dp = Array.new(cap + 1, 0)
  # State transitions
  for i in 1...(n + 1)
    # Traverse in increasing order
    for c in 1...(cap + 1)
      if wgt[i -1] > c
        # If item i exceeds the remaining capacity, do not choose it
        dp[c] = dp[c]
      else
        # Take the larger value obtained by excluding and including item i
        dp[c] = [dp[c], dp[c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1]].max
      end
    end
  end
  dp[cap]
end

items.title: 14.5.2   Coin change problem
items.text:
Knapsack represents a broad family of dynamic programming problems, with many variants such as coin change.

Question

Given \(n\) coin denominations, where denomination \(i\) has value \(coins[i - 1]\), and a target amount \(amt\), each denomination may be used repeatedly. What is the minimum number of coins needed to make the target? Return \(-1\) if it cannot be made. An example is shown in Figure 14-24.

Figure 14-24   Example input for coin change

items.title: 1.   Dynamic programming approach
items.text:
Coin change can be viewed as a special case of unbounded knapsack, with the following connections and differences.

  • The two problems can be translated into one another: items correspond to coins, item weights to coin denominations, and knapsack capacity to the target amount.
  • The optimization objectives are opposite: unbounded knapsack maximizes item value, while coin change minimizes the number of coins.
  • Unbounded knapsack must stay within a capacity limit, whereas coin change must reach the target amount exactly.

Step 1: Identify each decision, define the state, and establish the \(dp\) table

State \([i, a]\) represents the subproblem of finding the minimum number of coins needed to make amount \(a\) using the first \(i\) denominations, denoted by \(dp[i, a]\).

The two-dimensional \(dp\) table has size \((n+1) \times (amt+1)\).

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the state transition equation

The state transition differs from unbounded knapsack in two ways.

  • We want a minimum, so replace \(\max()\) with \(\min()\).
  • We optimize the coin count rather than item value, so choosing a coin adds \(+1\).
\[ dp[i, a] = \min(dp[i-1, a], dp[i, a - coins[i-1]] + 1) \]

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and evaluation order

A target amount of \(0\) requires \(0\) coins, so every entry \(dp[i, 0]\) in the first column is \(0\).

With no coins, any target amount \(> 0\) is impossible. To let \(\min()\) recognize and discard these infeasible solutions, represent them by \(+ \infty\): set the first-row entries \(dp[0, a]\) to \(+ \infty\).

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
items.text:
Most programming languages do not provide an integer value for \(+ \infty\), so the maximum int value is used instead. However, the \(+ 1\) in the transition may then overflow.

Instead, use \(amt + 1\) to represent an infeasible solution, since making \(amt\) requires at most \(amt\) coins. Before returning, check whether \(dp[n, amt]\) equals \(amt + 1\). If so, return \(-1\) to indicate that the target cannot be made. The code is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby coin_change.py
def coin_change_dp(coins: list[int], amt: int) -> int:
    """Coin change: dynamic programming"""
    n = len(coins)
    MAX = amt + 1
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * (amt + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # State transitions: first row and first column
    for a in range(1, amt + 1):
        dp[0][a] = MAX
    # State transitions: remaining rows and columns
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for a in range(1, amt + 1):
            if coins[i - 1] > a:
                # If the coin value exceeds the current amount a, do not choose coin i
                dp[i][a] = dp[i - 1][a]
            else:
                # Take the smaller result of not choosing and choosing coin i
                dp[i][a] = min(dp[i - 1][a], dp[i][a - coins[i - 1]] + 1)
    return dp[n][amt] if dp[n][amt] != MAX else -1

int coinChangeDPComp(int coins[], int amt, int coinsSize) {
    int n = coinsSize;
    int MAX = amt + 1;
    // Initialize the dp table
    int *dp = malloc((amt + 1) * sizeof(int));
    for (int j = 1; j <= amt; j++) {
        dp[j] = MAX;
    } 
    dp[0] = 0;

    // State transitions
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        for (int a = 1; a <= amt; a++) {
            if (coins[i - 1] > a) {
                // If the coin exceeds the target amount, do not choose coin i
                dp[a] = dp[a];
            } else {
                // Take the smaller result of not choosing and choosing coin i
                dp[a] = myMin(dp[a], dp[a - coins[i - 1]] + 1);
            }
        }
    }
    int res = dp[amt] != MAX ? dp[amt] : -1;
    // Free memory
    free(dp);
    return res;
}

items.title: 14.5.3   Coin change problem II
items.text:
Question

Given \(n\) coin denominations, where denomination \(i\) has value \(coins[i - 1]\), and a target amount \(amt\), each denomination may be used repeatedly. How many combinations of coins make the target amount? An example is shown in Figure 14-26.

Figure 14-26   Example input for coin change II

items.title: 1.   Dynamic programming approach
items.text:
This time, we count combinations, so the subproblem becomes the number of combinations that make amount \(a\) using the first \(i\) denominations. The \(dp\) table remains a two-dimensional matrix of size \((n+1) \times (amt + 1)\).

The number of combinations for the current state is the sum of those that exclude the current coin and those that include it. The state transition equation is:

\[ dp[i, a] = dp[i-1, a] + dp[i, a - coins[i-1]] \]

A target of \(0\) can be made by choosing no coins, so initialize every first-column entry \(dp[i, 0]\) to \(1\). With no coins, any target \(>0\) is impossible, so the first-row entries \(dp[0, a]\) are \(0\).

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
3.   Space optimization
items.text:
The space optimization is the same: remove the coin dimension:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby coin_change_ii.py
def coin_change_ii_dp_comp(coins: list[int], amt: int) -> int:
    """Coin change II: space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n = len(coins)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * (amt + 1)
    dp[0] = 1
    # State transitions
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # Traverse in increasing order
        for a in range(1, amt + 1):
            if coins[i - 1] > a:
                # If the coin value exceeds the current amount a, do not choose coin i
                dp[a] = dp[a]
            else:
                # Add the numbers of ways without and with coin i
                dp[a] = dp[a] + dp[a - coins[i - 1]]
    return dp[amt]

items.title: Chapter 9.   Graphs
items.text:
Abstract

On the journey of life, we are like nodes joined by countless invisible edges.

Every meeting and parting leaves a unique mark on this vast network.

items.title: 1.   Representing the same graph in two ways
items.text:
An undirected graph has four vertices A, B, C, D and edges A-B, A-C, B-C, C-D.

  1. Write its adjacency list.
  2. Fill in its adjacency matrix using only 0 and 1.
  3. Which representation lets us determine whether A and D are directly connected by inspecting just one stored entry?
  4. If a graph has many vertices but few edges, which representation usually uses less space?
Reference answer

  1. The adjacency list is:

    A: B, C
B: A, C
C: A, B, D
D: C

  2. The adjacency matrix is:

    A B C D A 0 1 1 0 B 1 0 1 0 C 1 1 0 1 D 0 0 1 0

  3. In the adjacency matrix, we can inspect row A, column D directly. This makes it well suited to checking whether any two vertices are directly connected.

  4. When there are many vertices but few edges, an adjacency list records only existing edges. It usually uses less space than an adjacency matrix, which reserves an entry for every pair of vertices.

items.title: 2.   Breadth-first and depth-first traversal orders
items.text:
An undirected graph has vertices A, B, C, D, E and edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, D-E.

Start at A. Whenever several unvisited neighbors are available, choose them in alphabetical order:

  1. Write the breadth-first traversal (BFS) order.
  2. Write the recursive depth-first traversal (DFS) order.
  3. Why must both traversals keep track of vertices already visited?
Reference answer

  1. The BFS order is A, B, C, D, E. It first visits B and C, which are one edge away from A, and then the more distant D and E.

  2. The DFS order is A, B, D, C, E. It proceeds into an unvisited neighbor of the current vertex, first following A → B → D → C. When C has no new neighbors to visit, it returns to D and then visits E.

  3. The graph contains cycles, such as A-B-D-C-A. Without recording visited vertices, traversal could repeatedly follow a cycle through the same vertices and fail to terminate.

items.title: 3.   Can one BFS visit the entire graph?
items.text:
An undirected graph has vertices A, B, C, D, E, F and only the edges A-B, B-C, D-E.

  1. Which vertices can a single BFS starting from A visit?
  2. Based on your answer, has this BFS visited every vertex in the graph? Why?
  3. Suppose we scan all vertices alphabetically and start a new BFS whenever we encounter an unvisited vertex. What are the starting vertices of these searches? How many separate connected parts, or connected components, does the graph have?
Reference answer

  1. Starting from A reaches only A, B, C.

  2. Not every vertex is visited. D, E form another connected part, and F is an isolated vertex. None has a path to A, so they cannot be reached from A.

  3. The three BFS starting vertices are A, D, F, in order, visiting {A, B, C}, {D, E}, and {F}, respectively. Thus, the graph has three connected components.

items.title: 1.   Checking for a path in an undirected graph
items.text:
You are given an undirected graph with \(n\) vertices numbered from \(0\) to \(n-1\). Each entry [u, v] in the array edges represents an undirected edge between vertices u and v.

You are also given a starting vertex source and an ending vertex destination. First build an adjacency list from edges, then use BFS or DFS to determine whether a path exists from source to destination. Return true if it does, or false otherwise. The graph may contain cycles and may be disconnected.

Hints
  1. Add each undirected edge in both directions.
  2. The graph may contain cycles, so keep track of vertices already visited.
  3. Starting from source, return true if you reach destination. Return false if traversal ends without reaching it.

items.title: 9.1   Graphs
items.text:
A graph is a nonlinear data structure made up of vertices and edges. We can represent a graph \(G\) abstractly using a set of vertices \(V\) and a set of edges \(E\). The following example describes a graph with 5 vertices and 7 edges.

\[ egin{aligned} V & = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \} ewline E & = \{ (1,2), (1,3), (1,5), (2,3), (2,4), (2,5), (4,5) \} ewline G & = \{ V, E \} ewline \end{aligned} \]

If we think of vertices as nodes and edges as references (pointers) connecting those nodes, a graph can be viewed as an extension of a linked list. As Figure 9-1 shows, network relationships (graphs) allow more freedom than linear relationships (linked lists) or divide-and-conquer relationships (trees), making them more complex.

Figure 9-1   Relationships between linked lists, trees, and graphs

items.title: 9.1.1   Common graph types and terminology
items.text:
Depending on whether their edges have a direction, graphs are classified as undirected graphs or directed graphs, as shown in Figure 9-2.

  • In an undirected graph, an edge represents a two-way connection between two vertices, such as a friendship on WeChat or QQ.
  • In a directed graph, edges have a direction: the edges \(A \rightarrow B\) and \(A \leftarrow B\) are independent of each other. Examples include following and being followed on Weibo or Douyin.

Figure 9-2   Directed and undirected graphs

Depending on whether all vertices are connected, graphs are classified as connected graphs or disconnected graphs, as shown in Figure 9-3.

  • In a connected graph, every other vertex can be reached from any starting vertex.
  • In a disconnected graph, at least one vertex cannot be reached from a given starting vertex.

Figure 9-3   Connected and disconnected graphs

We can also assign a weight to each edge to obtain a weighted graph, as shown in Figure 9-4. For example, mobile games such as Honor of Kings calculate an affinity score between players based on the time they spend playing together. A weighted graph can represent this network of affinities.

Figure 9-4   Weighted and unweighted graphs

The following terms are commonly used when discussing graphs.

  • Adjacency: Two vertices are adjacent if an edge connects them. In Figure 9-4, the vertices adjacent to vertex 1 are 2, 3, and 5.
  • Path: A sequence of edges followed from vertex A to vertex B is called a path from A to B. In Figure 9-4, the edge sequence 1-5-2-4 forms a path from vertex 1 to vertex 4.
  • Degree: The number of edges incident to a vertex. In a directed graph, the in-degree is the number of edges pointing to the vertex, and the out-degree is the number of edges pointing away from it.

items.title: 9.1.2   Representing a graph
items.text: Two common ways to represent a graph are an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list. We will use undirected graphs in the following examples.

items.title: 1.   Adjacency matrix
items.text:
For a graph with \(n\) vertices, an adjacency matrix represents the graph using an \(n \times n\) matrix. Each row (or column) represents a vertex, and the matrix entries represent edges: \(1\) or \(0\) indicates whether an edge exists between two vertices.

As shown in Figure 9-5, let \(M\) be the adjacency matrix and \(V\) the vertex list. The entry \(M[i, j] = 1\) means that an edge connects vertices \(V[i]\) and \(V[j]\), whereas \(M[i, j] = 0\) means that no edge connects them.

Figure 9-5   Representing a graph with an adjacency matrix

An adjacency matrix has the following properties.

  • In a simple graph, a vertex cannot connect to itself, so the entries on the main diagonal do not represent meaningful connections.
  • In an undirected graph, edges in the two directions are equivalent, so the adjacency matrix is symmetric about its main diagonal.
  • Replacing the \(1\) and \(0\) entries with weights allows the matrix to represent a weighted graph.

With an adjacency matrix, we can access a matrix entry directly to retrieve an edge. Adding, removing, looking up, and modifying edges are therefore efficient, each taking \(O(1)\) time. However, the matrix requires \(O(n^2)\) space and uses a substantial amount of memory.

items.title: 2.   Adjacency list
items.text:
An adjacency list represents a graph using \(n\) linked lists whose nodes represent vertices. The \(i\)-th linked list corresponds to vertex \(i\) and stores all of its adjacent vertices (the vertices connected to it). Figure 9-6 shows an example of a graph stored as an adjacency list.

Figure 9-6   Representing a graph with an adjacency list

An adjacency list stores only edges that actually exist. Since the total number of edges is usually much smaller than \(n^2\), it saves space. However, finding an edge requires traversing a linked list, so lookups are slower than with an adjacency matrix.

As Figure 9-6 shows, an adjacency list closely resembles separate chaining in a hash table, so similar techniques can improve its efficiency. For example, a long linked list can be replaced with an AVL tree or a red-black tree to improve lookup time from \(O(n)\) to \(O(\log n)\). Replacing it with a hash table can further reduce the time complexity to \(O(1)\).

items.title: 9.1.3   Common applications of graphs
items.text:
As shown in Table 9-1, many real-world systems can be modeled as graphs, and their associated problems can be reduced to graph computation problems.

Table 9-1   Common graphs in everyday life

Vertices Edges Graph computation problem Social network Users Friendships Recommending potential friends Subway network Stations Connections between stations Recommending the shortest route Solar system Celestial bodies Gravitational interactions between bodies Calculating planetary orbits

items.title: 9.2   Basic graph operations
items.text: Basic graph operations fall into two categories: operations on edges and operations on vertices. Their implementations differ depending on whether the graph is represented by an adjacency matrix or an adjacency list.

items.title: 9.2.1   Adjacency matrix implementation
items.text:
For an undirected graph with \(n\) vertices, the operations are implemented as shown in Figure 9-7.

  • Add or remove an edge: Modify the corresponding entry in the adjacency matrix directly, taking \(O(1)\) time. Since the graph is undirected, update the edge in both directions.
  • Add a vertex: Append one row and one column to the adjacency matrix and fill them with \(0\), taking \(O(n)\) time.
  • Remove a vertex: Delete the corresponding row and column from the adjacency matrix. The worst case occurs when deleting the first row and column: \((n-1)^2\) entries must be shifted up and to the left, taking \(O(n^2)\) time.
  • Initialize the graph: Given \(n\) vertices, initialize the vertex list vertices of length \(n\) in \(O(n)\) time, then initialize the \(n \times n\) adjacency matrix adjMat in \(O(n^2)\) time.
<1><2><3><4><5>

Figure 9-7   Initializing an adjacency matrix and adding or removing edges and vertices

The following code implements a graph using an adjacency matrix:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby graph_adjacency_matrix.py
class GraphAdjMat:
    """Undirected graph class implemented with an adjacency matrix"""

    def __init__(self, vertices: list[int], edges: list[list[int]]):
        """Constructor"""
        # Vertex list: elements are vertex values, and indices are vertex indices
        self.vertices: list[int] = []
        # Adjacency matrix: row and column indices correspond to vertex indices
        self.adj_mat: list[list[int]] = []
        # Add a vertex
        for val in vertices:
            self.add_vertex(val)
        # Add an edge
        # Note that the entries in edges are vertex indices, corresponding to element indices in vertices
        for e in edges:
            self.add_edge(e[0], e[1])

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the number of vertices"""
        return len(self.vertices)

    def add_vertex(self, val: int):
        """Add a vertex"""
        n = self.size()
        # Append the new vertex value to the vertex list
        self.vertices.append(val)
        # Add a row to the adjacency matrix
        new_row = [0] * n
        self.adj_mat.append(new_row)
        # Add a column to the adjacency matrix
        for row in self.adj_mat:
            row.append(0)

    def remove_vertex(self, index: int):
        """Remove a vertex"""
        if index >= self.size():
            raise IndexError()
        # Remove the vertex at index `index` from the vertex list
        self.vertices.pop(index)
        # Remove row `index` from the adjacency matrix
        self.adj_mat.pop(index)
        # Remove column `index` from the adjacency matrix
        for row in self.adj_mat:
            row.pop(index)

    def add_edge(self, i: int, j: int):
        """Add an edge"""
        # Parameters i and j are element indices in vertices
        # Handle out-of-bounds or equal indices
        if i < 0 or j < 0 or i >= self.size() or j >= self.size() or i == j:
            raise IndexError()
        # For an undirected graph, the adjacency matrix is symmetric about its main diagonal: entries (i, j) and (j, i) are equal
        self.adj_mat[i][j] = 1
        self.adj_mat[j][i] = 1

    def remove_edge(self, i: int, j: int):
        """Remove an edge"""
        # Parameters i and j are element indices in vertices
        # Handle out-of-bounds or equal indices
        if i < 0 or j < 0 or i >= self.size() or j >= self.size() or i == j:
            raise IndexError()
        self.adj_mat[i][j] = 0
        self.adj_mat[j][i] = 0

    def print(self):
        """Print the adjacency matrix"""
        print("Vertex list =", self.vertices)
        print("Adjacency matrix =")

/* Constructor */
GraphAdjMat *newGraphAdjMat() {
    GraphAdjMat *graph = (GraphAdjMat *)malloc(sizeof(GraphAdjMat));
    graph->size = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_SIZE; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < MAX_SIZE; j++) {
            graph->adjMat[i][j] = 0;
        }
    }
    return graph;
}

/* Destructor */
void delGraphAdjMat(GraphAdjMat *graph) {
    free(graph);
}

/* Add a vertex */
void addVertex(GraphAdjMat *graph, int val) {
    if (graph->size == MAX_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "The graph has reached its maximum number of vertices\n");
        return;
    }
    // Add the vertex at index n and set row n and column n to zero
    int n = graph->size;
    graph->vertices[n] = val;
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        graph->adjMat[n][i] = graph->adjMat[i][n] = 0;
    }
    graph->size++;
}

/* Remove a vertex */
void removeVertex(GraphAdjMat *graph, int index) {
    if (index < 0 || index >= graph->size) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Vertex index out of bounds\n");
        return;
    }
    // Remove the vertex at index `index` from the vertex list
    for (int i = index; i < graph->size - 1; i++) {
        graph->vertices[i] = graph->vertices[i + 1];
    }
    // Remove row `index` from the adjacency matrix
    for (int i = index; i < graph->size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < graph->size; j++) {
            graph->adjMat[i][j] = graph->adjMat[i + 1][j];
        }
    }
    // Remove column `index` from the adjacency matrix
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        for (int j = index; j < graph->size - 1; j++) {
            graph->adjMat[i][j] = graph->adjMat[i][j + 1];
        }
    }
    graph->size--;
}

        for (j in 0..<n) {

items.title: 9.2.2   Adjacency list implementation
items.text:
For an undirected graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges, the operations can be implemented as shown in Figure 9-8.

  • Add an edge: Append the edge to the linked list of the corresponding vertex, taking \(O(1)\) time. Since the graph is undirected, add the edge in both directions.
  • Remove an edge: Find and remove the specified edge in the corresponding vertex's linked list, taking \(O(m)\) time. For an undirected graph, remove the edge in both directions.
  • Add a vertex: Add a linked list to the adjacency list with the new vertex as its head node, taking \(O(1)\) time.
  • Remove a vertex: Traverse the entire adjacency list and remove every edge involving the specified vertex, taking \(O(n + m)\) time.
  • Initialize the graph: Create \(n\) vertices and \(2m\) edge entries in the adjacency list, taking \(O(n + m)\) time.
<1><2><3><4><5>

Figure 9-8   Initializing an adjacency list and adding or removing edges and vertices

The following code implements an adjacency list, with these differences from Figure 9-8.

  • To make adding and removing vertices easier and simplify the code, we use lists (dynamic arrays) in place of linked lists.
  • A hash table stores the adjacency list. Each key is a vertex instance, and its value is the list (linked list) of adjacent vertices.

We also use the Vertex class to represent vertices in the adjacency list. If we identified vertices by list indices, as in the adjacency matrix, deleting the vertex at index \(i\) would require traversing the entire adjacency list and subtracting \(1\) from every index greater than \(i\). This would be inefficient. When each vertex is a unique Vertex instance, deleting one vertex requires no changes to the other vertices.

class GraphAdjList:
    """Undirected graph class implemented with an adjacency list"""

    def __init__(self, edges: list[list[Vertex]]):
        """Constructor"""
        # Adjacency list: key is a vertex, value is the list of all its neighbors
        self.adj_list = dict[Vertex, list[Vertex]]()
        # Add all vertices and edges
        for edge in edges:
            self.add_vertex(edge[0])
            self.add_vertex(edge[1])
            self.add_edge(edge[0], edge[1])

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the number of vertices"""
        return len(self.adj_list)

    def add_edge(self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex):
        """Add an edge"""
        if vet1 not in self.adj_list or vet2 not in self.adj_list or vet1 == vet2:
            raise ValueError()
        # Add edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list[vet1].append(vet2)
        self.adj_list[vet2].append(vet1)

    def remove_edge(self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex):
        """Remove an edge"""
        if vet1 not in self.adj_list or vet2 not in self.adj_list or vet1 == vet2:
            raise ValueError()
        # Remove edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list[vet1].remove(vet2)
        self.adj_list[vet2].remove(vet1)

    def add_vertex(self, vet: Vertex):
        """Add a vertex"""
        if vet in self.adj_list:
            return
        # Add a new list to the adjacency list
        self.adj_list[vet] = []

    def remove_vertex(self, vet: Vertex):
        """Remove a vertex"""
        if vet not in self.adj_list:
            raise ValueError()
        # Remove the list corresponding to vertex vet from the adjacency list
        self.adj_list.pop(vet)
        # Traverse the lists of the other vertices and remove all edges incident to vet
        for vertex in self.adj_list:
            if vet in self.adj_list[vertex]:
                self.adj_list[vertex].remove(vet)

    def print(self):
        """Print the adjacency list"""
        print("Adjacency list =")
        for vertex in self.adj_list:
            tmp = [v.val for v in self.adj_list[vertex]]
            print(f"{vertex.val}: {tmp},")

    unordered_map<Vertex *, vector<Vertex *>> adjList;

    /* Remove the specified vertex from the vector */
    void remove(vector<Vertex *> &vec, Vertex *vet) {
        for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i++) {
            if (vec[i] == vet) {
                vec.erase(vec.begin() + i);
                break;
            }
        }
    }

    /* Constructor */
    GraphAdjList(const vector<vector<Vertex *>> &edges) {
        // Add all vertices and edges
        for (const vector<Vertex *> &edge : edges) {
            addVertex(edge[0]);
            addVertex(edge[1]);
            addEdge(edge[0], edge[1]);
        }
    }

    /* Get the number of vertices */
    int size() {
        return adjList.size();
    }

    /* Add an edge */
    void addEdge(Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
        if (!adjList.count(vet1) || !adjList.count(vet2) || vet1 == vet2)
            throw invalid_argument("Invalid vertex");
        // Add edge vet1 - vet2
        adjList[vet1].push_back(vet2);
        adjList[vet2].push_back(vet1);
    }

    /* Remove an edge */
    void removeEdge(Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
        if (!adjList.count(vet1) || !adjList.count(vet2) || vet1 == vet2)
            throw invalid_argument("Invalid vertex");
        // Remove edge vet1 - vet2
        remove(adjList[vet1], vet2);
        remove(adjList[vet2], vet1);
    }

    void addVertex(Vertex *vet) {
        if (adjList.count(vet))
            return;
        // Add a new list to the adjacency list
        adjList[vet] = vector<Vertex *>();

    /* Remove a vertex */
    void removeVertex(Vertex *vet) {
        if (!adjList.count(vet))
            throw invalid_argument("Invalid vertex");
        // Remove the list corresponding to vertex vet from the adjacency list
        adjList.erase(vet);
        // Traverse the lists of the other vertices and remove all edges incident to vet
        for (auto &adj : adjList) {
            remove(adj.second, vet);

            const auto &vec = adj.second;

            this.addEdge(edge[0], edge[1]);
        }
    }

    /* Get the number of vertices */
    size() {
        return this.adjList.size;
    }

    /* Add an edge */
    addEdge(vet1, vet2) {
        if (
            !this.adjList.has(vet1) ||
            !this.adjList.has(vet2) ||
            vet1 === vet2
        ) {
            throw new Error('Invalid argument');
        }
        // Add edge vet1 - vet2
        this.adjList.get(vet1).push(vet2);
        this.adjList.get(vet2).push(vet1);
    }

    /* Remove an edge */

        if (
            !this.adjList.has(vet1) ||
            !this.adjList.has(vet2) ||

        for (const set of this.adjList.values()) {

/* Undirected graph type implemented with an adjacency list */
pub struct GraphAdjList {
    // Adjacency list: key is a vertex, value is the list of all its neighbors
    pub adj_list: HashMap<Vertex, Vec<Vertex>>, // A HashSet<Vertex> may be a better choice for the neighbor collection
}

impl GraphAdjList {
    /* Constructor */
    pub fn new(edges: Vec<[Vertex; 2]>) -> Self {
        let mut graph = GraphAdjList {
            adj_list: HashMap::new(),
        };
        // Add all vertices and edges
        for edge in edges {
            graph.add_vertex(edge[0]);
            graph.add_vertex(edge[1]);
            graph.add_edge(edge[0], edge[1]);
        }

        graph
    }

    /* Get the number of vertices */
    #[allow(unused)]
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        self.adj_list.len()
    }

    /* Add an edge */
    pub fn add_edge(&mut self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex) {
        if vet1 == vet2 {
            panic!("Vertices must be distinct");
        }
        // Add edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list.entry(vet1).or_default().push(vet2);
        self.adj_list.entry(vet2).or_default().push(vet1);
    }

    /* Remove an edge */
    #[allow(unused)]
    pub fn remove_edge(&mut self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex) {
        if vet1 == vet2 {
            panic!("Vertices must be distinct");
        }
        // Remove edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list
            .entry(vet1)
            .and_modify(|v| v.retain(|&e| e != vet2));
        self.adj_list
            .entry(vet2)
            .and_modify(|v| v.retain(|&e| e != vet1));
    }

    /* Add a vertex */
    pub fn add_vertex(&mut self, vet: Vertex) {
        if self.adj_list.contains_key(&vet) {
            return;
        }
        // Add a new neighbor list to the adjacency list
        self.adj_list.insert(vet, vec![]);
    }

    /* Remove a vertex */
    #[allow(unused)]
    pub fn remove_vertex(&mut self, vet: Vertex) {
        // Remove the neighbor list for vertex vet from the adjacency list
        self.adj_list.remove(&vet);
        // Traverse the other neighbor lists and remove every edge incident to vet
        for list in self.adj_list.values_mut() {
            list.retain(|&v| v != vet);
        }
    }

    /* Print the adjacency list */
    pub fn print(&self) {
        println!("Adjacency list =");
        for (vertex, list) in &self.adj_list {
            let list = list.iter().map(|vertex| vertex.val).collect::<Vec<i32>>();
            println!("{}: {:?},", vertex.val, list);
        }
    }
}

/* Adjacency-list node structure */
typedef struct AdjListNode {
    Vertex *vertex;           // Vertex
    struct AdjListNode *next; // Next node
} AdjListNode;

/* Find the list node corresponding to a vertex */
AdjListNode *findNode(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        if (graph->heads[i]->vertex == vet) {
            return graph->heads[i];
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

/* Helper for adding an edge */
void addEdgeHelper(AdjListNode *head, Vertex *vet) {
    AdjListNode *node = (AdjListNode *)malloc(sizeof(AdjListNode));
    node->vertex = vet;
    // Insert at the front of the neighbor list
    node->next = head->next;
    head->next = node;
}

/* Helper for removing an edge */
void removeEdgeHelper(AdjListNode *head, Vertex *vet) {
    AdjListNode *pre = head;
    AdjListNode *cur = head->next;
    // Search the linked list for the node corresponding to vet
    while (cur != NULL && cur->vertex != vet) {
        pre = cur;
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    if (cur == NULL)
        return;
    // Remove the node corresponding to vet from the linked list
    pre->next = cur->next;
    // Free memory
    free(cur);
}

/* Undirected graph structure implemented with an adjacency list */
typedef struct {
    AdjListNode *heads[MAX_SIZE]; // Array of list heads
    int size;                     // Number of vertices
} GraphAdjList;

/* Constructor */
GraphAdjList *newGraphAdjList() {
    GraphAdjList *graph = (GraphAdjList *)malloc(sizeof(GraphAdjList));
    if (!graph) {
        return NULL;
    }
    graph->size = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_SIZE; i++) {
        graph->heads[i] = NULL;
    }
    return graph;
}

/* Destructor */
void delGraphAdjList(GraphAdjList *graph) {
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        AdjListNode *cur = graph->heads[i];
        while (cur != NULL) {
            AdjListNode *next = cur->next;
            if (cur != graph->heads[i]) {
                free(cur);
            }
            cur = next;
        }
        free(graph->heads[i]->vertex);
        free(graph->heads[i]);
    }
    free(graph);
}

/* Find the list node corresponding to a vertex */
AdjListNode *findNode(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        if (graph->heads[i]->vertex == vet) {
            return graph->heads[i];
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

/* Add an edge */
void addEdge(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
    AdjListNode *head1 = findNode(graph, vet1);
    AdjListNode *head2 = findNode(graph, vet2);
    assert(head1 != NULL && head2 != NULL && head1 != head2);
    // Add edge vet1 - vet2
    addEdgeHelper(head1, vet2);
    addEdgeHelper(head2, vet1);
}

/* Remove an edge */
void removeEdge(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
    AdjListNode *head1 = findNode(graph, vet1);
    AdjListNode *head2 = findNode(graph, vet2);
    assert(head1 != NULL && head2 != NULL);
    // Remove edge vet1 - vet2
    removeEdgeHelper(head1, head2->vertex);
    removeEdgeHelper(head2, head1->vertex);
}

/* Add a vertex */
void addVertex(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    assert(graph != NULL && graph->size < MAX_SIZE);
    AdjListNode *head = (AdjListNode *)malloc(sizeof(AdjListNode));
    head->vertex = vet;
    head->next = NULL;
    // Add a new list to the adjacency list
    graph->heads[graph->size++] = head;
}

/* Remove a vertex */
void removeVertex(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    AdjListNode *node = findNode(graph, vet);
    assert(node != NULL);
    // Remove the list corresponding to vertex vet from the adjacency list
    AdjListNode *cur = node, *pre = NULL;
    while (cur) {
        pre = cur;
        cur = cur->next;
        free(pre);
    }
    // Traverse the lists of the other vertices and remove all edges incident to vet
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        cur = graph->heads[i];
        pre = NULL;
        while (cur) {
            pre = cur;
            cur = cur->next;
            if (cur && cur->vertex == vet) {
                pre->next = cur->next;
                free(cur);
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    // Shift subsequent vertices forward to fill the gap
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        if (graph->heads[i] == node)
            break;
    }
    for (int j = i; j < graph->size - 1; j++) {
        graph->heads[j] = graph->heads[j + 1];
    }
    graph->size--;
    free(vet);
}

items.title: 9.2.3   Comparing efficiency
items.text:
For a graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges, Table 9-2 compares the time and space efficiency of adjacency matrices and adjacency lists. Here, "adjacency list (linked lists)" refers to the implementation in this section, while "adjacency list (hash tables)" specifically refers to an implementation in which every linked list is replaced by a hash table.

Table 9-2   Comparing adjacency matrices and adjacency lists

Adjacency matrix Adjacency list (linked lists) Adjacency list (hash tables) Check adjacency \(O(1)\) \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Add an edge \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) Remove an edge \(O(1)\) \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Add a vertex \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) Remove a vertex \(O(n^2)\) \(O(n + m)\) \(O(n)\) Memory usage \(O(n^2)\) \(O(n + m)\) \(O(n + m)\)

Table 9-2 suggests that an adjacency list using hash tables is the most efficient in both time and space. In practice, however, edge operations in an adjacency matrix are faster: each requires only a single array access or assignment. Overall, an adjacency matrix trades space for time, while an adjacency list trades time for space.

items.title: 9.3   Graph traversal
items.text:
A tree represents one-to-many relationships, whereas a graph allows more freedom and can represent arbitrary many-to-many relationships. We can therefore view a tree as a special case of a graph. Accordingly, tree traversal is also a special case of graph traversal.

Both graphs and trees use search algorithms for traversal. Graph traversal can likewise be divided into two types: breadth-first traversal and depth-first traversal.

items.title: 9.3.1   Breadth-first traversal
items.text:
Breadth-first traversal visits vertices from near to far. Starting from a vertex, it always visits the nearest vertices first and expands outward layer by layer. In Figure 9-9, we start at the top-left vertex and visit all its adjacent vertices, then visit all the adjacent vertices of the next vertex, and so on until every vertex has been visited.

Figure 9-9   Breadth-first traversal of a graph

items.title: 1.   Algorithm implementation
items.text:
BFS is usually implemented with a queue, as shown in the code below. A queue's first-in, first-out behavior fits the near-to-far order of BFS.

  1. Enqueue the starting vertex startVet and begin the loop.
  2. In each iteration, dequeue the vertex at the front and record the visit, then enqueue all its adjacent vertices at the rear.
  3. Repeat step 2. until every vertex has been visited.

To avoid visiting a vertex more than once, we use a hash set visited to track which vertices have already been visited.

Tip

A hash set can be viewed as a hash table that stores only key entries, with no value entries. Adding, removing, looking up, and modifying a key take \(O(1)\) time. Because every key is unique, hash sets are commonly used to remove duplicate data.

def graph_bfs(graph: GraphAdjList, start_vet: Vertex) -> list[Vertex]:
    """Breadth-first traversal"""
    # Represent the graph with an adjacency list to access all neighbors of a given vertex
    # Vertex traversal sequence
    res = []
    # Hash set recording visited vertices
    visited = set[Vertex]([start_vet])
    # Use a queue to implement BFS
    que = deque[Vertex]([start_vet])
    # Starting from start_vet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while len(que) > 0:
        vet = que.popleft()  # Dequeue the front vertex
        res.append(vet)  # Record the visited vertex
        # Traverse all neighbors of this vertex
        for adj_vet in graph.adj_list[vet]:
            if adj_vet in visited:
                continue  # Skip vertices that have already been visited
            que.append(adj_vet)  # Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            visited.add(adj_vet)  # Mark this vertex as visited
    # Return the vertex traversal sequence
    return res

/* Breadth-first traversal */
// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to access all neighbors of a given vertex
vector<Vertex *> graphBFS(GraphAdjList &graph, Vertex *startVet) {
    // Vertex traversal sequence
    vector<Vertex *> res;
    // Hash set recording visited vertices
    unordered_set<Vertex *> visited = {startVet};
    // Use a queue to implement BFS
    queue<Vertex *> que;
    que.push(startVet);
    // Starting from startVet, continue until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while (!que.empty()) {
        Vertex *vet = que.front();
        que.pop();          // Dequeue the front vertex
        res.push_back(vet); // Record the visited vertex
        // Traverse all neighbors of this vertex
        for (auto adjVet : graph.adjList[vet]) {
            if (visited.count(adjVet))
                continue;            // Skip vertices that have already been visited
            que.push(adjVet);        // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            visited.emplace(adjVet); // Mark this vertex as visited
        }
    }
    // Return the vertex traversal sequence
    return res;
}

List<Vertex> graphBFS(GraphAdjList graph, Vertex startVet) {
    // Vertex traversal sequence
    List<Vertex> res = new ArrayList<>();
    // Hash set recording visited vertices
    Set<Vertex> visited = new HashSet<>();
    visited.add(startVet);
    // Use a queue to implement BFS
    Queue<Vertex> que = new LinkedList<>();
    que.offer(startVet);
    // Starting from startVet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while (!que.isEmpty()) {
        Vertex vet = que.poll(); // Dequeue the front vertex
        res.add(vet);            // Record the visited vertex
        // Traverse all neighbors of this vertex
        for (Vertex adjVet : graph.adjList.get(vet)) {
            if (visited.contains(adjVet))
                continue;        // Skip vertices that have already been visited
            que.offer(adjVet);   // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            visited.add(adjVet); // Mark this vertex as visited
        }
    }
    // Return the vertex traversal sequence
    return res;
}

// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to access all neighbors of a given vertex
List<Vertex> GraphBFS(GraphAdjList graph, Vertex startVet) {
    // Vertex traversal sequence
    List<Vertex> res = [];
    // Hash set recording visited vertices
    HashSet<Vertex> visited = [startVet];
    // Use a queue to implement BFS
    Queue<Vertex> que = new();
    que.Enqueue(startVet);
    // Starting from startVet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while (que.Count > 0) {
        Vertex vet = que.Dequeue(); // Dequeue the front vertex
        res.Add(vet);               // Record the visited vertex
        foreach (Vertex adjVet in graph.adjList[vet]) {
            if (visited.Contains(adjVet)) {
                continue;          // Skip vertices that have already been visited
            }
            que.Enqueue(adjVet);   // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            visited.Add(adjVet);   // Mark this vertex as visited
        }
    }

    // Return the vertex traversal sequence
    return res;
