// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to access all neighbors of a given vertex
func graphBFS(g *graphAdjList, startVet Vertex) []Vertex {
    // Vertex traversal sequence
    res := make([]Vertex, 0)
    // Hash set recording visited vertices
    visited := make(map[Vertex]struct{})
    visited[startVet] = struct{}{}
    // Use a queue for BFS, represented here by a slice
    queue := make([]Vertex, 0)
    queue = append(queue, startVet)
    // Starting from startVet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    for len(queue) > 0 {
        // Dequeue the front vertex
        vet := queue[0]
        queue = queue[1:]
        // Record the visited vertex
        res = append(res, vet)
        // Traverse all neighbors of this vertex
        for _, adjVet := range g.adjList[vet] {
            _, isExist := visited[adjVet]
            // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            if !isExist {
                queue = append(queue, adjVet)
                visited[adjVet] = struct{}{}
            }
        }
    }
    // Return the vertex traversal sequence
    return res
}

/* Vertex queue structure */
typedef struct {
    Vertex *vertices[MAX_SIZE];
    int front, rear, size;
} Queue;

/* Constructor */
Queue *newQueue() {
    Queue *q = (Queue *)malloc(sizeof(Queue));
    q->front = q->rear = q->size = 0;
    return q;
}

/* Check whether the queue is empty */
int isEmpty(Queue *q) {
    return q->size == 0;
}

/* Enqueue operation */
void enqueue(Queue *q, Vertex *vet) {
    q->vertices[q->rear] = vet;
    q->rear = (q->rear + 1) % MAX_SIZE;
    q->size++;
}

/* Dequeue operation */
Vertex *dequeue(Queue *q) {
    Vertex *vet = q->vertices[q->front];
    q->front = (q->front + 1) % MAX_SIZE;
    q->size--;
    return vet;
}

/* Check whether a vertex has been visited */
int isVisited(Vertex **visited, int size, Vertex *vet) {
    // Search for the vertex with a linear scan in O(n) time
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (visited[i] == vet)
            return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Breadth-first traversal */
// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to access all neighbors of a given vertex
void graphBFS(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *startVet, Vertex **res, int *resSize, Vertex **visited, int *visitedSize) {
    // Use a queue to implement BFS
    Queue *queue = newQueue();
    enqueue(queue, startVet);
    visited[(*visitedSize)++] = startVet;
    // Starting from startVet, continue until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while (!isEmpty(queue)) {
        Vertex *vet = dequeue(queue); // Dequeue the front vertex
        res[(*resSize)++] = vet;      // Record the visited vertex
        // Traverse all neighbors of this vertex
        AdjListNode *node = findNode(graph, vet);
        while (node != NULL) {
            // Skip vertices that have already been visited
            if (!isVisited(visited, *visitedSize, node->vertex)) {
                enqueue(queue, node->vertex);             // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
                visited[(*visitedSize)++] = node->vertex; // Mark this vertex as visited
            }
            node = node->next;
        }
    }
    // Free memory
    free(queue);
}

  # Vertex traversal sequence

  while que.length > 0

      que << adj_vet # Enqueue only unvisited vertices
      visited.add(adj_vet) # Mark this vertex as visited
    end
  end

  res
end

Is the breadth-first traversal order unique?

No. Breadth-first traversal only requires vertices to be visited from near to far; vertices at the same distance may be visited in any order. In Figure 9-10, vertices \(1\) and \(3\) can be visited in either order, and vertices \(2\), \(4\), and \(6\) can also be visited in any order.

items.title: 2.   Complexity analysis
items.text:
Time complexity: Every vertex is enqueued and dequeued once, taking \(O(|V|)\) time. While traversing adjacent vertices, every edge is visited \(2\) times because the graph is undirected, taking \(O(2|E|)\) time. The total time is \(O(|V| + |E|)\).

Space complexity: The list res, hash set visited, and queue que each contain at most \(|V|\) vertices, requiring \(O(|V|)\) space.

items.title: 9.3.2   Depth-first traversal
items.text:
Depth-first traversal follows a path as far as possible and returns when it can go no farther. In Figure 9-11, we start at the top-left vertex and move to an adjacent vertex of the current vertex, continuing until we reach a dead end. We then return and explore another path as far as possible, repeating this process until every vertex has been visited.

Figure 9-11   Depth-first traversal of a graph

items.title: 1.   Algorithm implementation
items.text:
This pattern of going as far as possible and then returning is usually implemented with recursion. As with breadth-first traversal, we use a hash set visited to track visited vertices and avoid visiting them again.

def dfs(graph: GraphAdjList, visited: set[Vertex], res: list[Vertex], vet: Vertex):
    """Depth-first traversal helper function"""
    res.append(vet)  # Record the visited vertex
    visited.add(vet)  # Mark this vertex as visited
    # Traverse all neighbors of this vertex
    for adjVet in graph.adj_list[vet]:
        if adjVet in visited:
            continue  # Skip vertices that have already been visited
        # Recursively visit the neighboring vertex
        dfs(graph, visited, res, adjVet)

Is the depth-first traversal order unique?

Like breadth-first traversal, depth-first traversal does not have a unique order. From any vertex, we can explore in any direction first: rearranging the order of adjacent vertices still produces a depth-first traversal.

For example, in tree traversal, "root \(\rightarrow\) left \(\rightarrow\) right", "left \(\rightarrow\) root \(\rightarrow\) right", and "left \(\rightarrow\) right \(\rightarrow\) root" correspond to preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal. They use three different visiting priorities, yet all are depth-first traversals.

items.title: 2.   Complexity analysis
items.text:
Time complexity: Every vertex is visited \(1\) time, taking \(O(|V|)\) time, and every edge is visited \(2\) times, taking \(O(2|E|)\) time. The total time is \(O(|V| + |E|)\).

Space complexity: The list res and hash set visited each contain at most \(|V|\) vertices, and the maximum recursion depth is \(|V|\), so the space complexity is \(O(|V|)\).

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• A graph consists of vertices and edges and can be represented using a vertex set and an edge set.
  • Network relationships (graphs) allow more freedom than linear relationships (linked lists) or divide-and-conquer relationships (trees), making them more complex.
  • Edges in a directed graph have a direction; all vertices in a connected graph are reachable; and each edge in a weighted graph has a weight.
  • An adjacency matrix represents a graph with a matrix. Each row (or column) represents a vertex, and entries represent edges, with \(1\) or \(0\) indicating whether an edge exists between two vertices. Adding, removing, looking up, and modifying edges are efficient, but the matrix uses substantial space.
  • An adjacency list represents a graph with multiple linked lists. The \(i\)-th linked list corresponds to vertex \(i\) and stores all of its adjacent vertices. It uses less space than an adjacency matrix, but finding an edge requires traversing a linked list, making lookups slower.
  • A long linked list in an adjacency list can be replaced with a red-black tree or a hash table to speed up lookups.
  • In terms of algorithm design, an adjacency matrix trades space for time, while an adjacency list trades time for space.
  • Graphs can model many real-world systems, such as social networks and subway networks.
  • A tree is a special case of a graph, and tree traversal is a special case of graph traversal.
  • Breadth-first graph traversal searches from near to far, expanding layer by layer. It is usually implemented with a queue.
  • Depth-first graph traversal follows a path as far as possible and backtracks when it can go no farther. It is often implemented with recursion.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Is a path defined as a sequence of vertices or a sequence of edges?

Wikipedia's language editions give different definitions: the English edition defines a path as a sequence of edges, while the Chinese edition defines it as a sequence of vertices. The English wording is: In graph theory, a path in a graph is a finite or infinite sequence of edges which joins a sequence of vertices.

In this book, a path is treated as a sequence of edges rather than vertices. This is because multiple edges can connect the same two vertices, in which case each edge corresponds to a path.

Q: Can some vertices in a disconnected graph remain unvisited?

In a disconnected graph, at least one vertex cannot be reached from a given starting vertex. Traversing the entire graph requires multiple starting points so that all connected components are visited.

Q: Must the adjacent vertices in an adjacency list appear in a particular order?

They may appear in any order. In practice, however, it can be useful to sort them by a specific rule, such as the order in which vertices were added or their values. This helps us quickly find a vertex with a particular extreme value.

items.title: Chapter 15.   Greedy algorithms
items.text:
Abstract

A sunflower turns toward the sun, always seeking the greatest opportunity to grow.

Through a series of simple choices, a greedy strategy leads us step by step toward the best answer.

items.title: 1.   Is choosing the largest coin always best?
items.text:
The coin denominations are [1, 7, 10], and the target amount is 14.

  1. Follow the rule “always take the largest denomination that does not exceed the remaining amount,” and list the coins chosen.
  2. Is there a way to use fewer coins? If so, give one; if not, explain why.
  3. Can you conclude that this greedy strategy is correct for any set of coin denominations?
Reference answer

  1. The greedy strategy chooses 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, using 5 coins in total.

  2. There is a solution with fewer coins: 7 + 7, which uses only 2.

  3. No. This counterexample shows that choosing the largest available denomination at each step does not always minimize the number of coins for arbitrary denominations. The largest immediate choice can rule out a better combination later.

items.title: 2.   Which item should go into the knapsack first?
items.text:
A knapsack with a capacity of 4 kg can hold the following items. You may take part of an item, and the value obtained is proportional to the weight taken.

  • Item A weighs 4 kg and has a value of 20.
  • Item B weighs 3 kg and has a value of 18.
  1. What is each item's value per kilogram? Which item should you take first?
  2. If you fill the knapsack using the greedy strategy for fractional knapsack, what is the final value?
  3. When items can be divided and the knapsack limits total weight, should you compare total value or value per kilogram? Why?
Reference answer

  1. A's value per kilogram is 20 ÷ 4 = 5, and B's is 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Take B first because it has the higher value per unit of weight.

  2. Take all of B first, using 3 kg of capacity and gaining a value of 18. With 1 kg of capacity left, take 1 kg of A for a value of 5. The final value is 18 + 5 = 23.

  3. The knapsack limits total weight, and items can be divided, so compare value per unit of weight. Although A has a higher total value, its value per kilogram is lower than B's. Taking all of A first would give a value of only 20.

items.title: 3.   Which pointer should move next?
items.text:
The wall heights are [1, 8, 6, 2, 5]. Use two pointers, initially at opposite ends, to find the maximum container capacity. Capacity equals the height of the shorter of the two walls multiplied by the difference between their indices.

  1. Initially, the left pointer is at index 0 and the right pointer is at index 4. What is the current capacity? Which pointer should move next?
  2. After making the move you chose in question 1, what are the two pointer indices? What is the capacity now, and which pointer should move next?
  3. For the current pair of walls, you could move the pointer at the shorter wall or the pointer at the taller wall. Which move still has a chance of producing a larger capacity? Why?
Reference answer

  1. The current capacity is min(1, 5) × (4 - 0) = 4. The left wall is shorter, so move the left pointer.

  2. After moving the left pointer, the pointers are at indices 1 and 4. The current capacity is min(8, 5) × (4 - 1) = 15. The right wall is shorter, so move the right pointer next.

  3. Only moving the pointer at the shorter wall can still produce a larger capacity. Moving the pointer at the taller wall reduces the distance between the walls, while the container's height remains limited by the shorter wall that has not moved. That height can only stay the same or decrease, so the capacity cannot exceed its previous value. Moving the pointer at the shorter wall is the only way to have a chance of finding a taller wall.

items.title: 1.   Fractional knapsack
items.text:
You are given arrays wgt and val of equal length, where wgt[i] > 0 and val[i] >= 0, and a knapsack capacity cap >= 0. There is one of each item, but you may take just part of it. The value obtained is proportional to the fraction of the item's total weight that you take. Use a greedy algorithm to return the maximum total value the knapsack can hold, as a real number.

Hints
  1. First calculate each item's value per unit of weight, val[i] / wgt[i]. Preserve the fractional part of the division result.
  2. Take items with a higher value per unit of weight first.
  3. If the remaining capacity is less than the current item's weight, take just enough of the item to fill the knapsack, then stop.

items.title: 15.2   Fractional knapsack problem
items.text:
Question

Given \(n\) items, where item \(i\) has weight \(wgt[i-1]\) and value \(val[i-1]\), and a knapsack with capacity \(cap\), each item may be selected only once. However, you may take a fraction of an item, with its value proportional to the weight taken. What is the maximum total value that fits within the knapsack's capacity? An example is shown in Figure 15-3.

Figure 15-3   Example input for the fractional knapsack problem

The fractional knapsack problem is very similar to the 0-1 knapsack problem. The state consists of the current item \(i\) and capacity \(c\), and the goal is to maximize value within the knapsack's capacity.

The difference is that we may take only part of an item. As shown in Figure 15-4, we can divide items into arbitrary fractions and calculate their values in proportion to their weights.

  1. For item \(i\), the value per unit weight is \(val[i-1] / wgt[i-1]\), which we call its unit value.
  2. If we take a portion of item \(i\) weighing \(w\), the value added to the knapsack is \(w \times val[i-1] / wgt[i-1]\).

Figure 15-4   Value per unit weight of each item

items.title: 1.   Choosing a greedy strategy
items.text:
Maximizing the total value in the knapsack essentially means maximizing the value obtained per unit weight. This leads to the greedy strategy shown in Figure 15-5.

  1. Sort the items by unit value in descending order.
  2. Iterate through the items, greedily choosing the item with the highest unit value at each step.
  3. If the remaining capacity is insufficient, take just enough of the current item to fill the knapsack.

Figure 15-5   Greedy strategy for the fractional knapsack problem

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
items.text:
We define an Item class to make it easier to sort items by unit value. We repeatedly make greedy choices, stopping and returning the result when the knapsack is full:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby fractional_knapsack.py
class Item:
    """Item"""

    def __init__(self, w: int, v: int):
        self.w = w  # Item weight
        self.v = v  # Item value

def fractional_knapsack(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """Fractional knapsack: greedy algorithm"""
    # Create a list of items, each with two attributes: weight and value
    items = [Item(w, v) for w, v in zip(wgt, val)]
    # Sort by value per unit weight, item.v / item.w, in descending order
    items.sort(key=lambda item: item.v / item.w, reverse=True)
    # Repeatedly make greedy choices
    res = 0
    for item in items:
        if item.w <= cap:
            # If enough capacity remains, put the entire current item in the knapsack
            res += item.v
            cap -= item.w
        else:
            # If the remaining capacity is insufficient, put part of the current item in the knapsack
            res += (item.v / item.w) * cap
            # No capacity remains, so exit the loop
            break
    return res

            res += (double)item.v / item.w * cap;
            // No capacity remains, so exit the loop

        }
    }
    return res;
}

items.title: 3.   Proof of correctness
items.text:
We use proof by contradiction. Suppose item \(x\) has the highest unit value, and an algorithm produces a maximum value of res, but its solution does not include item \(x\).

Now remove one unit of weight of any item from the knapsack and replace it with one unit of weight of item \(x\). Since \(x\) has the highest unit value, the total value after replacement must exceed res. This contradicts the assumption that res is optimal, showing that an optimal solution must include item \(x\).

We can construct the same contradiction for other items in the solution. Thus, an item with a higher unit value is always a better choice, which establishes the greedy strategy.

As shown in Figure 15-6, if we plot item weight on the horizontal axis and unit value on the vertical axis, the fractional knapsack problem becomes a problem of maximizing the area within a limited horizontal interval. This analogy provides a geometric view of why the greedy strategy works.

Figure 15-6   Geometric representation of the fractional knapsack problem

items.title: 15.1   Greedy algorithms
items.text:
A greedy algorithm is a common approach to optimization problems. At each decision point, it chooses the option that looks best at that moment: it makes a locally optimal choice in the hope of reaching a globally optimal solution. Greedy algorithms are simple and efficient, with many practical applications.

Both greedy algorithms and dynamic programming are commonly used for optimization. They share some features, such as relying on optimal substructure, but work differently.

  • Dynamic programming considers the current decision in light of all decisions from earlier stages, using solutions to earlier subproblems to build the solution to the current subproblem.
  • A greedy algorithm does not reconsider past decisions. It keeps moving forward, making greedy choices and shrinking the problem until it is solved.

Let's explore how greedy algorithms work through the coin change problem, which you have already encountered in the section on the unbounded knapsack problem.

Question

Given \(n\) coin denominations, where denomination \(i\) has value \(coins[i - 1]\), and a target amount \(amt\), you may use each denomination any number of times. What is the minimum number of coins needed to make the target amount? Return \(-1\) if it cannot be made.

The greedy strategy is shown in Figure 15-1. Given the remaining target amount, we greedily choose the largest coin that does not exceed it, repeating this step until we have made the target amount.

Figure 15-1   Greedy strategy for coin change

The implementation is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby coin_change_greedy.py
def coin_change_greedy(coins: list[int], amt: int) -> int:
    """Coin change: greedy algorithm"""
    # Assume the coins list is sorted
    i = len(coins) - 1
    count = 0
    # Repeatedly make greedy choices until no amount remains
    while amt > 0:
        # Find the largest coin no greater than the remaining amount
        while i > 0 and coins[i] > amt:
            i -= 1
        # Choose coins[i]
        amt -= coins[i]
        count += 1
    # Return -1 if no feasible solution was found
    return count if amt == 0 else -1

items.title: 15.1.1   Strengths and limitations of greedy algorithms
items.text:
Greedy algorithms are straightforward, easy to implement, and usually efficient. In the code above, let \(\min(coins)\) be the smallest coin denomination. At most \(amt / \min(coins)\) greedy choices are made, giving a time complexity of \(O(amt / \min(coins))\). This is an order of magnitude lower than the dynamic programming solution's \(O(n \times amt)\) time complexity.

However, for some sets of coin denominations, a greedy algorithm cannot find the optimal solution. Figure 15-2 illustrates two examples.

  • Successful case: \(coins = [1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100]\). For these denominations, the greedy algorithm finds an optimal solution for any \(amt\).
  • Counterexample: \(coins = [1, 20, 50]\). For \(amt = 60\), the greedy algorithm produces \(50 + 1 \times 10\), using \(11\) coins. Dynamic programming finds the optimal solution \(20 + 20 + 20\), using only \(3\) coins.
  • Counterexample: \(coins = [1, 49, 50]\). For \(amt = 98\), the greedy algorithm produces \(50 + 1 \times 48\), using \(49\) coins. Dynamic programming finds the optimal solution \(49 + 49\), using only \(2\) coins.

Figure 15-2   Examples where the greedy algorithm fails to find the optimal solution

In other words, a greedy algorithm cannot guarantee a globally optimal solution to coin change and may produce a very poor solution. Dynamic programming is better suited to this problem.

In general, greedy algorithms are useful in two situations.

  1. An optimal solution is guaranteed: A greedy algorithm is often the best choice because it is usually more efficient than backtracking or dynamic programming.
  2. A near-optimal solution can be found: A greedy algorithm can still be useful. For many complex problems, finding a globally optimal solution is very difficult, so finding a good suboptimal solution efficiently is valuable.

items.title: 15.1.2   Properties required by greedy algorithms
items.text:
What kinds of problems are suitable for greedy algorithms? More specifically, when can a greedy algorithm guarantee an optimal solution?

Greedy algorithms have stricter requirements than dynamic programming. Two properties are particularly important.

  • Greedy-choice property: A greedy algorithm can guarantee an optimal solution only when locally optimal choices always lead to a globally optimal solution.
  • Optimal substructure: An optimal solution to the original problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems.

Optimal substructure was covered in the dynamic programming chapter, so we will not repeat that discussion here. Some problems have optimal substructure that is not immediately apparent, yet can still be solved greedily.

We will focus on how to determine whether the greedy-choice property holds. Its description may sound simple, but proving it is difficult for many problems.

For coin change, for example, it is easy to give counterexamples that disprove the greedy-choice property, but proving it is harder. If asked which conditions on the coin denominations allow a greedy solution, we may be able to give only a vague answer based on intuition or examples, rather than a rigorous mathematical proof.

Quote

One paper gives an \(O(n^3)\)-time algorithm for determining whether a set of coin denominations allows a greedy algorithm to find an optimal solution for every amount.

Pearson, D. A polynomial-time algorithm for the change-making problem[J]. Operations Research Letters, 2005, 33(3): 231-234.

items.title: 15.1.3   Steps for solving a problem greedily
items.text:
Solving a greedy problem generally involves three steps.

  1. Analyze the problem: Understand its properties, including the state definition, optimization objective, and constraints. This step also appears in backtracking and dynamic programming.
  2. Choose a greedy strategy: Decide how to make a greedy choice at each step. Each choice should reduce the problem's size, eventually solving the whole problem.
  3. Prove correctness: Usually, we must establish the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. This may require a mathematical proof, such as induction or proof by contradiction.

Choosing the greedy strategy is the central step, but it can be difficult for the following reasons.

  • Greedy strategies vary greatly from problem to problem. For many problems, the strategy is straightforward and can be found with a little thought and experimentation. For more complex problems, it may be well hidden, testing our problem-solving experience and algorithmic skills.
  • Some greedy strategies are misleading. We may confidently devise a strategy, implement it, and submit the code, only to find that it fails some test cases. The strategy is only partially correct; the coin change problem above is a typical example.

To ensure correctness, we should give the greedy strategy a rigorous mathematical proof, usually using contradiction or mathematical induction.

However, such a proof can itself be difficult. When we do not know where to start, we often debug against test cases, gradually refining and checking the greedy strategy.

items.title: 15.1.4   Typical greedy problems
items.text:
Greedy algorithms often solve optimization problems with the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Some typical examples follow.

  • Coin change: For certain sets of coin denominations, a greedy algorithm always finds an optimal solution.
  • Interval scheduling: Given tasks that each occupy a time interval, the goal is to complete as many tasks as possible. Always choosing the available task that finishes earliest yields an optimal solution.
  • Fractional knapsack: Given items and a weight limit, choose items to maximize total value without exceeding the limit. Choosing the item with the highest value-to-weight ratio at each step can yield an optimal solution in some settings.
  • Stock trading: Given historical stock prices, you may buy and sell multiple times, but cannot buy again while holding stock until you sell it. The goal is to maximize profit.
  • Huffman coding: This greedy algorithm is used for lossless data compression. It builds a Huffman tree by repeatedly merging the two nodes with the lowest frequencies. The resulting tree has the minimum weighted path length (encoding length).
  • Dijkstra's algorithm: This greedy algorithm finds shortest paths from a given source vertex to every other vertex in a graph whose edge weights are all nonnegative.

items.title: 15.3   Maximum capacity problem
items.text:
Question

Given an array \(ht\), each element represents the height of a vertical wall. Any two walls, together with the space between them, form a container.

The container's capacity is its height multiplied by its width (an area). Its height is determined by the shorter wall, and its width is the difference between the two walls' array indices.

Choose two walls from the array to maximize the container's capacity, and return that maximum capacity. An example is shown in Figure 15-7.

Figure 15-7   Example input for the maximum capacity problem

A container is formed by two walls, so the state of this problem is the pair of wall indices, denoted by \([i, j]\).

Capacity is height times width, with the height determined by the shorter wall and the width equal to the difference between the wall indices. Writing the capacity as \(cap[i, j]\), we have:

\[ cap[i, j] = \min(ht[i], ht[j]) \times (j - i) \]

For an array of length \(n\), there are \(C_n^2 = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\) pairs of walls (possible states). The most direct approach is to enumerate all states and find the maximum capacity, taking \(O(n^2)\) time.

items.title: 1.   Choosing a greedy strategy
items.text:
A more efficient solution is possible. Consider the state \([i, j]\) in Figure 15-8, where \(i < j\) and \(ht[i] < ht[j]\): wall \(i\) is shorter and wall \(j\) is taller.

Figure 15-8   Initial state

As shown in Figure 15-9, moving the taller wall \(j\) inward toward the shorter wall \(i\) must reduce the capacity.

Moving wall \(j\) inward always reduces the width \(j-i\). Since the shorter wall determines the height, the height can only stay the same (if \(i\) remains shorter) or decrease (if the new wall \(j\) is shorter).

Figure 15-9   State after moving the taller wall inward

Conversely, only moving the shorter wall \(i\) inward can potentially increase the capacity. Although the width must decrease, the height may increase if the new wall \(i\) is taller. Figure 15-10 shows an example where moving the shorter wall increases the area.

Figure 15-10   State after moving the shorter wall inward

This gives us a greedy strategy: initialize two pointers at opposite ends of the container. At each step, move the pointer at the shorter wall inward until the pointers meet.

Figure 15-11 illustrates the greedy process.

  1. Initially, pointers \(i\) and \(j\) are at opposite ends of the array.
  2. Calculate the current capacity \(cap[i, j]\) and update the maximum capacity.
  3. Compare the heights of walls \(i\) and \(j\), and move the shorter wall inward by one position.
  4. Repeat steps 2. and 3. until \(i\) and \(j\) meet.
<1><2><3><4><5><6><7><8><9>

Figure 15-11   Greedy steps for the maximum capacity problem

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
items.text:
The loop runs at most \(n\) times, so the time complexity is \(O(n)\).

The variables \(i\), \(j\), and \(res\) require constant extra space, so the space complexity is \(O(1)\).

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby max_capacity.py
def max_capacity(ht: list[int]) -> int:
    """Maximum container capacity: greedy algorithm"""
    # Initialize i and j at opposite ends of the array
    i, j = 0, len(ht) - 1
    # The initial maximum capacity is 0
    res = 0
    # Repeatedly make greedy choices until the two sides meet
    while i < j:
        # Update the maximum capacity
        cap = min(ht[i], ht[j]) * (j - i)
        res = max(res, cap)
        # Move the shorter side inward
        if ht[i] < ht[j]:
            i += 1
        else:
            j -= 1
    return res

items.title: 3.   Proof of correctness
items.text:
The greedy algorithm is faster than exhaustive search because each greedy choice skips some states.

For example, in state \(cap[i, j]\), suppose \(i\) is the shorter wall and \(j\) the taller one. Moving the shorter wall \(i\) inward by one position skips the states shown in Figure 15-12. Their capacities will never be checked later.

\[ cap[i, i+1], cap[i, i+2], \dots, cap[i, j-2], cap[i, j-1] \]

Figure 15-12   States skipped by moving the shorter wall

Observe that the skipped states are precisely those obtained by moving the taller wall \(j\) inward. We have already shown that moving the taller wall inward must reduce capacity. None of these skipped states can therefore be optimal, and skipping them cannot cause us to miss the optimal solution.

This shows that moving the shorter wall is safe, and that the greedy strategy is valid.

items.title: 15.4   Maximum product cutting problem
items.text:
Question

Given a positive integer \(n\), split it into a sum of at least two positive integers. What is the largest possible product of those integers? The problem is illustrated in Figure 15-13.

Figure 15-13   Definition of the maximum product cutting problem

Suppose we split \(n\) into \(m\) integers that will be factors in the product. Denote the \(i\)-th factor by \(n_i\), so that

\[ n = \sum_{i=1}^{m}n_i \]

Our goal is to maximize the product of all these integer factors:

\[ \max(\prod_{i=1}^{m}n_i) \]

We need to determine how many parts \(m\) to create and what each \(n_i\) should be.

items.title: 1.   Choosing a greedy strategy
items.text:
The product of two integers is often greater than their sum. Suppose we split off a factor of \(2\) from \(n\), giving the product \(2(n-2)\). Comparing this product with \(n\) gives:

\[ \begin{aligned} 2(n-2) & \geq n \newline 2n - n - 4 & \geq 0 \newline n & \geq 4 \end{aligned} \]

As shown in Figure 15-14, when \(n \geq 4\), splitting off a \(2\) increases the product. This suggests that every integer greater than or equal to \(4\) should be split further.

Greedy strategy 1: If a factor \(\geq 4\) appears in a split, divide it further. The final split should contain only the factors \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\).

Figure 15-14   Splitting increases the product

Next, consider which factor is best. Of \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\), clearly \(1\) is the worst: \(1 \times (n-1) < n\) always holds, so splitting off a \(1\) reduces the product.

As shown in Figure 15-15, when \(n = 6\), we have \(3 \times 3 > 2 \times 2 \times 2\). This means that splitting into factors of \(3\) is better than splitting into factors of \(2\).

Greedy strategy 2: A split should contain at most two factors of \(2\), because three \(2\)s can always be replaced with two \(3\)s to obtain a larger product.

Figure 15-15   Optimal factors

These observations lead to the following greedy strategy.

  1. Starting with \(n\), keep splitting off factors of \(3\) until the remainder is \(0\), \(1\), or \(2\).
  2. If the remainder is \(0\), then \(n\) is a multiple of \(3\), and no further action is needed.
  3. If the remainder is \(2\), keep it without splitting it further.
  4. If the remainder is \(1\), replace the last \(3\) and the remaining \(1\) with two \(2\)s, since \(2 \times 2 > 1 \times 3\).

items.title: 2.   Code implementation
items.text:
As shown in Figure 15-16, we do not need a loop to split the integer. Floor division gives the number of \(3\)s, denoted by \(a\), and the modulo operation gives the remainder \(b\). Thus:

\[ n = 3 a + b \]

For the boundary cases \(n \leq 3\), we must split off a \(1\), giving a product of \(1 \times (n - 1)\).

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby max_product_cutting.py
def max_product_cutting(n: int) -> int:
    """Maximum product after splitting: greedy algorithm"""
    # When n <= 3, one part must be 1
    if n <= 3:
        return 1 * (n - 1)
    # Greedily split off parts of size 3; a is the number of 3s and b is the remainder
    a, b = n // 3, n % 3
    if b == 1:
        # When the remainder is 1, replace one pair 1 * 3 with 2 * 2
        return int(math.pow(3, a - 1)) * 2 * 2
    if b == 2:
        # When the remainder is 2, no adjustment is needed
        return int(math.pow(3, a)) * 2
    # When the remainder is 0, no adjustment is needed
    return int(math.pow(3, a))

items.title: 3.   Proof of correctness
items.text:
We use proof by contradiction, considering only \(n \geq 4\).

  1. All factors are \(\leq 3\): Suppose an optimal split contains a factor \(x\) that is \(\geq 4\). We can split it further to obtain \(2(x-2)\), giving a greater (or equal) product. This contradicts the assumption.
  2. The split contains no \(1\): Suppose an optimal split contains a factor of \(1\). We can merge it into another factor to obtain a larger product, contradicting the assumption.
  3. The split contains at most two \(2\)s: Suppose an optimal split contains three \(2\)s. Replacing them with two \(3\)s gives a larger product, contradicting the assumption.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Greedy algorithms are commonly used for optimization. At each decision point, they make a locally optimal choice in the hope of reaching a globally optimal solution.
  • A greedy algorithm repeatedly makes greedy choices, turning the problem into a smaller subproblem at each step until it is solved.
  • Greedy algorithms are easy to implement and efficient. Their time complexity is usually lower than that of dynamic programming.
  • For some coin denominations, a greedy algorithm is guaranteed to find an optimal coin change solution. For others, it may produce a very poor solution.
  • Problems suited to greedy algorithms have two properties: the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. The greedy-choice property establishes that the strategy works.
  • Proving the greedy-choice property can be difficult for complex problems. Disproving it is often easier, as coin change illustrates.
  • Solving a greedy problem involves three main steps: analyze the problem, choose a greedy strategy, and prove correctness. Choosing the strategy is the central step, while proving correctness is often the hardest.
  • The fractional knapsack problem extends 0-1 knapsack by allowing fractions of items, making a greedy solution possible. The strategy can be proved correct by contradiction.
  • The maximum capacity problem can be solved by exhaustive search in \(O(n^2)\) time. A greedy strategy that moves the shorter wall inward at each step reduces this to \(O(n)\).
  • For the maximum product cutting problem, we derived two greedy strategies: continue splitting integers \(\geq 4\), and favor factors of \(3\). The implementation uses exponentiation, so its time complexity depends on the exponentiation method, usually \(O(1)\) or \(O(\log n)\).

Abstract

In the world of computers, a hash table is like a knowledgeable librarian.

Knowing how to calculate a call number lets the librarian find the desired book quickly.

items.title: 1.   Searching after a hash collision
items.text:
A hash table has five buckets and uses the hash function \(h(x)=x \bmod 5\). When elements collide, they are added in order to the list in that bucket. Insert [1, 6, 11, 7] in sequence:

  1. Write out the contents of buckets 0 through 4.
  2. When searching for 6, which bucket is visited first, and which elements are checked in order?
  3. Based on the bucket contents from question 1, did later elements overwrite earlier ones? Explain using this collision-handling method.
Reference answer

  1. Since \(1\bmod5=6\bmod5=11\bmod5=1\) and \(7\bmod5=2\), the buckets contain:

    0: []
1: [1, 6, 11]
2: [7]
3: []
4: []

  2. Searching for 6 first visits bucket 1 and compares against 1 and then 6, finding the target on the second comparison.

  3. Equal hash values mean only that the elements land in the same bucket, not that the elements themselves are equal. Separate chaining keeps all colliding elements in the bucket and compares them one by one during a search, so 1, 6, and 11 do not overwrite one another.

items.title: 2.   Where do elements go when a hash table grows?
items.text:
A hash table using separate chaining initially has five buckets and the hash function \(h(x)=x\bmod5\). The keys [1, 6, 11] are all in bucket 1.

The table is now expanded to seven buckets, and the hash function becomes \(h(x)=x\bmod7\):

  1. Calculate the new bucket number for each of 1, 6, and 11.
  2. Which buckets contain elements after the expansion?
  3. Can the list in the old bucket 1 simply be copied unchanged into the new bucket 1? Explain using your results from questions 1 and 2.
Reference answer

  1. The new bucket numbers are:

    • \(1\bmod7=1\);
    • \(6\bmod7=6\);
    • \(11\bmod7=4\).

  2. Bucket 1 holds 1, bucket 4 holds 11, and bucket 6 holds 6. The three keys no longer share one bucket.

  3. The list cannot simply be copied unchanged. A bucket number is the remainder of the key divided by the number of buckets. When that number changes from 5 to 7, a key's bucket may change, so every key's position must be recalculated. If we copied the old bucket 1 unchanged, subsequent searches for 6 and 11 using the new formula would visit buckets 6 and 4, respectively, and fail to find them.

items.title: 3.   Can we still find 11 after deleting 6?
items.text:
A hash table has five positions with indices 0-4 and uses the hash function \(h(x)=x\bmod5\). When a collision occurs, it starts at the computed index and searches to the right for the first empty position.

Insert [1, 6, 11] in order:

  1. At which index is each number ultimately stored?
  2. Which indices are checked, in order, when searching for 11?
  3. Suppose deleting 6 marks its position as an empty slot that has never been used, and a search stops on reaching an empty slot. What happens when we search for 11 again? Is the result correct? If not, how can we avoid the problem?
Reference answer

  1. The number 1 is stored at index 1. The number 6 also maps to index 1, so after the collision it is stored at index 2. The number 11 likewise starts at index 1, skips occupied indices 1 and 2, and is finally stored at index 3.

  2. Searching for 11 checks indices 1, 2, 3 in order and finds it at index 3.

  3. If index 2 is marked as an empty slot that has never been used, a search for 11 checks index 1 and then stops at index 2, incorrectly concluding that 11 is absent. Deletion should leave a deleted marker instead: a search continues to the next index when it encounters this marker, wrapping from index 4 to index 0. Later insertions can still reuse the position.

items.text:

Determine whether the rearrangement can produce t. Return true if it can, or false otherwise. Use a hash table to record the frequency of each letter; do not sort the characters in either string.

  2. Use a hash table to record each letter's count; increment the appropriate count by 1 while scanning s.
  3. Decrement the appropriate count by 1 while scanning t. The character frequencies match only if all counts end at 0.

items.title: 6.3   Hash algorithms
items.text:
The previous two sections explained how hash tables work and how collisions are resolved. Whether we use open addressing or separate chaining, these techniques keep the table working when collisions occur, but do not reduce how often collisions happen.

Frequent collisions can severely degrade performance. In the separate-chaining table shown below, the ideal case distributes pairs evenly among buckets for the best lookup efficiency. In the worst case, all pairs occupy the same bucket, degrading the time complexity to \(O(n)\).

Figure 6-8   Best and worst cases for hash collisions

The hash function determines how key-value pairs are distributed. Recall its two steps: calculate a hash value, then take it modulo the array length:

index = hash(key) % capacity

For a fixed capacity, the hash algorithm hash() determines the output, and therefore the distribution of pairs in the table.

To lower the likelihood of collisions, we should therefore focus on designing hash().

items.title: 6.3.1   Goals of a hash algorithm
items.text:
To build a hash table that is both fast and reliable, its hash algorithm should have these properties.

  • Determinism: The same input must always produce the same output, ensuring reliable lookup.
  • Efficiency: Calculating a hash should be fast. Lower computational overhead makes the table more practical.
  • Uniform distribution: The algorithm should distribute pairs evenly across the table. More uniform distribution means fewer collisions.

Hash algorithms also have many applications beyond hash tables.

  • Password storage: To protect passwords, systems usually store password hashes rather than plaintext passwords. When a user enters a password, the system hashes it and compares the result with the stored hash. A match means the password is accepted.
  • Data-integrity checking: A sender can calculate a hash of the data and send it alongside the data. The receiver recomputes the hash and compares it with the received hash. A match indicates that the data is intact.

Cryptographic applications require stronger security properties to prevent reverse engineering, such as recovering an original password from its hash.

  • One-wayness: The hash should not reveal any information about the input data.
  • Collision resistance: Finding two different inputs with the same hash should be extremely difficult.
  • Avalanche effect: A small input change should produce a large, unpredictable output change.

Uniform distribution and collision resistance are independent concepts. Uniform output does not guarantee collision resistance. For example, with random keys, key % 100 can produce uniform outputs. But this algorithm is too simple: all keys with the same last two digits give the same output. It is therefore easy to infer a usable key from a hash and crack a password.

items.title: 6.3.2   Designing a hash algorithm
items.text:
Designing a hash algorithm is complex and involves many factors. For less demanding uses, however, we can devise simple algorithms.

  • Additive hashing: Add the ASCII codes of all input characters and use the sum as the hash.
  • Multiplicative hashing: Use multiplication to mix values, multiplying by a constant each round and accumulating character ASCII codes into the hash.
  • XOR hashing: Accumulate each input element into a hash using exclusive OR.
  • Rotational hashing: Accumulate each character's ASCII code into a hash, rotating the hash before each accumulation.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby simple_hash.py
def add_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """Additive hash"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash += ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

def mul_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """Multiplicative hash"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash = 31 * hash + ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

def xor_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """XOR hash"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash ^= ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

def rot_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """Rotating hash"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash = (hash << 4) ^ (hash >> 28) ^ ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

Each algorithm ends by taking the result modulo the large prime \(1000000007\) to keep it within a suitable range. Why emphasize a prime modulus? What goes wrong with a composite modulus? This is an interesting question.

The conclusion is that using a large prime modulus helps make hash values as uniformly distributed as possible. Because a prime shares no nontrivial factors with other numbers, it reduces periodic patterns introduced by the modulo operation and thus avoids collisions.

For example, choose the composite modulus \(9\), which is divisible by \(3\). Every key divisible by \(3\) then maps to one of just three hash values: \(0\), \(3\), or \(6\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{modulus} & = 9 \newline \text{key} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, \dots \} \newline \text{hash} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 0, 3, 6, 0, 3, 6, 0, 3, 6,\dots \} \end{aligned} \]

If the input keys follow this arithmetic progression, the hash values cluster, increasing collisions. Now replace the modulus with the prime \(13\). With no common factor between the key pattern and the modulus, the output becomes noticeably more uniform.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{modulus} & = 13 \newline \text{key} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, \dots \} \newline \text{hash} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 2, 5, 8, 11, 1, 4, 7, \dots \} \end{aligned} \]

If the keys are already uniformly random, either a prime or a composite modulus can produce uniformly distributed hashes. When the keys have a periodic pattern, however, a composite modulus is more likely to cause clustering.

We therefore usually choose a prime modulus, preferably a large one, to suppress periodic patterns as much as possible and make the algorithm more robust.

items.title: 6.3.3   Common hash algorithms
items.text:
The simple algorithms above are fragile and fall well short of our design goals. Addition and XOR are commutative, for example, so additive and XOR hashing cannot distinguish strings containing the same characters in different orders. This can increase collisions and create security problems.

In practice, standard algorithms such as MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3 are commonly used. They map inputs of arbitrary length to fixed-length hash values.

Over nearly a century, hash algorithms have continually evolved. Some researchers work to improve their performance, while others, along with hackers, search for security weaknesses. Table 6-2 lists commonly used algorithms.

  • MD5 and SHA-1 have been successfully attacked repeatedly and have been retired from security applications.
  • SHA-256, part of the SHA-2 family, is among the most secure hash algorithms. No successful attack has been reported, so it is widely used in security applications and protocols.
  • SHA-3 has lower implementation overhead and higher computational efficiency than SHA-2, but is not yet as widely used.

Table 6-2   Common hash algorithms

MD5 SHA-1 SHA-2 SHA-3 Introduced 1992 1995 2002 2008 Output length 128 bit 160 bit 256/512 bit 224/256/384/512 bit Hash collisions More frequent More frequent Rare Rare Security Low; successfully attacked Low; successfully attacked High High Applications Deprecated; still used for integrity checks Deprecated Cryptocurrency transaction verification, digital signatures, and more Can replace SHA-2

items.title: 6.3.4   Hash values of data structures
items.text:
Hash-table keys can be integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and other types. Programming languages usually provide built-in hashing for these types to calculate bucket indices. In Python, for example, hash() calculates hash values for various types.

  • Integers and Booleans have hash values equal to their own values.
  • Hashing floating-point numbers and strings is more complex; interested readers can explore the details.
  • A tuple's hash combines the hashes of its individual elements into one value.
  • An object's hash is based on its memory address. Overriding its hash method allows hashing by content instead.

Tip

Built-in hash functions differ in their definitions and implementations across programming languages.

In many programming languages, only immutable objects can serve as hash-table keys. If a list, a dynamic array, were used as a key, changing its contents would change its hash, making the original value impossible to retrieve from the table.

Custom objects, such as linked-list nodes, can be hashable even though their member variables are mutable. Their hash is usually based on their memory address, which stays the same even when their contents change.

You may notice different hash values when running the program in different consoles. Each time the Python interpreter starts, it adds a random salt to its string hash function. This helps prevent HashDoS attacks and improves security.

items.title: 6.2   Hash collisions
items.text:
As discussed in the previous section, a hash function's input space is usually much larger than its output space, so collisions are theoretically unavoidable. For example, if the input space is all integers and the output space is limited to the array's capacity, multiple integers must map to the same bucket index.

Hash collisions can produce incorrect lookup results and make a hash table unusable. One solution is to expand the table whenever a collision occurs until the collision disappears. This simple, brute-force approach works, but is inefficient because expansion requires substantial data movement and hash computation. We can improve efficiency with the following strategies.

  1. Improve the data structure so that it works correctly even when collisions occur.
  2. Expand only when necessary, when collisions become sufficiently frequent.

The main structural approaches are “separate chaining” and “open addressing.”

items.title: 6.2.1   Separate chaining
items.text:
In the original hash table, each bucket holds only one key-value pair. Separate chaining replaces this single element with a linked list. Each pair becomes a node, and all colliding pairs are stored in the same list. An example is shown below.

Figure 6-5   A hash table using separate chaining

The operations change as follows.

  • Lookup: Hash the input key to obtain a bucket index, access the list's head, and traverse the list comparing keys to find the target pair.
  • Insertion: Use the hash function to access the list's head, then add the node containing the key-value pair to the list.
  • Deletion: Use the hash function to locate the list, traverse it to find the target node, and remove that node.

Separate chaining has the following limitations.

  • More space: Linked lists store node pointers and consume more memory than arrays.
  • Slower lookup: Finding an element requires a linear scan of the list.

The code below gives a simple implementation. Keep two points in mind.

  • Lists, implemented as dynamic arrays, replace linked lists to simplify the code. The hash table is an array of buckets, each of which is a list.
  • The implementation includes expansion: when the load factor exceeds \(\frac{2}{3}\), the table's capacity is doubled to \(2\) times its original size.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby hash_map_chaining.py
class HashMapChaining:
    """Hash table with separate chaining"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self.size = 0  # Number of key-value pairs
        self.capacity = 4  # Hash table capacity
        self.load_thres = 2.0 / 3.0  # Load factor threshold that triggers capacity growth
        self.extend_ratio = 2  # Capacity growth factor
        self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(self.capacity)]  # Bucket array

    def hash_func(self, key: int) -> int:
        """Hash function"""
        return key % self.capacity

    def load_factor(self) -> float:
        """Load factor"""
        return self.size / self.capacity

    def get(self, key: int) -> str | None:
        """Lookup operation"""
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        bucket = self.buckets[index]
        # Traverse the bucket; if key is found, return its corresponding val
        for pair in bucket:
            if pair.key == key:
                return pair.val
        # Return None if key is not found
        return None

    def put(self, key: int, val: str):
        """Insert operation"""
        # Grow the capacity when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if self.load_factor() > self.load_thres:
            self.extend()
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        bucket = self.buckets[index]
        # Traverse the bucket; if the specified key is found, update its val and return
        for pair in bucket:
            if pair.key == key:
                pair.val = val
                return
        # If key is absent, append the key-value pair at the end
        pair = Pair(key, val)
        bucket.append(pair)
        self.size += 1

    def remove(self, key: int):
        """Remove operation"""
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        bucket = self.buckets[index]
        # Traverse the bucket and remove the key-value pair
        for pair in bucket:
            if pair.key == key:
                bucket.remove(pair)
                self.size -= 1
                break

    def extend(self):
        """Grow the hash table capacity"""
        # Keep a reference to the original hash table
        buckets = self.buckets
        # Initialize a new hash table with the expanded capacity
        self.capacity *= self.extend_ratio
        self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(self.capacity)]
        self.size = 0
        # Move the key-value pairs from the original hash table to the new one
        for bucket in buckets:
            for pair in bucket:
                self.put(pair.key, pair.val)

    def print(self):
        """Print the hash table"""
        for bucket in self.buckets:

    }

    ~HashMapChaining() {
        for (auto &bucket : buckets) {
            for (Pair *pair : bucket) {
                // Free memory
                delete pair;
            }
        }
    }

    /* Hash function */
    int hashFunc(int key) {
        return key % capacity;
    }

    /* Load factor */
    double loadFactor() {
        return (double)size / (double)capacity;
    }

    string get(int key) {
        int index = hashFunc(key);
        // Traverse the bucket; if key is found, return its corresponding val
        for (Pair *pair : buckets[index]) {
            if (pair->key == key) {
                return pair->val;
            }
        }
        // Return an empty string if key is not found
        return "";
    }

    /* Insert operation */
    void put(int key, string val) {
        // Grow the capacity when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if (loadFactor() > loadThres) {
            extend();
        }
        int index = hashFunc(key);
        // Traverse the bucket; if the specified key is found, update its val and return
        for (Pair *pair : buckets[index]) {
            if (pair->key == key) {
                pair->val = val;
                return;
            }
        }
        // If key is absent, append the key-value pair at the end
        buckets[index].push_back(new Pair(key, val));

        auto &bucket = buckets[index];
        // Traverse the bucket and remove the key-value pair
        for (int i = 0; i < bucket.size(); i++) {

                bucket.erase(bucket.begin() + i); // Remove the key-value pair from the list
                delete tmp;                       // Free memory
                size--;
                return;
            }
        }
    }

    void extend() {
        // Keep a copy of the original bucket array
        vector<vector<Pair *>> bucketsTmp = buckets;

        buckets.resize(capacity);

        for (auto &bucket : bucketsTmp) {
            for (Pair *pair : bucket) {
                put(pair->key, pair->val);
                // Free memory
                delete pair;
            }
        }
    }

/* Hash function */

}

/* Load factor */

}

/* Lookup operation */
func (m *hashMapChaining) get(key int) string {

    bucket := m.buckets[idx]
    // Traverse the bucket; if key is found, return its corresponding val
    for _, p := range bucket {

            return p.val
        }
    }
    // If key is not found, return an empty string
    return ""
}

/* Insert operation */
func (m *hashMapChaining) put(key int, val string) {
    // Grow the capacity when the load factor exceeds the threshold
    if m.loadFactor() > m.loadThres {
        m.extend()
    }
    idx := m.hashFunc(key)
    // Traverse the bucket; if the specified key is found, update its val and return
    for i := range m.buckets[idx] {
        if m.buckets[idx][i].key == key {
            m.buckets[idx][i].val = val
            return
        }
    }
    // If key is absent, append the key-value pair at the end
    p := pair{
        key: key,
        val: val,
    }
    m.buckets[idx] = append(m.buckets[idx], p)
    m.size += 1
}

/* Remove operation */
func (m *hashMapChaining) remove(key int) {
    idx := m.hashFunc(key)
    // Traverse the bucket and remove the key-value pair
    for i, p := range m.buckets[idx] {
        if p.key == key {
            // Remove the element from the slice
            m.buckets[idx] = append(m.buckets[idx][:i], m.buckets[idx][i+1:]...)
            m.size -= 1
            break
        }
    }
}

/* Grow the hash table capacity */
func (m *hashMapChaining) extend() {
    // Save a copy of the original hash table
    tmpBuckets := make([][]pair, len(m.buckets))
    for i := 0; i < len(m.buckets); i++ {
        tmpBuckets[i] = make([]pair, len(m.buckets[i]))
        copy(tmpBuckets[i], m.buckets[i])
    }
    // Initialize a new hash table with the expanded capacity
    m.capacity *= m.extendRatio
    m.buckets = make([][]pair, m.capacity)
    for i := 0; i < m.capacity; i++ {
        m.buckets[i] = make([]pair, 0)
    }
    m.size = 0
    // Move the key-value pairs from the original hash table to the new one
    for _, bucket := range tmpBuckets {
        for _, p := range bucket {
            m.put(p.key, p.val)
        }
    }

    fn load_factor(&self) -> f32 {
        self.size as f32 / self.capacity as f32
    }

    /* Remove operation */
    fn remove(&mut self, key: i32) -> Option<String> {
        let index = self.hash_func(key);

        // Traverse the bucket and remove the key-value pair
        for (i, p) in self.buckets[index].iter_mut().enumerate() {
            if p.key == key {
                let pair = self.buckets[index].remove(i);
                self.size -= 1;
                return Some(pair.val);
            }
        }

        // Return None if key is not found
        None
    }

    /* Grow the hash table capacity */
    fn extend(&mut self) {
        // Temporarily take ownership of the original buckets
        let buckets_tmp = std::mem::take(&mut self.buckets);

        // Initialize a new hash table with the expanded capacity
        self.capacity *= self.extend_ratio;
        self.buckets = vec![Vec::new(); self.capacity as usize];
        self.size = 0;

        // Move the key-value pairs from the original hash table to the new one
        for bucket in buckets_tmp {
            for pair in bucket {
                self.put(pair.key, pair.val);
            }
        }
    }

    /* Print the hash table */
    fn print(&self) {
        for bucket in &self.buckets {
            let mut res = Vec::new();
            for pair in bucket {
                res.push(format!("{} -> {}", pair.key, pair.val));
            }
            println!("{:?}", res);
        }
    }

    /* Insert operation */
    fn put(&mut self, key: i32, val: String) {
        // Grow the capacity when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if self.load_factor() > self.load_thres {
            self.extend();
        }

        let index = self.hash_func(key);

        // Traverse the bucket; if the specified key is found, update its val and return
        for pair in self.buckets[index].iter_mut() {
            if pair.key == key {
                pair.val = val;
                return;
            }
        }

        // If key is absent, append the key-value pair at the end
        let pair = Pair { key, val };
        self.buckets[index].push(pair);
        self.size += 1;
    }

    /* Lookup operation */
    fn get(&self, key: i32) -> Option<&str> {
        let index = self.hash_func(key);

        // Traverse the bucket; if key is found, return its corresponding val
        for pair in self.buckets[index].iter() {
            if pair.key == key {
                return Some(&pair.val);
            }
        }

        // Return None if key is not found
        None
    }
}

    hashMap->buckets = (Node **)malloc(hashMap->capacity * sizeof(Node *));
    for (int i = 0; i < hashMap->capacity; i++) {
        hashMap->buckets[i] = NULL;
    }
    return hashMap;
}

/* Destructor */
void delHashMapChaining(HashMapChaining *hashMap) {
    for (int i = 0; i < hashMap->capacity; i++) {
        Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[i];
        while (cur) {
            Node *tmp = cur;
            cur = cur->next;
            free(tmp->pair);
            free(tmp);
        }
    }
    free(hashMap->buckets);
    free(hashMap);
}

/* Hash function */
int hashFunc(HashMapChaining *hashMap, int key) {
    return key % hashMap->capacity;
}

/* Load factor */
double loadFactor(HashMapChaining *hashMap) {
    return (double)hashMap->size / (double)hashMap->capacity;
}

/* Lookup operation */
char *get(HashMapChaining *hashMap, int key) {
    int index = hashFunc(hashMap, key);
    // Traverse the bucket; if key is found, return its corresponding val
    Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[index];
    while (cur) {
        if (cur->pair->key == key) {
            return cur->pair->val;
        }
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    return ""; // Return an empty string if key is not found
}

/* Insert operation */
void put(HashMapChaining *hashMap, int key, const char *val) {
    // Grow the capacity when the load factor exceeds the threshold
    if (loadFactor(hashMap) > hashMap->loadThres) {
        extend(hashMap);
    }
    int index = hashFunc(hashMap, key);
    // Traverse the bucket; if the specified key is found, update its val and return
    Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[index];
    while (cur) {
        if (cur->pair->key == key) {
            strcpy(cur->pair->val, val); // If the specified key is found, update its val and return
            return;
        }
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    // If key is absent, add the key-value pair at the head of the linked list
    Pair *newPair = (Pair *)malloc(sizeof(Pair));
    newPair->key = key;
    strcpy(newPair->val, val);
    Node *newNode = (Node *)malloc(sizeof(Node));
    newNode->pair = newPair;
    newNode->next = hashMap->buckets[index];
    hashMap->buckets[index] = newNode;
    hashMap->size++;
}

/* Grow the hash table capacity */
void extend(HashMapChaining *hashMap) {
    // Keep a reference to the original hash table
    int oldCapacity = hashMap->capacity;
    Node **oldBuckets = hashMap->buckets;
    // Initialize a new hash table with the expanded capacity
    hashMap->capacity *= hashMap->extendRatio;
    hashMap->buckets = (Node **)malloc(hashMap->capacity * sizeof(Node *));
    for (int i = 0; i < hashMap->capacity; i++) {
        hashMap->buckets[i] = NULL;
    }
    hashMap->size = 0;
    // Move the key-value pairs from the original hash table to the new one
    for (int i = 0; i < oldCapacity; i++) {
        Node *cur = oldBuckets[i];
        while (cur) {
            put(hashMap, cur->pair->key, cur->pair->val);
            Node *temp = cur;
            cur = cur->next;
            // Free memory
            free(temp->pair);
            free(temp);
        }
    }

    free(oldBuckets);
}

/* Remove operation */
void removeItem(HashMapChaining *hashMap, int key) {
    int index = hashFunc(hashMap, key);
    Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[index];
    Node *pre = NULL;
    while (cur) {
        if (cur->pair->key == key) {
            // Remove the key-value pair from the list
            if (pre) {
                pre->next = cur->next;
            } else {
                hashMap->buckets[index] = cur->next;
            }
            // Free memory
            free(cur->pair);
            free(cur);
            hashMap->size--;
            return;
        }
        pre = cur;
        cur = cur->next;
    }
}

/* Print the hash table */
void print(HashMapChaining *hashMap) {
    for (int i = 0; i < hashMap->capacity; i++) {
        Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[i];
        printf("[");
        while (cur) {
            printf("%d -> %s, ", cur->pair->key, cur->pair->val);
            cur = cur->next;
        }
        printf("]\n");
    }
}

        }
        // Return null if key is not found

        for (pair in bucket) {
            if (pair.key == key) {
                pair._val = _val

        // If key is absent, append the key-value pair at the end
        val pair = Pair(key, _val)

items.title: 6.2.2   Open addressing
items.text:
Open addressing handles collisions by probing multiple locations without introducing another data structure. Common strategies include linear probing, quadratic probing, and multiple hashing.

We use linear probing to explain how an open-addressing hash table works.

items.title: 1.   Linear probing
items.text:
Linear probing searches with a fixed step size. Its operations differ from those of a basic hash table.

  • Insertion: Calculate the bucket index using the hash function. If the bucket is occupied, scan forward from that position with a fixed step size, usually \(1\), until an empty bucket is found, then insert the element.
  • Lookup: If a collision is encountered, scan forward with the same step size until the target is found, then return its value. An empty bucket means the target is absent, so return None.

Figure 6-6 shows key-value pairs in an open-addressing table using linear probing. With this hash function, keys sharing the same last two digits map to the same bucket. Linear probing stores them successively in that bucket and the following buckets.

Figure 6-6   Distribution of key-value pairs with linear probing

However, linear probing is prone to clustering. The longer a run of occupied positions becomes, the more likely a collision is to occur within it, causing the cluster to grow further. This feedback loop eventually degrades insertion, deletion, lookup, and update performance.

We cannot simply delete an element from an open-addressing table. Deletion would leave an empty bucket, None. A lookup stops when linear probing reaches such a bucket, making later elements in the probe sequence inaccessible and potentially reporting them as absent, as shown below.

Figure 6-7   Lookup problems caused by deletion in open addressing

To solve this, use lazy deletion: rather than simply removing the entry, mark its bucket with the constant TOMBSTONE. Both None and TOMBSTONE represent available buckets that can hold a new pair. Unlike None, however, a TOMBSTONE does not stop a search, because further pairs may lie beyond it.

However, lazy deletion can accelerate performance degradation. Each deletion leaves a marker. As TOMBSTONE entries accumulate, searches may need to skip many of them before reaching the target, increasing search time.

To address this, record the first TOMBSTONE encountered during probing and swap the target entry with it when found. On each lookup or insertion, this moves the entry closer to its ideal location—the start of the probe sequence—and improves lookup efficiency.

The code below implements linear probing with lazy deletion. To use the table's space more fully, treat the array as circular: after reaching the end, wrap around to the beginning.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby hash_map_open_addressing.py
class HashMapOpenAddressing:
    """Hash table with open addressing"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self.size = 0  # Number of key-value pairs
        self.capacity = 4  # Hash table capacity
        self.load_thres = 2.0 / 3.0  # Load factor threshold that triggers capacity growth
        self.extend_ratio = 2  # Capacity growth factor
        self.buckets: list[Pair | None] = [None] * self.capacity  # Bucket array
        self.TOMBSTONE = Pair(-1, "-1")  # Tombstone marker

    def hash_func(self, key: int) -> int:
        """Hash function"""
        return key % self.capacity

    def load_factor(self) -> float:
        """Load factor"""
        return self.size / self.capacity

    def find_bucket(self, key: int) -> int:
        """Find the bucket index for key"""
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        first_tombstone = -1
        # Probe linearly until an empty bucket is reached
        while self.buckets[index] is not None:
            # If key is found, return its bucket index
            if self.buckets[index].key == key:
                # If a tombstone was encountered earlier, move the key-value pair to that index
                if first_tombstone != -1:
                    self.buckets[first_tombstone] = self.buckets[index]
                    self.buckets[index] = self.TOMBSTONE
                    return first_tombstone  # Return the bucket index after the move
                return index  # Return the bucket index
            # Record the first tombstone encountered
            if first_tombstone == -1 and self.buckets[index] is self.TOMBSTONE:
                first_tombstone = index
            # Calculate the bucket index, wrapping to the beginning after the end
            index = (index + 1) % self.capacity
        # If key is absent, return the index for insertion
        return index if first_tombstone == -1 else first_tombstone

    def get(self, key: int) -> str:
        """Lookup operation"""
        # Find the bucket index for key
        index = self.find_bucket(key)
        # If the key-value pair is found, return its val
        if self.buckets[index] not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
            return self.buckets[index].val
        # Return None if the key-value pair is absent
        return None

    def put(self, key: int, val: str):
        """Insert operation"""
        # Grow the capacity when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if self.load_factor() > self.load_thres:
            self.extend()
        # Find the bucket index for key
        index = self.find_bucket(key)
        # If the key-value pair is found, overwrite val and return
        if self.buckets[index] not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
            self.buckets[index].val = val
            return
        # If the key-value pair is absent, insert it
        self.buckets[index] = Pair(key, val)
        self.size += 1

    def remove(self, key: int):
        """Remove operation"""
        # Find the bucket index for key
        index = self.find_bucket(key)
        # If the key-value pair is found, replace it with a tombstone
        if self.buckets[index] not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
            self.buckets[index] = self.TOMBSTONE
            self.size -= 1

    def extend(self):
        """Grow the hash table capacity"""
        # Keep a reference to the original hash table
        buckets_tmp = self.buckets
        # Initialize a new hash table with the expanded capacity
        self.capacity *= self.extend_ratio
        self.buckets = [None] * self.capacity
        self.size = 0
        # Move the key-value pairs from the original hash table to the new one
        for pair in buckets_tmp:
            if pair not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
                self.put(pair.key, pair.val)

    def print(self):
        """Print the hash table"""
        for pair in self.buckets:
            if pair is None:
                print("None")
            elif pair is self.TOMBSTONE:
                print("TOMBSTONE")
            else:
                print(pair.key, "->", pair.val)

/* Hash table with open addressing */
class HashMapOpenAddressing {
  private:
    int size;                             // Number of key-value pairs
    int capacity = 4;                     // Hash table capacity
    const double loadThres = 2.0 / 3.0;     // Load factor threshold that triggers capacity growth
    const int extendRatio = 2;            // Capacity growth factor
    vector<Pair *> buckets;               // Bucket array
    Pair *TOMBSTONE = new Pair(-1, "-1"); // Tombstone marker

  public:
    /* Constructor */
    HashMapOpenAddressing() : size(0), buckets(capacity, nullptr) {
    }

    /* Destructor */
    ~HashMapOpenAddressing() {
        for (Pair *pair : buckets) {
            if (pair != nullptr && pair != TOMBSTONE) {
                delete pair;
            }
        }
        delete TOMBSTONE;
    }

    /* Hash function */
    int hashFunc(int key) {
        return key % capacity;
    }

    /* Load factor */
    double loadFactor() {
        return (double)size / capacity;
    }

    /* Find the bucket index for key */
    int findBucket(int key) {
        int index = hashFunc(key);
        int firstTombstone = -1;
        // Probe linearly until an empty bucket is reached
        while (buckets[index] != nullptr) {
            // If key is found, return its bucket index
            if (buckets[index]->key == key) {
                // If a tombstone was encountered earlier, move the key-value pair to that index
                if (firstTombstone != -1) {
                    buckets[firstTombstone] = buckets[index];
                    buckets[index] = TOMBSTONE;
                    return firstTombstone; // Return the bucket index after the move
                }
                return index; // Return the bucket index
            }
            // Record the first tombstone encountered
            if (firstTombstone == -1 && buckets[index] == TOMBSTONE) {
                firstTombstone = index;
            }
            // Calculate the bucket index, wrapping to the beginning after the end
            index = (index + 1) % capacity;
        }
        // If key is absent, return the index for insertion
        return firstTombstone == -1 ? index : firstTombstone;
    }

    /* Lookup operation */
    string get(int key) {
        // Find the bucket index for key
        int index = findBucket(key);
        // If the key-value pair is found, return its val
        if (buckets[index] != nullptr && buckets[index] != TOMBSTONE) {
            return buckets[index]->val;
        }
        // Return an empty string if the key-value pair does not exist
        return "";
    }

    /* Insert operation */
    void put(int key, string val) {
        // Grow the capacity when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if (loadFactor() > loadThres) {
            extend();
        }
        // Find the bucket index for key
        int index = findBucket(key);
        // If the key-value pair is found, overwrite val and return
        if (buckets[index] != nullptr && buckets[index] != TOMBSTONE) {
            buckets[index]->val = val;
            return;
        }
        // If the key-value pair is absent, insert it
        buckets[index] = new Pair(key, val);
        size++;
    }

    /* Remove operation */
    void remove(int key) {
        // Find the bucket index for key
        int index = findBucket(key);
        // If the key-value pair is found, replace it with a tombstone
        if (buckets[index] != nullptr && buckets[index] != TOMBSTONE) {
            delete buckets[index];
            buckets[index] = TOMBSTONE;
            size--;
        }
    }

    /* Grow the hash table capacity */
    void extend() {
        // Keep a copy of the original bucket array
        vector<Pair *> bucketsTmp = buckets;
        // Initialize a new hash table with the expanded capacity
        capacity *= extendRatio;
        buckets = vector<Pair *>(capacity, nullptr);
        size = 0;
        // Move the key-value pairs from the original hash table to the new one
        for (Pair *pair : bucketsTmp) {
            if (pair != nullptr && pair != TOMBSTONE) {
                put(pair->key, pair->val);
                delete pair;
            }
        }
    }

    /* Print the hash table */
    void print() {
        for (Pair *pair : buckets) {
            if (pair == nullptr) {
                cout << "nullptr" << endl;
            } else if (pair == TOMBSTONE) {
                cout << "TOMBSTONE" << endl;
            } else {
                cout << pair->key << " -> " << pair->val << endl;
            }
        }
    }
};

                }

            // Record the first tombstone encountered

                firstTombstone = index;

            // Calculate the bucket index, wrapping to the beginning after the end

    /* Lookup operation */

        int index = findBucket(key);

            return buckets[index].val;

        // Return null if the key-value pair is absent

        // If the key-value pair is found, overwrite val and return

func newHashMapOpenAddressing() *hashMapOpenAddressing {
