/* Get the k-th digit of num, where exp = 10^(k-1) */
int digit(int num, int exp) {
    // Passing exp instead of k avoids repeatedly performing expensive exponentiation here
    return (num / exp) % 10;
}

/* Counting sort (sort nums by the k-th digit) */
void countingSortDigit(vector<int> &nums, int exp) {
    // Decimal digits range from 0 to 9, so the bucket array needs length 10
    vector<int> counter(10, 0);
    int n = nums.size();
    // Count the occurrences of each digit from 0 to 9
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int d = digit(nums[i], exp); // Get the k-th digit of nums[i] and store it in d
        counter[d]++;                // Count the occurrences of digit d
    }
    // Compute prefix sums to convert occurrence counts into array positions
    for (int i = 1; i < 10; i++) {
        counter[i] += counter[i - 1];
    }
    // Traverse in reverse and place each element into res according to the bucket counts
    vector<int> res(n, 0);
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        int d = digit(nums[i], exp);
        int j = counter[d] - 1; // Get the destination index j for digit d in the array
        res[j] = nums[i];       // Place the current element at index j
        counter[d]--;           // Decrease the count for d by 1
    }
    // Overwrite the original array nums with the result
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        nums[i] = res[i];
}

/* Radix sort */
void radixSort(vector<int> &nums) {
    // Get the largest array element to determine the maximum number of digits
    int m = *max_element(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    // Process digits from least significant to most significant
    for (int exp = 1; exp <= m; exp *= 10)
        // Apply counting sort to the k-th digit of the array elements
        // k = 1 -> exp = 1
        // k = 2 -> exp = 10
        // That is, exp = 10^(k-1)
        countingSortDigit(nums, exp);
}

    int n = nums.length;
    // Count the occurrences of each digit from 0 to 9
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

        counter[i] += counter[i - 1];

    int[] res = new int[n];
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        int d = digit(nums[i], exp);

Why start with the least significant digit?

In successive rounds, a later sort takes precedence over an earlier one. For example, if the first round orders two elements as \(a < b\) but the second orders them as \(a > b\), the second result replaces the first. Higher digits have greater priority, so lower digits must be sorted first.

items.title: 11.10.2   Algorithm properties
items.text:
Compared with counting sort, radix sort handles a larger range of values, provided the data can be represented with a fixed number of digits and that number is not too large. For example, floating-point numbers are unsuitable because their digit count \(k\) may be so large that \(O(nk) \gg O(n^2)\).

  • Time complexity: \(O(nk)\); not adaptive. For \(n\) elements represented in base \(d\) with at most \(k\) digits, counting sort on one digit takes \(O(n + d)\) time. Sorting all \(k\) digits takes \(O((n + d)k)\). Usually \(d\) and \(k\) are relatively small, so the complexity approaches \(O(n)\).
  • Space complexity: \(O(n + d)\); not in-place. Like counting sort, radix sort requires arrays res and counter of lengths \(n\) and \(d\).
  • Stable. Radix sort is stable when the counting sort used within it is stable. If counting sort is not stable, radix sort cannot guarantee a correctly sorted result.

items.title: 11.2   Selection sort
items.text:
Selection sort works very simply: in each round, select the smallest element from the unsorted section and place it at the end of the sorted section.

For an array of length \(n\), the algorithm proceeds as shown below.

  1. Initially, all elements are unsorted, so the unsorted index interval is \([0, n-1]\).
  2. Select the smallest element in \([0, n-1]\) and swap it with the element at index \(0\). The first element is now sorted.
  3. Select the smallest element in \([1, n-1]\) and swap it with the element at index \(1\). The first two elements are now sorted.
  4. Continue in this way. After \(n - 1\) rounds of selection and swapping, the first \(n - 1\) elements are sorted.
  5. The remaining element must be the largest and needs no sorting. The array is now sorted.

def selection_sort(nums: list[int]):
    """Selection sort"""
    n = len(nums)
    # Outer loop: the unsorted range is [i, n-1]
    for i in range(n - 1):
        # Inner loop: find the smallest element in the unsorted range
        k = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if nums[j] < nums[k]:
                k = j  # Record the index of the smallest element
        # Swap the smallest element with the first element of the unsorted range
        nums[i], nums[k] = nums[k], nums[i]

        // Inner loop: find the smallest element in the unsorted range

        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[j] < nums[k])

    int n = nums.Length;
    // Outer loop: the unsorted range is [i, n-1]
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        // Inner loop: find the smallest element in the unsorted range
        int k = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[j] < nums[k])
                k = j; // Record the index of the smallest element
        }
        // Swap the smallest element with the first element of the unsorted range
        (nums[k], nums[i]) = (nums[i], nums[k]);
    }
}

items.title: 11.2.1   Algorithm properties
items.text:
• Time complexity: \(O(n^2)\); not adaptive. The outer loop runs \(n - 1\) times. The inner loop runs \(n - 1\) times in the first round and \(1\) time in the last, giving successive counts of \(n - 1\), \(n - 2\), \(\dots\), \(2\), and \(1\), which sum to \(\frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\).
  • Space complexity: \(O(1)\); in-place. Pointers \(i\) and \(j\) use constant extra space.
  • Not stable. As shown below, nums[i] may be swapped to the right of an equal element, changing their relative order.

Figure 11-3   An example showing that selection sort is not stable

items.title: 11.1   Sorting algorithms
items.text:
A sorting algorithm arranges a dataset in a specified order. Sorting is widely used because ordered data is often easier to search, analyze, and process efficiently.

As shown below, the data may consist of integers, floating-point numbers, characters, strings, and other types. The ordering rule can be chosen as needed: numerical magnitude, ASCII character order, or a custom rule.

Figure 11-1   Examples of data types and ordering rules

items.title: 11.1.1   Evaluation criteria
items.text:
Efficiency: We want low time complexity and few operations overall, corresponding to smaller constant factors in the complexity. Efficiency is especially important for large datasets.

In-place operation: An in-place sort works directly on the original array without an auxiliary array, saving memory. It usually moves data fewer times and runs faster as well.

Stability: A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements in the array.

Stable sorting is necessary for multilevel sorting. Suppose a table stores student names in its first column and ages in its second. An unstable sort may destroy the input's existing order:

# The input is already sorted by name
# (name, age)
  ('A', 19)
  ('B', 18)
  ('C', 21)
  ('D', 19)
  ('E', 23)

# Suppose an unstable algorithm sorts the list by age.
# The relative positions of ('D', 19) and ('A', 19) change,
# so the original ordering by name is lost
  ('B', 18)
  ('D', 19)
  ('A', 19)
  ('C', 21)
  ('E', 23)

Adaptiveness: An adaptive sort uses ordering already present in the input to reduce computation and improve efficiency. Its best-case time complexity is usually better than its average complexity.

Comparison-based or not: A comparison-based sort uses comparison operators (\(<\), \(=\), \(>\)) to determine the relative order of elements and sort the array. Its worst-case time complexity has a lower bound of \(\Omega(n \log n)\). A non-comparison sort does not use comparison operators and can achieve \(O(n)\) time, but is less broadly applicable.

items.title: 11.1.2   The ideal sorting algorithm
items.text:
Fast, in-place, stable, adaptive, and broadly applicable. No sorting algorithm with all these properties has yet been found. We must therefore choose according to the characteristics of the data and the requirements of the problem.

Next, we will study different sorting algorithms and analyze their strengths and weaknesses using these criteria.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Bubble sort sorts by swapping adjacent elements. Adding a flag to stop early improves its best-case time complexity to \(O(n)\).
  • Insertion sort inserts one element from the unsorted section into its correct position in the sorted section each round. Although its time complexity is \(O(n^2)\), its low operation count makes it popular for small datasets.
  • Quick sort sorts through partitioning. Repeatedly choosing the worst pivot can degrade its time complexity to \(O(n^2)\). Median or random pivot selection reduces this risk. Recursing on the shorter subarray reduces recursion depth and improves space complexity to \(O(\log n)\).
  • Merge sort has division and merging phases, exemplifying divide and conquer. Sorting an array requires an auxiliary array and \(O(n)\) space, while sorting a linked list can be optimized to use \(O(1)\) space.
  • Bucket sort has three steps: distribute data into buckets, sort within each bucket, and combine the results. It also uses divide and conquer and suits very large datasets. The key is distributing data evenly.
  • Counting sort is a special case of bucket sort that sorts by counting occurrences. It suits large datasets with a limited value range and requires data that can be converted to positive integers.
  • Radix sort sorts one digit at a time and requires data that can be represented as numbers with a fixed number of digits.
  • Ideally, a sorting algorithm would be efficient, stable, in-place, and adaptive. As with other data structures and algorithms, however, no single sorting algorithm meets all these requirements. In practice, choose one according to the data's properties.
  • Figure 11-19 compares common sorting algorithms in efficiency, stability, in-place operation, and adaptiveness.

Figure 11-19   Comparison of sorting algorithms

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: When is stability necessary in a sorting algorithm?

We often sort objects by one of their attributes. For example, students have names and heights, and we want a multilevel sort. First sort by name to obtain (A, 180) (B, 185) (C, 170) (D, 170), then sort by height. An unstable algorithm may produce (D, 170) (C, 170) (A, 180) (B, 185).

Students D and C have switched positions, breaking the ordering by name. This is not what we want.

Q: Can the right-to-left and left-to-right scans in partitioning be reversed?

No. When the leftmost element is the pivot, the right-to-left scan must come first. This may seem counterintuitive, so let us examine why.

The final step of partition() swaps nums[left] and nums[i]. Afterward, every element to the left of the pivot must be <= the pivot, so nums[left] >= nums[i] must hold before that swap. If we scan left to right first and fail to find a larger element, the loop stops at i == j, where it is possible that nums[j] == nums[i] > nums[left]. The final swap would then move an element larger than the pivot to the far left, causing partitioning to fail.

For example, given [0, 0, 0, 0, 1], scanning left to right first produces [1, 0, 0, 0, 0] after partitioning, which is incorrect.

Conversely, if we choose nums[right] as the pivot, we must scan left to right first.

Q: In the recursion-depth optimization for quick sort, why does choosing the shorter subarray keep the depth at most \(\log n\)?

Recursion depth is the number of recursive calls that have not yet returned. Each partition divides the array into two subarrays. After the optimization, the subarray chosen for recursion is at most half the original length. Even in the worst case, where it is always exactly half, the depth is \(\log n\).

In the original quick sort, we may repeatedly recurse on the larger subarray, with lengths \(n\), \(n - 1\), \(\dots\), \(2\), and \(1\) in the worst case, giving depth \(n\). The optimization prevents this.

Q: If all array elements are equal, does quick sort take \(O(n^2)\) time? How can we handle this degeneration?

Yes. In this case, consider partitioning into three sections: elements smaller than, equal to, and greater than the pivot. Recurse only on the smaller and greater sections. If all elements are equal, a single partition then completes the sort.

Q: Why is bucket sort's worst-case time complexity \(O(n^2)\)?

In the worst case, all elements fall into one bucket. If an \(O(n^2)\) algorithm is used to sort that bucket, the overall time complexity is \(O(n^2)\).

items.text:
Abstract

A stack is like cats piled on top of one another; a queue is like cats standing in line.

They represent last-in, first-out and first-in, first-out order, respectively.

items.title: 5.3   Deques
items.text:
A queue allows removal only at the front and insertion only at the rear. As shown below, a double-ended queue, or deque, is more flexible: elements can be added or removed at either end.

items.title: 5.3.2   Implementing a deque *
items.text: A deque is implemented much like a queue, using either a linked list or an array as the underlying structure.

items.title: 1.   Implementation with a doubly linked list
items.text:
In the previous section, we used a singly linked list for a queue because it easily supports removing the head for dequeueing and adding after the tail for enqueueing.

A deque supports both insertion and removal at both ends. It therefore needs the symmetric operations in the other direction as well. For this reason, we use a doubly linked list.

As shown below, treat the list's head and tail as the deque's front and rear, and support adding and removing nodes at both ends.

<1><2><3><4><5>

Figure 5-8   Insertion and removal in a linked-list deque

The implementation is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linkedlist_deque.py
class ListNode:
    """Doubly linked list node"""

    def __init__(self, val: int):
        """Constructor"""
        self.val: int = val
        self.next: ListNode | None = None  # Reference to the next node
        self.prev: ListNode | None = None  # Reference to the previous node

class LinkedListDeque:
    """Deque implemented with a doubly linked list"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self._front: ListNode | None = None  # Head node front
        self._rear: ListNode | None = None  # Tail node rear
        self._size: int = 0  # Deque size

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the deque size"""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the deque is empty"""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, num: int, is_front: bool):
        """Enqueue operation"""
        node = ListNode(num)
        # If the linked list is empty, make both front and rear point to node
        if self.is_empty():
            self._front = self._rear = node
        # Enqueue at the front
        elif is_front:
            # Add node to the head of the linked list
            self._front.prev = node
            node.next = self._front
            self._front = node  # Update the head node
        # Enqueue at the rear
        else:
            # Add node to the tail of the linked list
            self._rear.next = node
            node.prev = self._rear
            self._rear = node  # Update the tail node
        self._size += 1  # Update the deque size

    def push_first(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue at the front"""
        self.push(num, True)

    def push_last(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue at the rear"""
        self.push(num, False)

    def pop(self, is_front: bool) -> int:
        """Dequeue operation"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        # When the deque size is 1, the head and tail point to the same node
        if self._size == 1:
            val: int = self._front.val
            self._front = None
            self._rear = None
        # Dequeue from the front
        elif is_front:
            val: int = self._front.val  # Save the head node value
            # Remove the head node
            fnext: ListNode | None = self._front.next
            fnext.prev = None
            self._front.next = None
            self._front = fnext  # Update the head node
        # Dequeue from the rear
        else:
            val: int = self._rear.val  # Save the tail node value
            # Remove the tail node
            rprev: ListNode | None = self._rear.prev
            rprev.next = None

class LinkedListDeque {
  private:
    DoublyListNode *front, *rear; // Head node front and tail node rear
    int queSize = 0;              // Deque size

  public:
    /* Constructor */
    LinkedListDeque() : front(nullptr), rear(nullptr) {
    }

    /* Destructor */
    ~LinkedListDeque() {
        // Traverse the linked list and delete each node to free its memory
        DoublyListNode *pre, *cur = front;
        while (cur != nullptr) {
            pre = cur;
            cur = cur->next;
            delete pre;
        }
    }

    /* Get the deque size */
    int size() {
        return queSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the deque is empty */
    bool isEmpty() {
        return size() == 0;
    }

    /* Enqueue operation */
    void push(int num, bool isFront) {
        DoublyListNode *node = new DoublyListNode(num);
        // If the linked list is empty, make both front and rear point to node
        if (isEmpty())
            front = rear = node;
        // Enqueue at the front
        else if (isFront) {
            // Add node to the head of the linked list
            front->prev = node;
            node->next = front;
            front = node; // Update the head node
        // Enqueue at the rear
        } else {
            // Add node to the tail of the linked list
            rear->next = node;
            node->prev = rear;
            rear = node; // Update the tail node
        }
        queSize++; // Update the deque size
    }

    /* Enqueue at the front */
    void pushFirst(int num) {
        push(num, true);
    }

    /* Enqueue at the rear */
    void pushLast(int num) {
        push(num, false);
    }

    /* Dequeue operation */
    int pop(bool isFront) {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Deque is empty");
        int val;
        // When the deque size is 1, the head and tail point to the same node
        if (queSize == 1) {
            val = front->val;
            delete front; // Both point to the same node, so free it only once
            front = nullptr;
            rear = nullptr;
        }
        // Dequeue from the front
        else if (isFront) {
            val = front->val; // Save the head node value
            // Remove the head node
            DoublyListNode *fNext = front->next;
            fNext->prev = nullptr;
            front->next = nullptr;
            delete front;
            front = fNext; // Update the head node
        // Dequeue from the rear
        } else {
            val = rear->val; // Save the tail node value
            // Remove the tail node
            DoublyListNode *rPrev = rear->prev;
            rPrev->next = nullptr;
            rear->prev = nullptr;
            delete rear;
            rear = rPrev; // Update the tail node
        }
        queSize--; // Update the deque size
        return val;
    }

    /* Dequeue from the front */
    int popFirst() {
        return pop(true);
    }

    /* Dequeue from the rear */
    int popLast() {
        return pop(false);
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    int peekFirst() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Deque is empty");
        return front->val;
    }

    /* Access the rear element */
    int peekLast() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Deque is empty");
        return rear->val;
    }

      node.prev = _rear;
      _rear = node; // Update the tail node
    }
    _queSize++; // Update the queue size
  }

  /* Enqueue at the front */
  void pushFirst(int _num) {
    push(_num, true);
  }

  /* Enqueue at the rear */
  void pushLast(int _num) {
    push(_num, false);
  }

  /* Dequeue operation */
  int? pop(bool isFront) {
    // If the queue is empty, return null immediately
    if (isEmpty()) {
      return null;
    }
    final int val;
    // When the queue size is 1, the head and tail point to the same node
    if (_queSize == 1) {
      val = _front!.val;
      _front = null;
      _rear = null;
    }
    // Dequeue from the front
    else if (isFront) {
      val = _front!.val; // Save the head node value
      // Remove the head node
      ListNode? fNext = _front!.next;
      fNext!.prev = null;
      _front!.next = null;
      _front = fNext; // Update the head node
    // Dequeue from the rear
    } else {
      val = _rear!.val; // Save the tail node value
      // Remove the tail node
      ListNode? rPrev = _rear!.prev;
      rPrev!.next = null;
      _rear!.prev = null;
      _rear = rPrev; // Update the tail node
    }
    _queSize--; // Update the queue size
    return val;
  }

  /* Dequeue from the front */
  int? popFirst() {
    return pop(true);
  }

  /* Dequeue from the rear */
  int? popLast() {
    return pop(false);
  }

  /* Access the front element */
  int? peekFirst() {
    return _front?.val;
  }

  /* Access the rear element */
  int? peekLast() {
    return _rear?.val;
  }

  /* Return an array for printing */
  List<int> toArray() {
    ListNode? node = _front;
    final List<int> res = [];
    for (int i = 0; i < _queSize; i++) {
      res.add(node!.val);
      node = node.next;
    }

#[allow(dead_code)]
pub struct LinkedListDeque<T> {
    front: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, // Head node front
    rear: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>,  // Tail node rear
    que_size: usize,                         // Deque size
}

impl<T: Copy> LinkedListDeque<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            front: None,
            rear: None,
            que_size: 0,
        }
    }

    /* Get the deque size */
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        return self.que_size;
    }

    /* Check whether the deque is empty */
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        return self.que_size == 0;
    }

    /* Enqueue operation */
    fn push(&mut self, num: T, is_front: bool) {
        let node = ListNode::new(num);
        // Enqueue at the front
        if is_front {
            match self.front.take() {
                // If the linked list is empty, make both front and rear point to node
                None => {
                    self.rear = Some(node.clone());
                    self.front = Some(node);
                }
                // Add node to the head of the linked list
                Some(old_front) => {
                    old_front.borrow_mut().prev = Some(node.clone());
                    node.borrow_mut().next = Some(old_front);
                    self.front = Some(node); // Update the head node
                }
            }
        }
        // Enqueue at the rear
        else {
            match self.rear.take() {
                // If the linked list is empty, make both front and rear point to node
                None => {
                    self.front = Some(node.clone());
                    self.rear = Some(node);
                }
                // Add node to the tail of the linked list
                Some(old_rear) => {
                    old_rear.borrow_mut().next = Some(node.clone());
                    node.borrow_mut().prev = Some(old_rear);
                    self.rear = Some(node); // Update the tail node
                }
            }
        }
        self.que_size += 1; // Update the deque size
    }

    /* Enqueue at the front */
    pub fn push_first(&mut self, num: T) {
        self.push(num, true);
    }

    /* Enqueue at the rear */
    pub fn push_last(&mut self, num: T) {
        self.push(num, false);
    }

    /* Dequeue operation */
    fn pop(&mut self, is_front: bool) -> Option<T> {
        // If the deque is empty, return None immediately
        if self.is_empty() {
            return None;
        };
        // Dequeue from the front
        if is_front {
            self.front.take().map(|old_front| {
                match old_front.borrow_mut().next.take() {
                    Some(new_front) => {
                        new_front.borrow_mut().prev.take();
                        self.front = Some(new_front); // Update the head node
                    }
                    None => {
                        self.rear.take();
                    }
                }
                self.que_size -= 1; // Update the deque size
                old_front.borrow().val
            })
        }
        // Dequeue from the rear
        else {
            self.rear.take().map(|old_rear| {
                match old_rear.borrow_mut().prev.take() {
                    Some(new_rear) => {
                        new_rear.borrow_mut().next.take();
                        self.rear = Some(new_rear); // Update the tail node
                    }
                    None => {
                        self.front.take();
                    }
                }
                self.que_size -= 1; // Update the deque size
                old_rear.borrow().val
            })
        }
    }

    /* Dequeue from the front */
    pub fn pop_first(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        return self.pop(true);
    }

    /* Dequeue from the rear */
    pub fn pop_last(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        return self.pop(false);
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    pub fn peek_first(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.front.as_ref()
    }

    /* Access the rear element */
    pub fn peek_last(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.rear.as_ref()
    }

    /* Return a vector for printing */
    pub fn to_array(&self, head: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>) -> Vec<T> {
        let mut res: Vec<T> = Vec::new();
        fn recur<T: Copy>(cur: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, res: &mut Vec<T>) {
            if let Some(cur) = cur {
                res.push(cur.borrow().val);
                recur(cur.borrow().next.as_ref(), res);
            }
        }

        recur(head, &mut res);
        res
    }
}

typedef struct {

    int queSize;                  // Deque size
} LinkedListDeque;

/* Constructor */
LinkedListDeque *newLinkedListDeque() {
    LinkedListDeque *deque = (LinkedListDeque *)malloc(sizeof(LinkedListDeque));
    deque->front = NULL;
    deque->rear = NULL;
    deque->queSize = 0;
    return deque;
}

/* Destructor */
void delLinkedListdeque(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    // Free all nodes
    for (int i = 0; i < deque->queSize && deque->front != NULL; i++) {
        DoublyListNode *tmp = deque->front;
        deque->front = deque->front->next;
        free(tmp);
    }
    // Free the deque structure
    free(deque);
}

/* Get the queue size */
int size(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return deque->queSize;
}

/* Check whether the queue is empty */
bool empty(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return (size(deque) == 0);
}

/* Enqueue */
void push(LinkedListDeque *deque, int num, bool isFront) {
    DoublyListNode *node = newDoublyListNode(num);
    // If the list is empty, make both front and rear point to node
    if (empty(deque)) {
        deque->front = deque->rear = node;
    }
    // Enqueue at the front
    else if (isFront) {
        // Add node to the head of the linked list
        deque->front->prev = node;
        node->next = deque->front;
        deque->front = node; // Update the head node
    }
    // Enqueue at the rear
    else {
        // Add node to the tail of the linked list
        deque->rear->next = node;
        node->prev = deque->rear;
        deque->rear = node;
    }
    deque->queSize++; // Update the queue size
}

void pushFirst(LinkedListDeque *deque, int num) {
    push(deque, num, true);
}

/* Enqueue at the rear */
void pushLast(LinkedListDeque *deque, int num) {
    push(deque, num, false);
}

    assert(size(deque) && deque->front);
    return deque->front->val;
}

/* Access the rear element */
int peekLast(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    assert(size(deque) && deque->rear);
    return deque->rear->val;
}

/* Dequeue */
int pop(LinkedListDeque *deque, bool isFront) {
    if (empty(deque))
        return -1;
    int val;
    // When the queue size is 1, the head and tail point to the same node
    if (deque->queSize == 1) {
        val = deque->front->val;
        delDoublyListNode(deque->front); // Both point to the same node, so free it only once
        deque->front = NULL;
        deque->rear = NULL;
    }
    // Dequeue from the front
    else if (isFront) {
        val = peekFirst(deque); // Save the head node value
        DoublyListNode *fNext = deque->front->next;
        fNext->prev = NULL;
        deque->front->next = NULL;
        delDoublyListNode(deque->front);
        deque->front = fNext; // Update the head node
    }
    // Dequeue from the rear
    else {
        val = peekLast(deque); // Save the tail node value
        DoublyListNode *rPrev = deque->rear->prev;
        rPrev->next = NULL;
        deque->rear->prev = NULL;
        delDoublyListNode(deque->rear);
        deque->rear = rPrev; // Update the tail node
    }
    deque->queSize--; // Update the queue size
    return val;
}

/* Dequeue from the front */
int popFirst(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return pop(deque, true);
}

/* Dequeue from the rear */
int popLast(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return pop(deque, false);
}

void printLinkedListDeque(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    int *arr = malloc(sizeof(int) * deque->queSize);
    // Copy the linked list data into an array
    int i;
    DoublyListNode *node;
    for (i = 0, node = deque->front; i < deque->queSize; i++) {
        arr[i] = node->val;
        node = node->next;
    }
    printArray(arr, deque->queSize);
    free(arr);
}

class ArrayDeque:
    """Deque implemented with a circular array"""

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        """Constructor"""
        self._nums: list[int] = [0] * capacity
        self._front: int = 0
        self._size: int = 0

    def capacity(self) -> int:
        """Get the deque capacity"""
        return len(self._nums)

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the deque size"""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the deque is empty"""
        return self._size == 0

    def index(self, i: int) -> int:
        """Calculate an index in the circular array"""
        # Use modulo to connect the end of the array to its beginning
        # When i passes the end of the array, wrap around to the beginning
        # When i passes the beginning of the array, wrap around to the end
        return (i + self.capacity()) % self.capacity()

    def push_first(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue at the front"""
        if self._size == self.capacity():
            print("Deque is full")
            return
        # Move the front pointer one position to the left
        # Use modulo to wrap front to the end when it passes the beginning of the array
        self._front = self.index(self._front - 1)
        # Add num to the front
        self._nums[self._front] = num
        self._size += 1

    def push_last(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue at the rear"""
        if self._size == self.capacity():
            print("Deque is full")
            return
        # Calculate the rear pointer, which points one position past the last element
        rear = self.index(self._front + self._size)
        # Add num to the rear
        self._nums[rear] = num
        self._size += 1

    def pop_first(self) -> int:
        """Dequeue from the front"""
        num = self.peek_first()
        # Advance the front pointer by one position
        self._front = self.index(self._front + 1)
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def pop_last(self) -> int:
        """Dequeue from the rear"""
        num = self.peek_last()
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek_first(self) -> int:
        """Access the front element"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        return self._nums[self._front]

    def peek_last(self) -> int:
        """Access the rear element"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        # Calculate the index of the last element
        last = self.index(self._front + self._size - 1)
        return self._nums[last]

    def to_array(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return an array for printing"""
        # Convert only the list elements within the occupied range
        res = []
        for i in range(self._size):
            res.append(self._nums[self.index(self._front + i)])
        return res

  public:
    /* Constructor */

        front = queSize = 0;
    }

    }

        return queSize;
    }

    bool isEmpty() {
        return queSize == 0;
    }

    /* Calculate an index in the circular array */
    int index(int i) {
        // Use modulo to connect the end of the array to its beginning
        // When i passes the end of the array, wrap around to the beginning
        // When i passes the beginning of the array, wrap around to the end
        return (i + capacity()) % capacity();
    }

    /* Enqueue at the front */
    void pushFirst(int num) {
        if (queSize == capacity()) {
            cout << "Deque is full" << endl;
            return;
        }
        // Move the front index one position to the left
        // Use modulo to wrap front to the end when it passes the beginning of the array
        front = index(front - 1);
        // Add num to the front
        nums[front] = num;
        queSize++;
    }

    /* Enqueue at the rear */
    void pushLast(int num) {
        if (queSize == capacity()) {
            cout << "Deque is full" << endl;
            return;
        }
        // Calculate the rear index, one position past the last element
        int rear = index(front + queSize);
        // Add num to the rear
        nums[rear] = num;
        queSize++;
    }

    /* Dequeue from the front */
    int popFirst() {
        int num = peekFirst();
        // Advance the front index by one position
        front = index(front + 1);
        queSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Dequeue from the rear */
    int popLast() {
        int num = peekLast();
        queSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    int peekFirst() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Deque is empty");
        return nums[front];
    }

    /* Access the rear element */
    int peekLast() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Deque is empty");
        // Calculate the index of the last element
        int last = index(front + queSize - 1);
        return nums[last];
    }

    /* Return a vector for printing */
    vector<int> toVector() {
        // Copy only the elements in the occupied range
        vector<int> res(queSize);
        for (int i = 0, j = front; i < queSize; i++, j++) {
            res[i] = nums[index(j)];
        }
        return res;
    }

        // When i passes the end of the array, wrap around to the beginning
        // When i passes the beginning of the array, wrap around to the end
        ((i + self.capacity() as i32) % self.capacity() as i32) as usize
    }

    assert(empty(deque) == 0);
    return deque->nums[deque->front];
}

/* Access the rear element */
int peekLast(ArrayDeque *deque) {
    // Access error: the deque is empty
    assert(empty(deque) == 0);
    int last = dequeIndex(deque, deque->front + deque->queSize - 1);
    return deque->nums[last];
}

/* Dequeue from the front */
int popFirst(ArrayDeque *deque) {
    int num = peekFirst(deque);
    // Advance the front pointer by one position
    deque->front = dequeIndex(deque, deque->front + 1);
    deque->queSize--;
    return num;
}

/* Dequeue from the rear */
int popLast(ArrayDeque *deque) {
    int num = peekLast(deque);
    deque->queSize--;
    return num;
}

/* Return an array for printing */
int *toArray(ArrayDeque *deque, int *queSize) {
    *queSize = deque->queSize;
    int *res = (int *)calloc(deque->queSize, sizeof(int));
    int j = deque->front;
    for (int i = 0; i < deque->queSize; i++) {
        res[i] = deque->nums[j % deque->queCapacity];
        j++;
    }
    return res;
}

/* Constructor */
class ArrayDeque(capacity: Int) {
    private var nums: IntArray = IntArray(capacity) // Array that stores the deque elements
    private var front: Int = 0 // Front pointer, pointing to the first element
    private var queSize: Int = 0 // Deque size

    /* Get the deque capacity */
    fun capacity(): Int {
        return nums.size
    }

    /* Get the deque size */
    fun size(): Int {
        return queSize
    }

    /* Check whether the deque is empty */
    fun isEmpty(): Boolean {
        return queSize == 0
    }

    /* Calculate an index in the circular array */
    private fun index(i: Int): Int {
        // Use modulo to connect the end of the array to its beginning
        // When i passes the end of the array, wrap around to the beginning
        // When i passes the beginning of the array, wrap around to the end
        return (i + capacity()) % capacity()
    }

    /* Enqueue at the front */
    fun pushFirst(num: Int) {
        if (queSize == capacity()) {
            println("Deque is full")
            return
        }
        // Move the front pointer one position to the left
        // Use modulo to wrap front to the end when it passes the beginning of the array
        front = index(front - 1)
        // Add num to the front
        nums[front] = num
        queSize++
    }

    /* Enqueue at the rear */
    fun pushLast(num: Int) {
        if (queSize == capacity()) {
            println("Deque is full")
            return
        }
        // Calculate the rear pointer, which points one position past the last element
        val rear = index(front + queSize)
        // Add num to the rear
        nums[rear] = num
        queSize++
    }

    /* Dequeue from the front */
    fun popFirst(): Int {
        val num = peekFirst()
        // Advance the front pointer by one position
        front = index(front + 1)
        queSize--
        return num
    }

    /* Dequeue from the rear */
    fun popLast(): Int {
        val num = peekLast()
        queSize--
        return num
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    fun peekFirst(): Int {
        if (isEmpty()) throw IndexOutOfBoundsException()
        return nums[front]
    }

    /* Access the rear element */
    fun peekLast(): Int {
        if (isEmpty()) throw IndexOutOfBoundsException()
        // Calculate the index of the last element
        val last = index(front + queSize - 1)
        return nums[last]
    }

    /* Return an array for printing */
    fun toArray(): IntArray {
        // Copy only the elements within the occupied range
        val res = IntArray(queSize)
        var i = 0
        var j = front
        while (i < queSize) {
            res[i] = nums[index(j)]
            i++
            j++
        }
        return res
    }
}

items.title: 5.3.3   Applications
items.text:
A deque combines stack and queue behavior, so it supports all their applications while offering greater flexibility.

Software undo is usually implemented with a stack: the system uses push to record each change and pop to undo it. Because resources are limited, software often restricts the history to a fixed number of steps, such as \(50\). When the stack grows beyond \(50\), the oldest entry must be removed from the bottom, the front of the deque. A stack cannot provide this operation, so a deque is needed instead. The core undo behavior still follows last-in, first-out order; the deque simply provides flexibility for the additional logic.

items.title: 1.   Which element comes out first in a stack or queue?
items.text:
Start with an empty stack S and an empty queue Q. Perform the same operations on each:

Step 1: Add A. Step 2: Add B. Step 3: Remove and record one element. Step 4: Add C. Step 5: Keep removing and recording elements until the container is empty.

Write the order in which elements are removed from S and from Q. Explain the difference using last in, first out or first in, first out.

Reference answer

The removal order for stack S is B, C, A. After adding A, B, we first pop B, the most recently added element, and then add C. We then pop C, A in order. This is last in, first out.

The removal order for queue Q is A, B, C. After adding A, B, we first remove A, the earliest element added. We then add C and remove B, C in order. This is first in, first out.

items.title: 2.   What happens when the rear passes the end of the array?
items.text:
A queue uses a circular array of length 5, with indices 0-4. Currently, front = 3 and size = 2, with queue elements A, B at indices 3 and 4, respectively.

  1. When enqueueing C, at which index should C be placed? What is size afterward?
  2. If we then dequeue once, which element is removed? What are the new values of front and size?
  3. What is the logical order from front to rear now? Does dequeuing require moving the other array elements? Why?
Reference answer

  1. The new element's position is (front + size) % 5 = (3 + 2) % 5 = 0, so C goes at index 0. After enqueueing, size = 3.

  2. Dequeueing removes the current front element, A. The new front index is (3 + 1) % 5 = 4, so front = 4 and size = 2.

  3. The valid elements are logically ordered as B, C, with B at index 4 and C at index 0. Dequeueing only advances front and updates size. The circular array uses the remainder operation to wrap indices back to the beginning, so the other elements do not need to shift forward together.

items.title: 3.   Operations at both ends of a deque
items.text:
Here, push_first adds at the front, push_last adds at the rear, pop_first removes from the front, and pop_last removes from the rear.

Starting with an empty deque deq, perform:

  1. push_last(A)
  2. push_last(B)
  3. push_first(C)
  4. pop_last()
  5. push_last(D)
  6. pop_first()
  1. Which elements are removed by the two pop operations?
  2. Which elements remain, from front to rear, after all the operations?
  3. Examine these six steps. Can a queue that allows additions only at the rear and removals only at the front perform them all? If not, identify the unsupported operations. Then explain whether a deque can perform them all, and why.
Reference answer

After the first three steps, the deque contains [C, A, B] from front to rear.

  1. pop_last() removes B. After adding D, the deque is [C, A, D]. Then pop_first() removes C.

  2. The remaining elements are [A, D].

  3. A queue that allows additions only at the rear and removals only at the front cannot perform every operation: step 3, push_first(C), adds at the front, and step 4, pop_last(), removes from the rear. Neither operation is supported by that queue. A deque supports additions and removals at both ends, so it can perform all six steps.

A valid sequence must satisfy both conditions: each closing bracket matches the type of the most recent unmatched opening bracket, and no unmatched opening brackets remain at the end. Return a Boolean result.

items.title: 5.2   Queues
items.text:
A queue is a linear data structure that follows a first-in, first-out rule. It models a line of people: newcomers join at the back, while those at the front leave one by one.

As shown below, the two ends are called the “front” and the “rear.” Adding an element at the rear is called “enqueueing,” and removing an element from the front is called “dequeueing.”

Figure 5-4   The first-in, first-out rule of a queue

items.title: 5.2.2   Implementing a queue
items.text: A queue needs a data structure that allows insertion at one end and deletion at the other. Both linked lists and arrays can meet this requirement.

items.title: 1.   Implementation with a linked list
items.text:
As shown below, treat the linked list's head and tail as the queue's front and rear. Nodes may be added only at the rear and removed only from the front.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-5   Enqueue and dequeue in a linked-list queue

Here is an implementation using a linked list:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linkedlist_queue.py
class LinkedListQueue:
    """Queue implemented with a linked list"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self._front: ListNode | None = None  # Head node front
        self._rear: ListNode | None = None  # Tail node rear
        self._size: int = 0

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the queue size"""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the queue is empty"""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue"""
        # Add num after the tail node
        node = ListNode(num)
        # If the queue is empty, make both the head and tail point to this node
        if self._front is None:
            self._front = node
            self._rear = node
        # If the queue is not empty, add this node after the tail node
        else:
            self._rear.next = node
            self._rear = node
        self._size += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Dequeue"""
        num = self.peek()
        # Remove the head node
        self._front = self._front.next
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Access the front element"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Queue is empty")
        return self._front.val

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Convert to a list for printing"""
        queue = []
        temp = self._front
        while temp:
            queue.append(temp.val)
            temp = temp.next
        return queue

/* Queue implemented with a linked list */
class LinkedListQueue {
  private:
    ListNode *front, *rear; // Head node front and tail node rear
    int queSize;

  public:
    LinkedListQueue() {
        front = nullptr;
        rear = nullptr;
        queSize = 0;
    }

    ~LinkedListQueue() {
        // Traverse the linked list and delete each node to free its memory
        freeMemoryLinkedList(front);
    }

    /* Get the queue size */
    int size() {
        return queSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the queue is empty */
    bool isEmpty() {
        return queSize == 0;
    }

    /* Enqueue */
    void push(int num) {
        // Add num after the tail node
        ListNode *node = new ListNode(num);
        // If the queue is empty, make both the head and tail point to this node
        if (front == nullptr) {
            front = node;
            rear = node;
        }
        // If the queue is not empty, add this node after the tail node
        else {
            rear->next = node;
            rear = node;
        }
        queSize++;
    }

    /* Dequeue */
    int pop() {
        int num = peek();
        // Remove the head node
        ListNode *tmp = front;
        front = front->next;
        // Free memory
        delete tmp;
        queSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    int peek() {
        if (size() == 0)
            throw out_of_range("Queue is empty");
        return front->val;
    }

    /* Convert the linked list to a vector and return it */
    vector<int> toVector() {
        ListNode *node = front;
        vector<int> res(size());
        for (int i = 0; i < res.size(); i++) {
            res[i] = node->val;
            node = node->next;
        }
        return res;
    }
};

/* Queue implemented with a linked list */
class LinkedListQueue {
    ListNode? front, rear;  // Head node front and tail node rear 
    int queSize = 0;

    public LinkedListQueue() {
        front = null;
        rear = null;
    }

    /* Get the queue size */
    public int Size() {
        return queSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the queue is empty */
    public bool IsEmpty() {
        return Size() == 0;
    }

    /* Enqueue */
    public void Push(int num) {
        // Add num after the tail node
        ListNode node = new(num);
        // If the queue is empty, make both the head and tail point to this node
        if (front == null) {
            front = node;
            rear = node;
            // If the queue is not empty, add this node after the tail node
        } else if (rear != null) {
            rear.next = node;
            rear = node;
        }
        queSize++;
    }

    /* Dequeue */
    public int Pop() {
        int num = Peek();
        // Remove the head node
        front = front?.next;
        queSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    public int Peek() {
        if (IsEmpty())
            throw new Exception();
        return front!.val;
    }

    /* Convert the linked list to an array and return it */
    public int[] ToArray() {
        if (front == null)
            return [];

        ListNode? node = front;
        int[] res = new int[Size()];
        for (int i = 0; i < res.Length; i++) {
            res[i] = node!.val;
            node = node.next;
        }
        return res;
    }
}

class LinkedListQueue {
    private var front: ListNode? // Head node
    private var rear: ListNode? // Tail node
    private var _size: Int

    init() {
        _size = 0
    }

    /* Get the queue size */
    func size() -> Int {
        _size
    }

    /* Check whether the queue is empty */
    func isEmpty() -> Bool {
        size() == 0
    }

    /* Enqueue */
    func push(num: Int) {
        // Add num after the tail node
        let node = ListNode(x: num)
        // If the queue is empty, make both the head and tail point to this node
        if front == nil {
            front = node
            rear = node
        }
        // If the queue is not empty, add this node after the tail node
        else {
            rear?.next = node
            rear = node
        }
        _size += 1
    }

    /* Dequeue */
    @discardableResult
    func pop() -> Int {
        let num = peek()
        // Remove the head node
        front = front?.next
        _size -= 1
        return num
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    func peek() -> Int {
        if isEmpty() {
            fatalError("Queue is empty")
        }
        return front!.val
    }

    /* Convert the linked list to an array and return it */
    func toArray() -> [Int] {
        var node = front
        var res = Array(repeating: 0, count: size())
        for i in res.indices {
            res[i] = node!.val
            node = node?.next
        }
        return res
    }
}

/* Queue implemented with a linked list */
#[allow(dead_code)]
pub struct LinkedListQueue<T> {
    front: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, // Head node front
    rear: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>,  // Tail node rear
    que_size: usize,                         // Queue size
}

impl<T: Copy> LinkedListQueue<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            front: None,
            rear: None,
            que_size: 0,
        }
    }

    /* Get the queue size */
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        return self.que_size;
    }

    /* Check whether the queue is empty */
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        return self.que_size == 0;
    }

    /* Enqueue */
    pub fn push(&mut self, num: T) {
        // Add num after the tail node
        let new_rear = ListNode::new(num);
        match self.rear.take() {
            // If the queue is not empty, add this node after the tail node
            Some(old_rear) => {
                old_rear.borrow_mut().next = Some(new_rear.clone());
                self.rear = Some(new_rear);
            }
            // If the queue is empty, make both the head and tail point to this node
            None => {
                self.front = Some(new_rear.clone());
                self.rear = Some(new_rear);
            }
        }
        self.que_size += 1;
    }

    /* Dequeue */
    pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        self.front.take().map(|old_front| {
            match old_front.borrow_mut().next.take() {
                Some(new_front) => {
                    self.front = Some(new_front);
                }
                None => {
                    self.rear.take();
                }
            }
            self.que_size -= 1;
            old_front.borrow().val
        })
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    pub fn peek(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.front.as_ref()
    }

    /* Convert the linked list to a vector and return it */
    pub fn to_array(&self, head: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>) -> Vec<T> {
        let mut res: Vec<T> = Vec::new();

        fn recur<T: Copy>(cur: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, res: &mut Vec<T>) {
            if let Some(cur) = cur {
                res.push(cur.borrow().val);
                recur(cur.borrow().next.as_ref(), res);
            }
        }

        recur(head, &mut res);

        res
    }
}

items.title: 2.   Implementation with an array
items.text:
Removing the first element of an array takes \(O(n)\) time, which would make dequeueing inefficient. A useful technique avoids this problem.

Use a variable front for the index of the front element and a variable size for the queue's length. Define rear = front + size, so rear points to the position immediately after the last element.

With this design, the occupied interval is [front, rear - 1]. Operations work as shown below.

  • Enqueue: assign the new element to index rear and increase size by 1.
  • Dequeue: increase front by 1 and decrease size by 1.

Both operations require only a constant amount of work and take \(O(1)\) time.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-6   Enqueue and dequeue in an array-based queue

There is a problem: repeated enqueueing and dequeueing move both front and rear to the right, and they cannot continue once they reach the end of the array. To solve this, treat the array as circular, with its end connected to its beginning.

When front or rear passes the array's end, wrap it back to the beginning. The remainder operation implements this cyclic behavior:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array_queue.py
class ArrayQueue:
    """Queue implemented with a circular array"""

    def __init__(self, size: int):
        """Constructor"""
        self._nums: list[int] = [0] * size  # Array that stores the queue elements
        self._front: int = 0  # Front pointer, pointing to the first element
        self._size: int = 0  # Queue size

    def capacity(self) -> int:
        """Get the queue capacity"""
        return len(self._nums)

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the queue size"""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the queue is empty"""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue"""
        if self._size == self.capacity():
            raise IndexError("Queue is full")
        # Calculate the rear pointer, which points one position past the last element
        # Use modulo to wrap rear to the beginning when it passes the end of the array
        rear: int = (self._front + self._size) % self.capacity()
        # Add num to the rear
        self._nums[rear] = num
        self._size += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Dequeue"""
        num: int = self.peek()
        # Advance the front pointer by one position, wrapping to the beginning if it passes the end
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % self.capacity()
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Access the front element"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Queue is empty")
        return self._nums[self._front]

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return a list for printing"""
        res = [0] * self.size()
        j: int = self._front
        for i in range(self.size()):
            res[i] = self._nums[(j % self.capacity())]
            j += 1
        return res

    /* Return an array */
    func toArray() -> [Int] {
        // Include only the elements in the occupied range
        (front ..< front + size()).map { nums[$0 % capacity()] }
    }

impl<T: Copy + Default> ArrayQueue<T> {
    /* Constructor */
    fn new(capacity: i32) -> ArrayQueue<T> {
        ArrayQueue {
            nums: vec![T::default(); capacity as usize],
            front: 0,
            que_size: 0,
            que_capacity: capacity,
        }
    }

    /* Get the queue capacity */
    fn capacity(&self) -> i32 {
        self.que_capacity
    }

    /* Get the queue size */
    fn size(&self) -> i32 {
        self.que_size
    }

    /* Check whether the queue is empty */
    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.que_size == 0
    }

    /* Enqueue */
    fn push(&mut self, num: T) {
        if self.que_size == self.capacity() {
            println!("Queue is full");
            return;
        }
        // Calculate the rear index, one position past the last element
        // Use modulo to wrap rear to the beginning when it passes the end of the array
        let rear = (self.front + self.que_size) % self.que_capacity;
        // Add num to the rear
        self.nums[rear as usize] = num;
        self.que_size += 1;
    }

    /* Dequeue */
    fn pop(&mut self) -> T {
        let num = self.peek();
        // Advance the front index by one position, wrapping to the beginning if it passes the end
        self.front = (self.front + 1) % self.que_capacity;
        self.que_size -= 1;
        num
    }

    /* Access the front element */
    fn peek(&self) -> T {
        if self.is_empty() {
            panic!("Index out of bounds");
        }
        self.nums[self.front as usize]
    }

    fn to_vector(&self) -> Vec<T> {
        let cap = self.que_capacity;
        let mut j = self.front;
        let mut arr = vec![T::default(); cap as usize];
        for i in 0..self.que_size {
            arr[i as usize] = self.nums[(j % cap) as usize];
            j += 1;

items.title: 5.2.3   Typical applications
items.text:
• Taobao orders. When a shopper places an order, it enters a queue, and the system processes orders in sequence. During the Singles' Day shopping festival, enormous numbers of orders arrive in a short time, making high concurrency a major engineering challenge.
  • Tasks awaiting processing. Queues preserve processing order wherever first-come, first-served behavior is needed, such as printer jobs or restaurant orders.

items.title: 5.1   Stacks
items.text:
A stack is a linear data structure that follows a last-in, first-out rule.

Think of a stack of plates on a table. If we can move only one plate at a time, reaching the bottom plate requires removing all the plates above it first. Replace the plates with elements such as integers, characters, or objects, and we have a stack.

As shown below, the upper end is the “top” of the stack and the lower end is the “bottom.” Adding an element to the top is called “pushing,” and removing the top element is called “popping.”

Figure 5-1   The last-in, first-out rule of a stack

items.title: 5.1.1   Common stack operations

items.title: 5.1.2   Implementing a stack
items.text:
To understand how a stack works more deeply, let us implement a stack class ourselves.

A stack follows last-in, first-out order, so elements can be added or removed only at the top. Arrays and linked lists allow insertion and deletion at arbitrary positions, so a stack can be viewed as a restricted array or linked list. By hiding irrelevant operations, we make its public behavior conform to the stack's rules.

items.title: 1.   Implementation with a linked list
items.text:
When implementing a stack with a linked list, treat the head as the top and the tail as the bottom.

As shown below, pushing simply inserts a node at the head, an operation called “head insertion.” Popping removes the head node.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-2   Push and pop in a linked-list stack

Here is an implementation using a linked list:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linkedlist_stack.py
class LinkedListStack:
    """Stack implemented with a linked list"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self._peek: ListNode | None = None
        self._size: int = 0

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the stack size"""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the stack is empty"""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, val: int):
        """Push"""
        node = ListNode(val)
        node.next = self._peek
        self._peek = node
        self._size += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Pop"""
        num = self.peek()
        self._peek = self._peek.next
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Access the top element"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack is empty")
        return self._peek.val

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Convert to a list for printing"""
        arr = []
        node = self._peek
        while node:
            arr.append(node.val)
            node = node.next
        arr.reverse()
        return arr

/* Stack implemented with a linked list */
class LinkedListStack {
  private:
    ListNode *stackTop; // Use the head node as the stack top
    int stkSize;        // Stack size

  public:
    LinkedListStack() {
        stackTop = nullptr;
        stkSize = 0;
    }

    ~LinkedListStack() {
        // Traverse the linked list and delete each node to free its memory
        freeMemoryLinkedList(stackTop);
    }

    /* Get the stack size */
    int size() {
        return stkSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the stack is empty */
    bool isEmpty() {
        return size() == 0;
    }

    /* Push */
    void push(int num) {
        ListNode *node = new ListNode(num);
        node->next = stackTop;
        stackTop = node;
        stkSize++;
    }

    /* Pop */
    int pop() {
        int num = top();
        ListNode *tmp = stackTop;
        stackTop = stackTop->next;
        // Free memory
        delete tmp;
        stkSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Access the top element */
    int top() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Stack is empty");
        return stackTop->val;
    }

    /* Convert the linked list to a vector and return it */
    vector<int> toVector() {
        ListNode *node = stackTop;
        vector<int> res(size());
        for (int i = res.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            res[i] = node->val;
            node = node->next;
        }
        return res;
    }
};

class LinkedListStack {
    private ListNode stackPeek; // Use the head node as the stack top
    private int stkSize = 0; // Stack size

    public LinkedListStack() {
        stackPeek = null;
    }

    /* Get the stack size */
    public int size() {
        return stkSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the stack is empty */
    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return size() == 0;
    }

    /* Push */
    public void push(int num) {
        ListNode node = new ListNode(num);
        node.next = stackPeek;
        stackPeek = node;
        stkSize++;
    }

    /* Pop */
    public int pop() {
        int num = peek();
        stackPeek = stackPeek.next;
        stkSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Access the top element */
    public int peek() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException();
        return stackPeek.val;
    }

    /* Convert the list to an array and return it */
    public int[] toArray() {
        ListNode node = stackPeek;
        int[] res = new int[size()];
        for (int i = res.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            res[i] = node.val;
            node = node.next;
        }
        return res;
    }
}

    ListNode? stackPeek;  // Use the head node as the stack top
    int stkSize = 0;   // Stack size

    public LinkedListStack() {
        stackPeek = null;
    }

    /* Get the stack size */
    public int Size() {
        return stkSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the stack is empty */
    public bool IsEmpty() {
        return Size() == 0;
    }

    /* Push */
    public void Push(int num) {
        ListNode node = new(num) {
            next = stackPeek
        };
        stackPeek = node;
        stkSize++;
    }

    /* Pop */
    public int Pop() {
        int num = Peek();
        stackPeek = stackPeek!.next;
        stkSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Access the top element */
    public int Peek() {
        if (IsEmpty())
            throw new Exception();
        return stackPeek!.val;
    }

    /* Convert the linked list to an array and return it */
    public int[] ToArray() {
        if (stackPeek == null)
            return [];

        ListNode? node = stackPeek;
        int[] res = new int[Size()];
        for (int i = res.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            res[i] = node!.val;
            node = node.next;
        }
        return res;
    }
}

#[allow(dead_code)]
pub struct LinkedListStack<T> {
    stack_peek: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, // Use the head node as the stack top
    stk_size: usize,                              // Stack size
}

impl<T: Copy> LinkedListStack<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            stack_peek: None,
            stk_size: 0,
        }
    }

    /* Get the stack size */
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        return self.stk_size;
    }

    /* Check whether the stack is empty */
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        return self.size() == 0;
    }

    /* Push */
    pub fn push(&mut self, num: T) {
        let node = ListNode::new(num);
        node.borrow_mut().next = self.stack_peek.take();
        self.stack_peek = Some(node);
        self.stk_size += 1;
    }

    /* Pop */
    pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        self.stack_peek.take().map(|old_head| {
            self.stack_peek = old_head.borrow_mut().next.take();
            self.stk_size -= 1;

            old_head.borrow().val
        })
    }

    /* Access the top element */
    pub fn peek(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.stack_peek.as_ref()
    }

    /* Convert the linked list to a vector and return it */
    pub fn to_array(&self) -> Vec<T> {
        fn _to_array<T: Sized + Copy>(head: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>) -> Vec<T> {
            if let Some(node) = head {
                let mut nums = _to_array(node.borrow().next.as_ref());
                nums.push(node.borrow().val);
                return nums;
            }
            return Vec::new();
        }

        _to_array(self.peek())
    }
}

typedef struct {

        free(s->top);
        s->top = n;
    }
    free(s);

    node->next = s->top; // Set the new node's pointer field
    node->val = num;     // Set the new node's data field
    s->top = node;       // Update the stack top

items.title: 2.   Implementation with an array
items.text:
For an array-based stack, use the end of the array as the top. As shown below, pushing and popping correspond to adding and removing the last element, both taking \(O(1)\) time.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-3   Push and pop in an array-based stack

Since elements may keep arriving, use a dynamic array so that resizing is handled for us. An implementation follows:

class ArrayStack:
    """Stack implemented with an array"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self._stack: list[int] = []

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the stack size"""
        return len(self._stack)

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the stack is empty"""
        return self.size() == 0

    def push(self, item: int):
        """Push"""
        self._stack.append(item)

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Pop"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack is empty")
        return self._stack.pop()

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Access the top element"""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack is empty")
        return self._stack[-1]

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return a list for printing"""
        return self._stack

  def size
    @stack.length
  end

  ### Check whether the stack is empty ###
  def is_empty?
    @stack.empty?
  end

  ### Push ###
  def push(item)
    @stack << item
  end

  ### Pop ###
  def pop
    raise IndexError, 'Stack is empty' if is_empty?

    @stack.pop
  end

  ### Access the top element ###
  def peek
    raise IndexError, 'Stack is empty' if is_empty?

    @stack.last
  end

  ### Return a list for printing ###
  def to_array
    @stack
  end
end

items.title: 5.1.3   Comparing the implementations
items.text:
Supported operations

Both implementations support all stack operations. An array also allows random access, but that is outside the stack abstraction and is generally not used.

Time efficiency

In an array-based stack, pushes and pops operate in preallocated contiguous memory, giving good cache locality and high efficiency. However, a push that exceeds the array's capacity triggers expansion, making that particular push an \(O(n)\) operation.

A linked list grows flexibly and avoids the slowdown associated with array expansion. However, pushing requires creating a node object and updating pointers, so it is relatively slower. If the element is already a node object, the creation step can be skipped to improve efficiency.

For elements of primitive types such as int or double, we can therefore draw the following conclusions.

  • An array-based stack slows down when expansion is triggered, but expansion is infrequent, so average efficiency is higher.
  • A linked-list stack provides more consistent performance.

Space efficiency

When a dynamic array is initialized, its initial capacity may exceed actual needs. Expansion typically multiplies the capacity by a fixed factor, such as 2, which may again leave excess space. An array-based stack can therefore waste some space.

However, linked-list nodes also store pointers, so each node occupies relatively more space.

We cannot say universally which implementation uses less memory; the answer depends on the situation.

items.title: 5.1.4   Typical applications
items.text:
• Browser back and forward navigation, and software undo and redo. When a new web page is opened, the browser pushes the previous page onto a stack. Going back pops that page. Supporting both back and forward requires two stacks working together.
  • Program memory management. Each function call adds a stack frame containing the function's context. During recursion, frames are pushed as calls descend and popped as they return.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• A stack follows last-in, first-out order and can be implemented with an array or linked list.
  • An array-based stack offers higher average time efficiency, but a push that triggers expansion takes \(O(n)\) time. A linked-list stack provides more consistent performance.
  • An array-based stack may waste some space. However, linked-list nodes require more memory than individual array elements.
  • A queue follows first-in, first-out order and can also be implemented with an array or linked list. Their time and space tradeoffs resemble those of stack implementations.
  • A deque is a more flexible queue that allows insertion and removal at both ends.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Are browser back and forward navigation implemented with a doubly linked list?

Browser navigation fundamentally reflects stack behavior. Visiting a new page adds it to the top of a stack; clicking Back removes it. A deque conveniently supports additional operations, as discussed in the deque section.

Q: After popping a node, do we need to free its memory?

If the node will still be used, do not free it. If it is no longer needed, languages such as Java and Python use automatic garbage collection, so manual deallocation is unnecessary. In C and C++, memory must be released manually.

Q: A deque looks like two stacks joined together. What is it useful for?

A deque resembles a combination of a stack and a queue, or two stacks joined together. It combines stack and queue behavior, supporting all their applications with greater flexibility.

Q: How exactly do undo and redo work?

Use two stacks: A for undo and B for redo.

  1. Whenever the user performs an action, push it onto A and clear B.
  2. To undo, pop the most recent action from A and push it onto B.
  3. To redo, pop the most recent action from B and push it onto A.

items.title: 7.3   Array representation of a binary tree
items.text:
In a linked representation, a binary tree stores data in TreeNode nodes connected by pointers. The previous section introduced basic operations on binary trees in this form.

Can we represent a binary tree with an array instead? Yes.
path: 7.3   Array representation of a binary tree

items.title: 7.3.1   Representing a perfect binary tree
items.text:
Start with a simple case. Store every node of a perfect binary tree in an array in level order. Each node then corresponds to a unique array index.

Level-order traversal gives us a mapping between parent and child indices: if a node has index \(i\), its left child has index \(2i + 1\) and its right child has index \(2i + 2\). Figure 7-12 illustrates this relationship.

Figure 7-12   Array representation of a perfect binary tree

The mapping formulas serve the same role as node references or pointers in a linked representation. Given any node in the array, we can use them to access its left or right child.
path: 7.3   Array representation of a binary tree

items.title: 7.3.2   Representing an arbitrary binary tree
items.text:
A perfect binary tree is a special case. Other binary trees often contain many missing nodes, None, at intermediate levels. Ordinary level-order traversal omits these positions, so its sequence alone cannot tell us their number or locations. Multiple tree structures can therefore produce the same level-order sequence.

As shown below, the array representation above no longer works for a non-perfect binary tree.

Figure 7-13   Multiple binary trees can share a level-order sequence

To solve this, include every None position explicitly in the level-order sequence. The sequence then represents the tree uniquely, as shown below. Example code follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby

Figure 7-14   Array representation of an arbitrary binary tree

Complete binary trees are particularly well suited to array representation. By definition, missing positions occur only at the right end of the lowest level, so all None entries appear at the end of the level-order sequence.

We can therefore omit all None entries when storing a complete binary tree in an array. An example is shown below.

Figure 7-15   Array representation of a complete binary tree

The following code implements an array-based binary tree with these operations.

  • Given a node, get its value, left or right child, and parent.
  • Obtain preorder, inorder, postorder, and level-order traversal sequences.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array_binary_tree.py
class ArrayBinaryTree:
    """Binary tree class using an array representation"""

    def __init__(self, arr: list[int | None]):
        """Constructor"""
        self._tree = list(arr)

    def size(self):
        """Length of the backing list"""
        return len(self._tree)

    def val(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the value of the node at index i"""
        # If the index is out of bounds, return None to represent an empty position
        if i < 0 or i >= self.size():
            return None
        return self._tree[i]

    def left(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the left child index of the node at index i"""
        return 2 * i + 1

    def right(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the right child index of the node at index i"""
        return 2 * i + 2

    def parent(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the parent index of the node at index i"""
        return (i - 1) // 2

    def level_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Level-order traversal"""
        self.res = []
        # Traverse the array directly
        for i in range(self.size()):
            if self.val(i) is not None:
                self.res.append(self.val(i))
        return self.res

    def dfs(self, i: int, order: str):
        """Depth-first traversal"""
        if self.val(i) is None:
            return
        # Preorder traversal
        if order == "pre":
            self.res.append(self.val(i))
        self.dfs(self.left(i), order)
        # Inorder traversal
        if order == "in":
            self.res.append(self.val(i))
        self.dfs(self.right(i), order)
        # Postorder traversal
        if order == "post":
            self.res.append(self.val(i))

    def pre_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Preorder traversal"""
        self.res = []
        self.dfs(0, order="pre")
        return self.res

    def in_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Inorder traversal"""
        self.res = []
        self.dfs(0, order="in")
        return self.res

    def post_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Postorder traversal"""
        self.res = []
        self.dfs(0, order="post")
        return self.res

            res.push_back(val(i));

            res.push_back(val(i));
    }

        return this.#tree[i];
    }

    /* Get the left child index of the node at index i */
    left(i: number): number {
        return 2 * i + 1;
    }

    /* Get the right child index of the node at index i */
    right(i: number): number {
        return 2 * i + 2;
    }

    /* Get the parent index of the node at index i */
    parent(i: number): number {
        return Math.floor((i - 1) / 2); // Floor division
    }

    /* Level-order traversal */
    levelOrder(): number[] {
        let res = [];
        // Traverse the array directly
        for (let i = 0; i < this.size(); i++) {
            if (this.val(i) !== null) res.push(this.val(i));
        }
        return res;
    }

    /* Depth-first traversal */
    #dfs(i: number, order: Order, res: (number | null)[]): void {
        // Return if this position is empty
        if (this.val(i) === null) return;
        // Preorder traversal
        if (order === 'pre') res.push(this.val(i));
        this.#dfs(this.left(i), order, res);
        // Inorder traversal
        if (order === 'in') res.push(this.val(i));
        this.#dfs(this.right(i), order, res);
        // Postorder traversal
        if (order === 'post') res.push(this.val(i));
    }

    /* Preorder traversal */
    preOrder(): (number | null)[] {
        const res = [];
        this.#dfs(0, 'pre', res);
        return res;
    }

    /* Inorder traversal */
    inOrder(): (number | null)[] {
        const res = [];
        this.#dfs(0, 'in', res);
        return res;
    }

    /* Postorder traversal */
    postOrder(): (number | null)[] {
        const res = [];
        this.#dfs(0, 'post', res);
        return res;
    }
}
