        // If the index is out of bounds, return None to represent an empty position
        if i < 0 || i >= self.size() {
            None
        } else {
            self.tree[i as usize]
        }

    fn left(&self, i: i32) -> i32 {
        2 * i + 1
    }

    fn right(&self, i: i32) -> i32 {

        self.tree.iter().filter_map(|&x| x).collect()
    }

        if self.val(i).is_none() {
            return;

        let val = self.val(i).unwrap();
        // Preorder traversal
        if order == "pre" {
            res.push(val);

        self.dfs(self.left(i), order, res);
        // Inorder traversal
        if order == "in" {
            res.push(val);
        }
        self.dfs(self.right(i), order, res);
        // Postorder traversal
        if order == "post" {
            res.push(val);
        }
    }

        let mut res = vec![];
        self.dfs(0, "pre", &mut res);
        res

        self.dfs(0, "in", &mut res);

    if (i < 0 || i >= size(abt))
        return INT_MAX;

int *levelOrder(ArrayBinaryTree *abt, int *returnSize) {
    int *res = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int) * size(abt));
    int index = 0;
    // Traverse the array directly
    for (int i = 0; i < size(abt); i++) {
        if (val(abt, i) != INT_MAX)
            res[index++] = val(abt, i);
    }
    *returnSize = index;
    return res;

    // Return if this position is empty

    if (strcmp(order, "pre") == 0)
        res[(*index)++] = val(abt, i);
    dfs(abt, left(i), order, res, index);
    // Inorder traversal
    if (strcmp(order, "in") == 0)
        res[(*index)++] = val(abt, i);
    dfs(abt, right(i), order, res, index);
    // Postorder traversal
    if (strcmp(order, "post") == 0)
        res[(*index)++] = val(abt, i);

items.title: 7.3.3   Strengths and limitations
items.text:
Array representation offers the following advantages.

  • Contiguous memory is cache-friendly, making access and traversal fast.
  • No pointers need to be stored, saving space.
  • Nodes can be accessed randomly by index.

However, it also has limitations.

  • Arrays require contiguous memory, making them unsuitable for extremely large trees.
  • Adding and removing nodes requires array insertion and deletion operations, which are inefficient.
  • If the tree has many missing nodes, actual node data occupies only a small fraction of the array, wasting space.

items.title: 7.5   AVL trees *
items.text:
The binary-search-tree section explained that repeated insertions and deletions can make a tree degenerate into a linked list. All operations then degrade from \(O(\log n)\) to \(O(n)\) time.

In the example below, just two deletions turn the binary search tree into a linked list.

Figure 7-24   An AVL-tree example degenerating after deletions

Likewise, inserting two nodes into the perfect binary tree below makes it heavily skewed to the left, degrading lookup performance.

Figure 7-25   An AVL-tree example degenerating after insertions

In 1962, G. M. Adelson-Velsky and E. M. Landis introduced the AVL tree in their paper “An algorithm for the organization of information.” They described operations that prevent degeneration through repeated insertions and deletions, keeping the time complexity of operations at \(O(\log n)\). AVL trees therefore maintain efficient data operations when insertions, deletions, lookups, and updates are frequent, making them valuable in practice.

items.title: 7.5.1   AVL tree terminology
items.text: An AVL tree is both a binary search tree and a balanced binary tree, satisfying the properties of both. It is therefore a balanced binary search tree.

A node's height is the distance to its farthest leaf, measured in edges. A leaf has height \(0\), while a missing node has height \(-1\). We create two helper functions to retrieve and update a node's height:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def height(self, node: TreeNode | None) -> int:
    """Get the node height"""
    # An empty subtree has height -1; a leaf has height 0
    if node is not None:
        return node.height
    return -1

def update_height(self, node: TreeNode | None):
    """Update the node height"""
    # The node height equals the height of its taller subtree + 1
    node.height = max([self.height(node.left), self.height(node.right)]) + 1

items.text:

items.title: 7.5.2   AVL tree rotations
items.text:
The defining operation of an AVL tree is rotation, which restores balance without changing the inorder traversal sequence. A rotation preserves the binary-search-tree property while restoring the balanced-tree property.

A node whose balance factor has absolute value \(> 1\) is “unbalanced.” Depending on the imbalance, we use one of four rotations: right, left, right-then-left, or left-then-right. Let us examine them in detail.

items.title: 1.   Right rotation
items.text:
In Figure 7-26, balance factors appear beneath the nodes. Viewed from the bottom up, node 3 is the first unbalanced node. Focus on the subtree rooted there, naming its root node and its left child child. A right rotation restores balance while preserving the binary-search-tree property.

<1><2><3><4>

Figure 7-26   Steps of a right rotation

If child has a right child, denoted by grand_child, add one step to the rotation: make grand_child the left child of node, as shown below.

Figure 7-27   A right rotation with grand_child

“Rotating right” is a visual description; the implementation updates node pointers:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def right_rotate(self, node: TreeNode | None) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Right rotation"""
    child = node.left
    grand_child = child.right
    # Rotate node to the right around child
    child.right = node
    node.left = grand_child
    # Update the node height
    self.update_height(node)
    self.update_height(child)
    # Return the root of the rotated subtree
    return child

items.title: 3.   Left-then-right rotation
items.text:
For unbalanced node 3 below, neither a left nor a right rotation alone restores balance. First rotate child to the left, then rotate node to the right.

Figure 7-30   A left-then-right rotation

items.title: 4.   Right-then-left rotation
items.text:
For the mirror-image case below, first rotate child to the right, then rotate node to the left.

Figure 7-31   A right-then-left rotation

items.title: 5.   Choosing a rotation
items.text:
The four cases below correspond to the examples above and require, respectively, right, left-then-right, right-then-left, and left rotations.

Figure 7-32   The four AVL rotation cases

As Table 7-3 shows, the signs of the unbalanced node's balance factor and that of the child on its taller side determine the case.

Table 7-3   Conditions for choosing a rotation

Unbalanced node's balance factor Child's balance factor Rotation \(> 1\) (left-heavy) \(\geq 0\) Right \(> 1\) (left-heavy) \(<0\) Left, then right \(< -1\) (right-heavy) \(\leq 0\) Left \(< -1\) (right-heavy) \(>0\) Right, then left

Wrap the rotation logic in one function. It can then handle every imbalance and restore the affected node's balance. The code is as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def rotate(self, node: TreeNode | None) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Perform rotations to restore balance in this subtree"""
    # Get the balance factor of node
    balance_factor = self.balance_factor(node)
    # Left-heavy tree
    if balance_factor > 1:
        if self.balance_factor(node.left) >= 0:
            # Rotate right
            return self.right_rotate(node)
        else:
            # Rotate left, then right
            node.left = self.left_rotate(node.left)
            return self.right_rotate(node)
    # Right-heavy tree
    elif balance_factor < -1:
        if self.balance_factor(node.right) <= 0:
            # Rotate left
            return self.left_rotate(node)
        else:
            # Rotate right, then left
            node.right = self.right_rotate(node.right)
            return self.left_rotate(node)
    # The tree is balanced; return without rotating
    return node

  // Left-heavy tree
  if (factor > 1) {
    if (balanceFactor(node!.left) >= 0) {
      // Rotate right
      return rightRotate(node);
    } else {
      // Rotate left, then right
      node.left = leftRotate(node.left);
      return rightRotate(node);
    }
  }
  // Right-heavy tree
  if (factor < -1) {
    if (balanceFactor(node!.right) <= 0) {
      // Rotate left
      return leftRotate(node);
    } else {
      // Rotate right, then left
      node.right = rightRotate(node.right);
      return leftRotate(node);
    }
  }
  // The tree is balanced; return without rotating
  return node;
}

items.title: 1.   Inserting a node
items.text:
Insertion largely follows the binary-search-tree procedure. The difference is that inserting a node may unbalance nodes along the path to the root. Starting at the inserted node, work upward and perform rotations to restore balance at every affected node:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def insert(self, val):
    """Insert a node"""
    self._root = self.insert_helper(self._root, val)

def insert_helper(self, node: TreeNode | None, val: int) -> TreeNode:
    """Insert a node recursively (helper method)"""
    if node is None:
        return TreeNode(val)
    # 1. Find the insertion position and insert the node
    if val < node.val:
        node.left = self.insert_helper(node.left, val)
    elif val > node.val:
        node.right = self.insert_helper(node.right, val)
    else:
        # Return without inserting a duplicate node
        return node
    # Update the node height
    self.update_height(node)
    # 2. Perform rotations to restore balance in this subtree
    return self.rotate(node)

    root = insertHelper(root, val);

        node->left = insertHelper(node->left, val);
    else if (val > node->val)

    else
        return node;    // Return without inserting a duplicate node
    updateHeight(node); // Update the node height
    /* 2. Perform rotations to restore balance in this subtree */
    node = rotate(node);
    // Return the root of the subtree
    return node;
}

items.title: 2.   Deleting a node
items.text:
Similarly, extend binary-search-tree deletion with rotations from the bottom up to restore balance at every affected node:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def remove(self, val: int):
    """Remove a node"""
    self._root = self.remove_helper(self._root, val)

def remove_helper(self, node: TreeNode | None, val: int) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Remove a node recursively (helper method)"""
    if node is None:
        return None
    # 1. Find and remove the node
    if val < node.val:
        node.left = self.remove_helper(node.left, val)
    elif val > node.val:
        node.right = self.remove_helper(node.right, val)
    else:
        if node.left is None or node.right is None:
            child = node.left or node.right
            # Number of children = 0: remove node and return
            if child is None:
                return None
            # Number of children = 1: remove node directly
            else:
                node = child
        else:
            # Number of children = 2: remove the inorder successor and use its value to replace the current node value
            temp = node.right
            while temp.left is not None:
                temp = temp.left
            node.right = self.remove_helper(node.right, temp.val)
            node.val = temp.val
    # Update the node height
    self.update_height(node)
    # 2. Perform rotations to restore balance in this subtree
    return self.rotate(node)

    /* 1. Find and remove the node */
    if (val < node->val)
        node->left = removeHelper(node->left, val);
    else if (val > node->val)
        node->right = removeHelper(node->right, val);
    else {
        if (node->left == nullptr || node->right == nullptr) {
            TreeNode *child = node->left != nullptr ? node->left : node->right;
            // Number of children = 0: remove node and return
            if (child == nullptr) {
                delete node;
                return nullptr;
            }
            // Number of children = 1: remove node directly
            else {
                delete node;
                node = child;
            }
        } else {
            // Number of children = 2: remove the inorder successor and use its value to replace the current node value
            TreeNode *temp = node->right;
            while (temp->left != nullptr) {
                temp = temp->left;
            }
            int tempVal = temp->val;
            node->right = removeHelper(node->right, temp->val);
            node->val = tempVal;
        }
    }
    updateHeight(node); // Update the node height
    /* 2. Perform rotations to restore balance in this subtree */
    node = rotate(node);
    // Return the root of the subtree
    return node;
}

            node.val = temp.val;

    /* 2. Perform rotations to restore balance in this subtree */

/* Remove a node recursively (helper method) */
fn remove_helper(node: OptionTreeNodeRc, val: i32) -> OptionTreeNodeRc {
    match node {
        Some(mut node) => {
            /* 1. Find and remove the node */
            if val < node.borrow().val {
                let left = node.borrow().left.clone();
                node.borrow_mut().left = Self::remove_helper(left, val);
            } else if val > node.borrow().val {
                let right = node.borrow().right.clone();
                node.borrow_mut().right = Self::remove_helper(right, val);
            } else if node.borrow().left.is_none() || node.borrow().right.is_none() {
                let child = if node.borrow().left.is_some() {
                    node.borrow().left.clone()
                } else {
                    node.borrow().right.clone()
                };
                match child {
                    // Number of children = 0: remove node and return
                    None => {
                        return None;
                    }
                    // Number of children = 1: remove node directly
                    Some(child) => node = child,
                }
            } else {
                // Number of children = 2: remove the inorder successor and use its value to replace the current node value
                let mut temp = node.borrow().right.clone().unwrap();
                loop {
                    let temp_left = temp.borrow().left.clone();
                    if temp_left.is_none() {
                        break;
                    }
                    temp = temp_left.unwrap();
                }
                let right = node.borrow().right.clone();
                node.borrow_mut().right = Self::remove_helper(right, temp.borrow().val);
                node.borrow_mut().val = temp.borrow().val;
            }
            Self::update_height(Some(node.clone())); // Update the node height

            /* 2. Perform rotations to restore balance in this subtree */
            node = Self::rotate(Some(node)).unwrap();
            // Return the root of the subtree
            Some(node)
        }
        None => None,
    }
}

items.title: 7.5.4   Typical applications
items.text:
• Organizing and storing large datasets, particularly when lookups are frequent and insertions and deletions are less frequent.
  • Building database indexing systems.
  • Red-black trees are another common kind of balanced binary search tree. Their balance requirements are looser than those of AVL trees, so insertion and deletion need fewer rotations and are more efficient on average.

items.title: 7.4   Binary search trees
items.text:
A binary search tree satisfies the following conditions, as shown below.

  1. Every value in the left subtree is \(<\) the root value, which is \(<\) every value in the right subtree.
  2. The left and right subtrees of every node are also binary search trees and satisfy condition 1..

Figure 7-16   A binary search tree

items.title: 7.4.1   Binary search tree operations
items.text: We encapsulate the tree in a BinarySearchTree class with a member variable root pointing to its root node.

items.title: 1.   Finding a node
items.text:
To find a target value num, use the tree's ordering property. As shown below, initialize a node reference cur at root and repeatedly compare cur.val with num.

  • If cur.val < num, the target lies in the right subtree, so set cur = cur.right.
  • If cur.val > num, the target lies in the left subtree, so set cur = cur.left.
  • If cur.val = num, the target has been found; exit the loop and return the node.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 7-17   Finding a node in a binary search tree

Searching a binary search tree follows the same principle as binary search: each round eliminates half the possibilities. The number of iterations is at most the tree's height, giving \(O(\log n)\) time when the tree is balanced. An implementation follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_tree.py
def search(self, num: int) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Find a node"""
    cur = self._root
    # Search in a loop, stopping if cur becomes None
    while cur is not None:
        # If present, the target node is in the right subtree of cur
        if cur.val < num:
            cur = cur.right
        # If present, the target node is in the left subtree of cur
        elif cur.val > num:
            cur = cur.left
        # The target node was found; exit the loop
        else:
            break
    return cur

items.title: 2.   Inserting a node
items.text:
To insert num while preserving the ordering “left subtree < root < right subtree,” follow the process below.

  1. Find the insertion position: as in a search, start at the root and move down according to comparisons with num. Stop when the traversal passes a leaf and reaches None.
  2. Insert at that position: create a node containing num and place it at the None position.

Figure 7-18   Inserting a node into a binary search tree

Keep two details in mind when implementing this.

  • Duplicate values are not allowed under this definition. If the value already exists, return without inserting it.
  • Keep a reference pre to the node from the previous iteration. When the traversal reaches None, pre gives its parent so that the new node can be attached.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_tree.py
def insert(self, num: int):
    """Insert a node"""
    # If the tree is empty, initialize the root node
    if self._root is None:
        self._root = TreeNode(num)
        return
    # Search in a loop, stopping if cur becomes None
    cur, pre = self._root, None
    while cur is not None:
        # Return immediately if a duplicate node is found
        if cur.val == num:
            return
        pre = cur
        # The insertion position lies in the right subtree of cur
        if cur.val < num:
            cur = cur.right
        # The insertion position lies in the left subtree of cur
        else:
            cur = cur.left
    # Insert a node
    node = TreeNode(num)
    if pre.val < num:
        pre.right = node
    else:
        pre.left = node

/* Insert a node */
pub fn insert(&mut self, num: i32) {
    // If the tree is empty, initialize the root node
    if self.root.is_none() {
        self.root = Some(TreeNode::new(num));
        return;
    }
    let mut cur = self.root.clone();
    let mut pre = None;
    // Search while cur refers to a node
    while let Some(node) = cur.clone() {
        match num.cmp(&node.borrow().val) {
            // Return immediately if a duplicate node is found
            Ordering::Equal => return,
            // The insertion position lies in the right subtree of cur
            Ordering::Greater => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().right.clone();
            }
            // The insertion position lies in the left subtree of cur
            Ordering::Less => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().left.clone();
            }
        }
    }
    // Insert a node
    let pre = pre.unwrap();
    let node = Some(TreeNode::new(num));

items.title: 3.   Deleting a node
items.text:
First locate the target node, then remove it while preserving “left subtree < root < right subtree.” The procedure depends on whether the target has 0, 1, or 2 children.

As shown below, a node of degree \(0\) is a leaf and can be removed directly.

Figure 7-19   Deleting a node of degree 0

As shown below, replace a node of degree \(1\) with its only child.

Figure 7-20   Deleting a node of degree 1

A node of degree \(2\) cannot simply be removed; another node must replace it. To preserve “left subtree \(<\) root \(<\) right subtree,” use either the smallest node in the right subtree or the largest node in the left subtree.

Suppose we choose the smallest node in the right subtree, the next node in inorder traversal. The process is shown below.

  1. Find the target node's successor in inorder traversal and call it tmp.
  2. Replace the target node's value with tmp's value, then recursively delete tmp from the tree.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 7-21   Deleting a node of degree 2

Deletion also takes \(O(\log n)\) time: locating the target takes \(O(\log n)\), and finding its inorder successor takes \(O(\log n)\). An implementation follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_tree.py
def remove(self, num: int):
    """Remove a node"""
    # Return immediately if the tree is empty
    if self._root is None:
        return
    # Search in a loop, stopping if cur becomes None
    cur, pre = self._root, None
    while cur is not None:
        # The node to remove was found; exit the loop
        if cur.val == num:
            break
        pre = cur
        # If present, the node to remove is in the right subtree of cur
        if cur.val < num:
            cur = cur.right
        # If present, the node to remove is in the left subtree of cur
        else:
            cur = cur.left
    # Return immediately if the node to remove does not exist
    if cur is None:
        return

    # Number of children = 0 or 1
    if cur.left is None or cur.right is None:
        # With 0 or 1 child, child is None or that child, respectively
        child = cur.left or cur.right
        # Remove node cur
        if cur != self._root:
            if pre.left == cur:
                pre.left = child
            else:
                pre.right = child
        else:
            # If the removed node is the root, assign the new root
            self._root = child
    # Number of children = 2
    else:
        # Get the inorder successor of cur
        tmp: TreeNode = cur.right
        while tmp.left is not None:
            tmp = tmp.left
        # Recursively remove node tmp
        self.remove(tmp.val)
        # Replace the value of cur with the value of tmp
        cur.val = tmp.val

    // Track the parent of the node to remove
    var pre *TreeNode = nil
    // Continue searching while the current node is not nil
    for cur != nil {
        if cur.Val == num {
            break
        }
        pre = cur
        if cur.Val.(int) < num {
            // The node to remove is in the right subtree
            cur = cur.Right
        } else {
            // The node to remove is in the left subtree
            cur = cur.Left
        }
    }
    // Return immediately if the node to remove does not exist
    if cur == nil {
        return
    }
    // The node has 0 or 1 child
    if cur.Left == nil || cur.Right == nil {
        var child *TreeNode = nil

        if cur.Left != nil {
            child = cur.Left
        } else {
            child = cur.Right

            if pre.Left == cur {

            bst.root = child

        tmp := cur.Right
        for tmp.Left != nil {
            tmp = tmp.Left

        // Recursively remove node tmp
        bst.remove(tmp.Val.(int))

        cur.Val = tmp.Val

/* Remove a node */
pub fn remove(&mut self, num: i32) {
    // Return immediately if the tree is empty
    if self.root.is_none() {
        return;
    }
    let mut cur = self.root.clone();
    let mut pre = None;
    // Search while cur refers to a node
    while let Some(node) = cur.clone() {
        match num.cmp(&node.borrow().val) {
            // The node to remove was found; exit the loop
            Ordering::Equal => break,
            // The node to remove lies in the right subtree of cur
            Ordering::Greater => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().right.clone();
            }
            // The node to remove lies in the left subtree of cur
            Ordering::Less => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().left.clone();
            }
        }
    }
    // Return immediately if the node to remove does not exist
    if cur.is_none() {
        return;
    }
    let cur = cur.unwrap();
    let (left_child, right_child) = (cur.borrow().left.clone(), cur.borrow().right.clone());
    match (left_child.clone(), right_child.clone()) {
        // Number of children = 0 or 1
        (None, None) | (Some(_), None) | (None, Some(_)) => {
            // With 0 or 1 child, child is None or that child, respectively
            let child = left_child.or(right_child);
            let pre = pre.unwrap();
            // Remove node cur
            if !Rc::ptr_eq(&cur, self.root.as_ref().unwrap()) {
                let left = pre.borrow().left.clone();
                if left.is_some() && Rc::ptr_eq(left.as_ref().unwrap(), &cur) {
                    pre.borrow_mut().left = child;
                } else {
                    pre.borrow_mut().right = child;
                }
            } else {
                // If the removed node is the root, assign the new root
                self.root = child;
            }
        }
        // Number of children = 2
        (Some(_), Some(_)) => {
            // Get the inorder successor of cur
            let mut tmp = cur.borrow().right.clone();
            while let Some(node) = tmp.clone() {
                if node.borrow().left.is_some() {
                    tmp = node.borrow().left.clone();
                } else {
                    break;
                }
            }
            let tmp_val = tmp.unwrap().borrow().val;
            // Recursively remove node tmp
            self.remove(tmp_val);
            // Replace the value of cur with the value of tmp
            cur.borrow_mut().val = tmp_val;
        }
    }
}

items.title: 4.   Inorder traversal produces sorted data
items.text:
As shown below, inorder traversal visits “left \(\rightarrow\) root \(\rightarrow\) right,” while a binary search tree obeys “left child \(<\) root \(<\) right child.”

Thus, inorder traversal always visits the next smallest node, giving an important property: the inorder traversal of a binary search tree is in ascending order.

This lets us retrieve sorted data from the tree in just \(O(n)\) time, with no additional sorting.

Figure 7-22   Inorder traversal of a binary search tree

items.title: 7.4.2   Efficiency
items.text:
Suppose we want to store a dataset in an array or a binary search tree. As Table 7-2 shows, the tree's operations take logarithmic time, offering consistent and efficient performance. An array is faster only when insertions are frequent but lookups and deletions are infrequent.

Table 7-2   Efficiency of arrays and search trees

Unsorted array Binary search tree Find an element \(O(n)\) \(O(\log n)\) Insert an element \(O(1)\) \(O(\log n)\) Delete an element \(O(n)\) \(O(\log n)\)

Ideally, the tree is balanced, allowing any node to be found within \(\log n\) iterations.

However, repeated insertions and deletions may cause it to degenerate into a linked list, as shown below. The time complexity of its operations then degrades to \(O(n)\).

Figure 7-23   Degeneration of a binary search tree

items.title: 7.4.3   Common applications
items.text:
• Multilevel indexes in systems, supporting efficient lookup, insertion, and deletion.
  • The underlying data structure for certain search algorithms.
  • Storing a data stream while maintaining its order.

items.title: 7.1   Binary trees
items.text:
A binary tree is a nonlinear data structure representing relationships between ancestors and descendants. It embodies the divide-and-conquer idea of splitting in two. Like a linked list, it is built from nodes, each containing a value and references to its left and right children.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby 
class TreeNode:
    """Binary tree node class"""
    def __init__(self, val: int):
        self.val: int = val                # Node value
        self.left: TreeNode | None = None  # Left child reference
        self.right: TreeNode | None = None # Right child reference

/* Binary tree node struct */
struct TreeNode {
    int val;          // Node value
    TreeNode *left;   // Left child pointer
    TreeNode *right;  // Right child pointer
    TreeNode(int x) : val(x), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
};

/* Binary tree node class */
class TreeNode {
    int val;         // Node value
    TreeNode left;   // Left child reference
    TreeNode right;  // Right child reference
    TreeNode(int x) { val = x; }
}

/* Binary tree node class */
class TreeNode(int? x) {
    public int? val = x;    // Node value
    public TreeNode? left;  // Left child reference
    public TreeNode? right; // Right child reference
}

/* Binary tree node struct */
type TreeNode struct {
    Val   int
    Left  *TreeNode
    Right *TreeNode
}
/* Constructor */
func NewTreeNode(v int) *TreeNode {
    return &TreeNode{
        Left:  nil, // Left child pointer
        Right: nil, // Right child pointer
        Val:   v,   // Node value
    }
}

/* Binary tree node class */

    var val: Int // Node value
    var left: TreeNode? // Left child reference
    var right: TreeNode? // Right child reference

    init(x: Int) {

}

    val; // Node value
    left; // Left child pointer
    right; // Right child pointer
    constructor(val, left, right) {
        this.val = val === undefined ? 0 : val;
        this.left = left === undefined ? null : left;
        this.right = right === undefined ? null : right;
    }
}

/* Binary tree node class */
class TreeNode {
    val: number;
    left: TreeNode | null;
    right: TreeNode | null;

    constructor(val?: number, left?: TreeNode | null, right?: TreeNode | null) {
        this.val = val === undefined ? 0 : val; // Node value
        this.left = left === undefined ? null : left; // Left child reference
        this.right = right === undefined ? null : right; // Right child reference
    }
}

/* Binary tree node class */
class TreeNode {
  int val;         // Node value
  TreeNode? left;  // Left child reference
  TreeNode? right; // Right child reference
  TreeNode(this.val, [this.left, this.right]);
}

use std::rc::Rc;
use std::cell::RefCell;

/* Binary tree node struct */
struct TreeNode {
    val: i32,                               // Node value
    left: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,    // Left child reference
    right: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,   // Right child reference
}

impl TreeNode {
    /* Constructor */
    fn new(val: i32) -> Rc<RefCell<Self>> {
        Rc::new(RefCell::new(Self {
            val,
            left: None,
            right: None
        }))
    }
}

/* Binary tree node struct */
typedef struct TreeNode {
    int val;                // Node value
    int height;             // Node height
    struct TreeNode *left;  // Left child pointer
    struct TreeNode *right; // Right child pointer
} TreeNode;

/* Constructor */
TreeNode *newTreeNode(int val) {
    TreeNode *node;

    node = (TreeNode *)malloc(sizeof(TreeNode));
    node->val = val;
    node->height = 0;
    node->left = NULL;
    node->right = NULL;
    return node;
}

/* Binary tree node class */
class TreeNode(val _val: Int) {  // Node value
    var left: TreeNode? = null   // Left child reference
    var right: TreeNode? = null  // Right child reference
}

### Binary tree node class ###
class TreeNode
  attr_accessor :val    # Node value
  attr_accessor :left   # Left child reference
  attr_accessor :right  # Right child reference

  def initialize(val)
    @val = val
  end
end

Each node has two references or pointers, one to its left child and one to its right child. The node is their parent. Its left child and all nodes below that child form its left subtree; the right subtree is defined similarly.

Every non-leaf node has children and at least one nonempty subtree. In Figure 7-1, if node 2 is the parent, its left and right children are nodes 4 and 5. Its left subtree consists of node 4 and everything below it, and its right subtree consists of node 5 and everything below it.

Figure 7-1   Parents, children, and subtrees

items.title: 7.1.1   Common terminology
items.text:
Figure 7-2 illustrates common binary-tree terminology.

  • Root: the topmost node, which has no parent.
  • Leaf: a node with no children; both of its child references point to None.
  • Edge: a connection between two nodes, represented by a reference or pointer.
  • A node's level: levels increase from top to bottom, with the root at level 1.
  • A node's degree: its number of children, which is 0, 1, or 2 in a binary tree.
  • A tree's height: the number of edges from the root to its farthest leaf.
  • A node's depth: the number of edges from the root to that node.
  • A node's height: the number of edges from that node to its farthest leaf.

Figure 7-2   Common binary-tree terminology

Tip

Height and depth are usually measured in edges, but some problems or textbooks count nodes instead. Under that convention, add 1 to both height and depth.

items.title: 1.   Perfect binary trees
items.text:
In a perfect binary tree, every level is completely filled, as shown below. Leaves have degree \(0\), and all other nodes have degree \(2\). A tree of height \(h\) has \(2^{h+1} - 1\) nodes, an exponential relationship reminiscent of cell division in nature.

Tip

In Chinese-language resources, a perfect binary tree is often called 满二叉树.

Figure 7-4   A perfect binary tree

items.title: 2.   Complete binary trees
items.text:
Only the lowest level of a complete binary tree may be incomplete, and its nodes must fill that level consecutively from left to right, as shown below. Every perfect binary tree is also complete.

Figure 7-5   A complete binary tree

items.title: 3.   Full binary trees
items.text:
In a full binary tree, every node other than a leaf has exactly two children, as shown below.

Figure 7-6   A full binary tree

items.title: 4.   Balanced binary trees
items.text:
In a balanced binary tree, the heights of the left and right subtrees of every node differ by at most 1, as shown below.

Figure 7-7   A balanced binary tree

items.title: 7.1.4   Degeneration of a binary tree
items.text:
Figure 7-8 shows ideal and degenerate tree structures. When every level is full, the tree is perfect. When every node lies along one side, the tree degenerates into a linked list.

  • A perfect binary tree is the ideal case, making full use of divide and conquer.
  • A linked list is the opposite extreme: operations become linear, with time complexity degrading to \(O(n)\).

Figure 7-8   Best and worst binary-tree structures

As Table 7-1 shows, quantities such as leaf count, total node count, and height reach their maximum or minimum values in these best and worst structures.

Table 7-1   Best and worst binary-tree structures

Perfect binary tree Linked list Nodes at level \(i\) \(2^{i-1}\) \(1\) Leaves in a tree of height \(h\) \(2^h\) \(1\) Total nodes in a tree of height \(h\) \(2^{h+1} - 1\) \(h + 1\) Height of a tree with \(n\) nodes \(\log_2 (n+1) - 1\) \(n - 1\)

items.title: 7.2   Traversing a binary tree
items.text:
In its physical representation, a tree is a linked data structure, so traversal follows pointers from node to node. Unlike a linked list, however, a tree is nonlinear. Traversing it is more complex and requires a search algorithm.

Common binary-tree traversals include level-order, preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal.

items.title: 7.2.1   Level-order traversal
items.text:
As shown below, level-order traversal visits the tree level by level from top to bottom, moving from left to right within each level.

Level-order traversal is a form of breadth-first traversal, also called breadth-first search (BFS). It explores outward one layer at a time.

Figure 7-9   Level-order traversal of a binary tree

items.title: 1.   Implementation
items.text:
Breadth-first traversal usually uses a queue. A queue's first-in, first-out rule matches the traversal's level-by-level progression. The implementation follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_tree_bfs.py
def level_order(root: TreeNode | None) -> list[int]:
    """Level-order traversal"""
    # Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    queue: deque[TreeNode] = deque()
    queue.append(root)
    # Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    res = []
    while queue:
        node: TreeNode = queue.popleft()  # Dequeue from the queue
        res.append(node.val)  # Store the node value
        if node.left is not None:
            queue.append(node.left)  # Enqueue the left child
        if node.right is not None:
            queue.append(node.right)  # Enqueue the right child
    return res
binary_tree_bfs.cpp
/* Level-order traversal */
vector<int> levelOrder(TreeNode *root) {
    // Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    queue<TreeNode *> queue;
    queue.push(root);
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    vector<int> vec;
    while (!queue.empty()) {
        TreeNode *node = queue.front();
        queue.pop();              // Dequeue from the queue
        vec.push_back(node->val); // Store the node value
        if (node->left != nullptr)
            queue.push(node->left); // Enqueue the left child
        if (node->right != nullptr)
            queue.push(node->right); // Enqueue the right child
    }
    return vec;
}

/* Level-order traversal */
List<Integer> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    // Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    Queue<TreeNode> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    queue.add(root);
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = queue.poll(); // Dequeue from the queue
        list.add(node.val);           // Store the node value
        if (node.left != null)
            queue.offer(node.left);   // Enqueue the left child
        if (node.right != null)
            queue.offer(node.right);  // Enqueue the right child
    }
    return list;
}

/* Level-order traversal */
List<int> LevelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    // Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    Queue<TreeNode> queue = new();
    queue.Enqueue(root);
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    List<int> list = [];
    while (queue.Count != 0) {
        TreeNode node = queue.Dequeue(); // Dequeue from the queue
        list.Add(node.val!.Value);       // Store the node value
        if (node.left != null)
            queue.Enqueue(node.left);    // Enqueue the left child
        if (node.right != null)
            queue.Enqueue(node.right);   // Enqueue the right child
    }
    return list;
}

/* Level-order traversal */
func levelOrder(root *TreeNode) []any {
    // Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    queue := list.New()
    queue.PushBack(root)
    // Initialize a slice to store the traversal sequence
    nums := make([]any, 0)
    for queue.Len() > 0 {
        // Dequeue from the queue
        node := queue.Remove(queue.Front()).(*TreeNode)
        // Store the node value
        nums = append(nums, node.Val)
        if node.Left != nil {
            // Enqueue the left child
            queue.PushBack(node.Left)
        }
        if node.Right != nil {
            // Enqueue the right child
            queue.PushBack(node.Right)
        }
    }
    return nums
}

/* Level-order traversal */
func levelOrder(root: TreeNode) -> [Int] {
    // Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    var queue: [TreeNode] = [root]
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    var list: [Int] = []
    while !queue.isEmpty {
        let node = queue.removeFirst() // Dequeue from the queue
        list.append(node.val) // Store the node value
        if let left = node.left {
            queue.append(left) // Enqueue the left child
        }
        if let right = node.right {
            queue.append(right) // Enqueue the right child
        }
    }
    return list
}

/* Level-order traversal */
fn level_order(root: &Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>) -> Vec<i32> {
    // Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    let mut que = VecDeque::new();
    que.push_back(root.clone());
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    let mut vec = Vec::new();

    while let Some(node) = que.pop_front() {
        // Dequeue from the queue
        vec.push(node.borrow().val); // Store the node value
        if let Some(left) = node.borrow().left.as_ref() {
            que.push_back(left.clone()); // Enqueue the left child
        }
        if let Some(right) = node.borrow().right.as_ref() {
            que.push_back(right.clone()); // Enqueue the right child
        };
    }
    vec
}
binary_tree_bfs.c
/* Level-order traversal */
int *levelOrder(TreeNode *root, int *size) {
    /* Auxiliary queue */
    int front, rear;
    int index, *arr;
    TreeNode *node;
    TreeNode **queue;

    /* Auxiliary queue */
    queue = (TreeNode **)malloc(sizeof(TreeNode *) * MAX_SIZE);
    // Queue indices
    front = 0, rear = 0;
    // Enqueue the root node
    queue[rear++] = root;
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    /* Auxiliary array */
    arr = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int) * MAX_SIZE);
    // Array index
    index = 0;
    while (front < rear) {
        // Dequeue from the queue
        node = queue[front++];
        // Store the node value
        arr[index++] = node->val;
        if (node->left != NULL) {
            // Enqueue the left child
            queue[rear++] = node->left;
        }
        if (node->right != NULL) {
            // Enqueue the right child
            queue[rear++] = node->right;
        }
    }
    // Update the array length
    *size = index;
    arr = realloc(arr, sizeof(int) * (*size));

    // Free the auxiliary queue array
    free(queue);
    return arr;
}

/* Level-order traversal */
fun levelOrder(root: TreeNode?): MutableList<Int> {
    // Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
    val queue = LinkedList<TreeNode?>()
    queue.add(root)
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    val list = mutableListOf<Int>()
    while (queue.isNotEmpty()) {
        val node = queue.poll()      // Dequeue from the queue
        list.add(node?._val!!)       // Store the node value
        if (node.left != null)
            queue.offer(node.left)   // Enqueue the left child
        if (node.right != null)
            queue.offer(node.right)  // Enqueue the right child
    }
    return list
}

### Level-order traversal ###
def level_order(root)
  # Initialize a queue and enqueue the root
  queue = [root]
  # Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
  res = []
  while !queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift # Dequeue from the queue
    res << node.val # Store the node value
    queue << node.left unless node.left.nil? # Enqueue the left child
    queue << node.right unless node.right.nil? # Enqueue the right child
  end
  res
end

items.title: 7.2.2   Preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal
items.text:
Preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal are forms of depth-first traversal, also called depth-first search (DFS). They follow a path to its end, then backtrack and continue.

Figure 7-10 illustrates depth-first traversal. Imagine walking once around the outside of the entire binary tree. At each node, you encounter three positions corresponding to preorder, inorder, and postorder visits.

Figure 7-10   Preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal of a binary search tree

fn pre_order(root: Option<&Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut result = vec![];

    fn dfs(root: Option<&Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, res: &mut Vec<i32>) {
        if let Some(node) = root {
            // Visit order: root -> left subtree -> right subtree
            let node = node.borrow();
            res.push(node.val);
            dfs(node.left.as_ref(), res);
            dfs(node.right.as_ref(), res);
        }
    }
    dfs(root, &mut result);

    result
}

items.title: 2.   Complexity analysis
items.text:
• Time complexity: \(O(n)\). Every node is visited once, taking \(O(n)\) time.
  • Space complexity: \(O(n)\). In the worst case, the tree degenerates into a linked list, recursion reaches depth \(n\), and stack frames require \(O(n)\) space.

items.title: 1.   Complete, full, and perfect binary trees
items.text:
The following arrays represent binary trees in level order, with None marking an empty position:

  • Tree A: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
  • Tree B: [1, 2, 3, None, None, 6, 7]
  1. Which tree is a complete binary tree?
  2. Which is a full binary tree, meaning that every non-leaf node has two children?
  3. Is either tree a perfect binary tree? Explain for each tree.
Reference answer

  1. Tree A is complete. Only its bottom level is not full, and the nodes occupy consecutive positions from left to right. Tree B is not complete: its bottom level has empty positions on the left but still has nodes farther to the right.

  2. Tree B is full: nodes 1 and 3 each have two children, and all the other nodes are leaves. Tree A is not full because node 3 has only its left child, 6.

  3. Neither tree is perfect, because neither has a completely filled bottom level.

items.title: 2.   Three traversal orders for the same tree
items.text:
Store the array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] in a complete binary tree in level order.

  1. Draw the tree.
  2. Write its preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal sequences.
  3. In the inorder sequence, which parts of the tree do the sequences to the left and right of root node 1 correspond to?
Reference answer

  1. The tree is:

          1
    /   \
   2     3
  / \   / \
 4   5 6   7

  2. Preorder: 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 7; inorder: 4, 2, 5, 1, 6, 3, 7; postorder: 4, 5, 2, 6, 7, 3, 1.

  3. The sequence 4, 2, 5 to the left of root node 1 is the inorder traversal of the left subtree. The sequence 6, 3, 7 to its right is the inorder traversal of the right subtree.

items.title: 3.   Comparing two binary search trees
items.text:
Insert each of the following sequences from left to right into an empty binary search tree:

  • Sequence A: [4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7]
  • Sequence B: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
  1. Write the nodes visited when searching for 7 in each tree.
  2. If height is measured by the number of edges from the root to the farthest leaf, what is each tree's height?
  3. Based on your answers, do the two trees search for 7 equally efficiently? Explain using their shapes and search paths.
Reference answer

  1. In the tree built from sequence A, the search path is 4 → 6 → 7. In the tree built from sequence B, it is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7.

  2. The first tree has every level filled and a height of 2. The second tree has only right children and a height of 6.

  3. The searches for 7 are not equally efficient. Insertion order changes the shape and height of a binary search tree. Searching for 7 visits only three nodes in the first tree, but must visit seven in sequence in the second. The taller the tree, the more nodes may need to be compared along a path in the worst case.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• A binary tree is a nonlinear data structure that embodies the divide-and-conquer idea of splitting in two. Each node contains a value and two pointers, one to each child.
  • A node's left or right child, together with everything below it, forms its left or right subtree.
  • Tree terminology includes root, leaf, level, degree, edge, height, and depth.
  • Initializing a binary tree and inserting or deleting nodes resemble linked-list operations.
  • Common types include perfect, complete, full, and balanced binary trees. A perfect tree is the ideal form; a linked list is the worst degenerate form.
  • A binary tree can be represented by an array of node values and empty positions in level order. Index mappings between parents and children replace pointers.
  • Level-order traversal is breadth-first search: it expands outward one layer at a time and usually uses a queue.
  • Preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal are depth-first search: they follow paths to their ends before backtracking and usually use recursion.
  • A binary search tree supports efficient lookup, insertion, and deletion in \(O(\log n)\) time. If it degenerates into a linked list, all these operations degrade to \(O(n)\).
  • An AVL tree is a balanced binary search tree that uses rotations to maintain balance through insertions and deletions.
  • AVL rotations include right rotation, left rotation, right-then-left rotation, and left-then-right rotation. After an insertion or deletion, rotations are performed from the bottom up to restore balance.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: For a binary tree with only one node, are both the tree's height and the root's depth \(0\)?

Yes. Height and depth are usually defined by the number of edges traversed.

Q: The text says binary-tree insertion and deletion usually involve a sequence of coordinated operations. What does that mean? Does it refer to releasing resources held by child nodes?

For example, deleting a node from a binary search tree has three cases, and each case requires several steps involving nodes.

Q: Why does depth-first traversal have preorder, inorder, and postorder variants? What is each used for?

Just as an array can be traversed forward or backward, these are three ways to visit a binary tree and obtain a particular ordering. In a binary search tree, values satisfy left child value < root value < right child value, so visiting “left \(\rightarrow\) root \(\rightarrow\) right” produces a sorted node sequence.

Q: A right rotation adjusts node, child, and grand_child. What happens to the link between node and its parent? Doesn't the rotation break it?

View the operation recursively. right_rotate(root) receives a subtree's root and ends with return child, returning the new root of that subtree. The connection to its parent is updated after the function returns; it is outside the rotation function's responsibility.

Q: In C++, how do you decide which methods are private and which are public? Why is height() public but updateHeight() private?

The main consideration is where the method is used. A method used only within the class should be private. Calling updateHeight() alone is not meaningful to a user; it is just one step of insertion or deletion. In contrast, height() retrieves a node's height, much like vector.size(), so it is public for convenient access.

Q: How do you build a binary search tree from input data? Is choosing the root important?

Yes. The construction is provided by the build_tree() method in the binary-search-tree code. Usually, we sort the input, choose its middle element as the root, and recursively construct the left and right subtrees. This keeps the tree as balanced as possible.

Q: Must strings in Java always be compared with equals()?

For primitive types in Java, == compares variable values. For reference types, the two forms work differently.

  • == compares whether two variables refer to the same object, meaning the same location in memory.
  • equals() compares whether two objects have equal values.

Use equals() when comparing values. However, strings initialized with String a = "hi"; String b = "hi"; are stored in the string pool and refer to the same object, so a == b also works for these strings.

Q: Just before breadth-first traversal reaches the lowest level, does the queue contain \(2^h\) nodes?

Yes. For example, a perfect binary tree of height \(h = 2\) has \(n = 7\) nodes, with \(4 = 2^h = (n + 1) / 2\) nodes on its lowest level.
